title: Appraising Generosity Norms in Online Charitable Giving
affiliations: , University of Oklahoma and

detail.title: Appraising Generosity Norms in Online Charitable Giving
detail.abstract:
Online charitable-giving platforms increasingly surface large prior contributions in an effort to solicit larger gifts from subsequent individual donors. Yet empirical evidence diverges on whether such generosity-benchmarking artifacts achieve their intended effect. We develop an appraisal-based framework to explain why these artifacts can produce opposing effects across charitable contexts. We theorize a two-stage cognitive process in which the displayed benchmark first heightens the salience of a generosity norm, giving rise to a perceived generosity standard. Campaign cause orientation, which reflects whether a campaign invites donors to support an aspiration or respond to hardship, then shapes how donors appraise that standard. In want-based campaigns centered on aspirations, donors appraise the standard in terms of expressing personal values by supporting another's aspiration, leading to larger gifts. In need-based campaigns centered on hardship, they instead appraise the same standard in terms of fulfilling a moral obligation by alleviating another's hardship, leading to smaller gifts. Anonymity then emerges downstream as a way to avoid scrutiny over the adequacy of their giving. 

To test these predictions, we leverage GoFundMe's Top Donation List (TDL), a norm-salience feature activated when a campaign receives at least ten donations within a rolling three-day window. Applying a regression discontinuity design to donation-level data, we find that TDL activation produces opposite effects on contribution amounts across campaign orientations. It increases contribution amounts in want-based campaigns, with the rise concentrated among public donations; by contrast, it decreases them in need-based campaigns, with the decline concentrated among anonymous donations. A randomized online experiment supports the proposed mechanisms: TDL activation heightens perceptions of a generosity standard in both campaign orientations, but donors appraise the same standard through distinct, cause-specific pathways. Together, our study extends prior literature by reconciling divergent evidence on the effects of generosity-benchmarking artifacts, cautioning platform designers against deploying such features uniformly across charitable contexts.

title: Beyond the Application Programming Interface: The Intelligence Execution Network as a New Category of Sovereign AI Infrastructure

detail.title: Beyond the Application Programming Interface: The Intelligence Execution Network as a New Category of Sovereign AI Infrastructure

detail.abstract: Since the publication of Fielding's foundational dissertation on Representational State Transfer (REST) in 2000, the application programming interface (API) has served as the dominant paradigm for software interoperability. APIs expose capabilities; callers invoke them; data moves. This architecture proved sufficient for a generation of software integration. It does not prove sufficient for the age of artificial intelligence. When the fundamental unit of computation is no longer data retrieval but intelligence execution — the coordination of multiple trained agents, contextual business graph traversal, autonomous reasoning chains, and cryptographically auditable output — the API abstraction collapses under the weight of what it cannot represent. This paper introduces the Intelligence Execution Network (IEN™), a novel architectural category pioneered by 25 Alpha LLC and commercially launched on June 19, 2026, that replaces the request-response paradigm with an intelligence-execution paradigm. We argue that the IEN constitutes a genuine category discontinuity, and examine the five architectural properties — NAICS-native domain encoding, contextual business graph traversal, autonomous agent chain orchestration, compliance inheritance, and cryptographic provenance — that together distinguish intelligence execution from data transport. We draw on current analyst research confirming the urgency of this transition: Gartner's 2026 Hype Cycle for Agentic AI places agentic AI at the Peak of Inflated Expectations and identifies agent orchestration as the critical unfilled infrastructure layer; the EU AI Act's Article 50 transparency obligations took effect on August 2, 2026 and are now enforceable across the EU, while the Digital Omnibus (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force July 27, 2026) deferral of high-risk obligations to December 2, 2027 confirms that the market cannot yet operationalize the compliance infrastructure those rules require; McKinsey estimates a $500–$600 billion sovereign AI infrastructure market by 2030; Gartner confirms 40 percent of enterprise applications will embed AI agents by end of 2026, up from less than 5 percent in 2025. 25 Alpha LLC asserts trademark rights in Intelligence Execution Network™ and IEN™ and is pursuing federal registration in Class 42.

title: Privacy Capital

detail.title: Privacy Capital
detail.abstract: Privacy is the governance of personal data firms hold and use in production. In this paper, I show that privacy is capital, beyond compliance obligation. I construct the first firm-year measure of privacy capital via a hybrid-LLM approach from the texts of around 90,000 privacy policies. By exploiting the 2018-2023 regulatory wave, I provide causal evidence that investment in privacy pays. A one-standard-deviation within-firm increase in privacy capital increases asset turnover by 0.06 standard deviations and ROA by 0.10 standard deviations. The mechanism is consistent with governed data being utilized more productively. Effects are more pronounced for collection-intensive, sharing-intensive, and consumer-facing firms. The market initially discounts privacy capital, consistent with concerns that privacy regulation constrains data use and growth opportunities. As its productive benefits become apparent, investors gradually correct this initial assessment and the discount dissipates. Where prior work shows that bad privacy is punished, I show that good privacy is rewarded. Findings carry implications for the ongoing regulatory debate around privacy in the AI era. Privacy regulation imposes real costs, but it can also induce productive capital formation.

title: The Fallback as Signal: Preserved Human Skill, Liability, and Competence Signaling in Credence-Good Markets under Improving AI

detail.title: The Fallback as Signal: Preserved Human Skill, Liability, and Competence Signaling in Credence-Good Markets under Improving AI
detail.abstract: Firms that deploy improving but imperfect AI must decide how much to keep human workers engaged. Engagement lowers current output yet builds the fallback skill the firm needs when AI fails. We ask what that fallback skill signals to two audiences at once: mobile workers, who sort across firms on the skill trajectory a job builds, and clients, who cannot observe skill in a credence-good market and must infer competence. We embed the engagement-skill dynamics of Singh et al. (2026) in a signaling game and add a liability commitment. Because a more-skilled provider fails less often precisely in the states where AI is down, the expected cost of a liability pledge is decreasing in fallback skill. This restores Spence-Mirrlees single crossing on a type that is endogenous-built, not drawnand yields a separating equilibrium in which liability certifies preserved human competence that no artifact can certify once AI writes as well as the expert. We characterize the least-cost separating pledge schedule, show that client stakes shift engagement toward or away from the least-skilled worker depending on the size of the pledge, and derive a stakes threshold above which building skill dominates free-riding on a rival's training-reversing the asymmetric-specialization result of the underlying labor model. Two boundaries close the market from both sides: small tickets cannot fund enforcement, and large tickets exceed the provider's solvency. An agent-based version of the market reproduces the analytical thresholds under noisy beliefs, learning-by-record and worker churn.

title: Large Language Models Polarize Ideologically but Moderate Affectively in Online Political Discourse
affiliations: , HEC Paris, University of Pennsylvania - The Wharton School, HEC Paris and University of Pennsylvania

detail.title: Large Language Models Polarize Ideologically but Moderate Affectively in Online Political Discourse
detail.abstract: The emergence of large language models (LLMs) is reshaping how people engage in political discourse online. We examine how the release of ChatGPT altered ideological and emotional patterns in Reddit's largest political forum. Analysis of millions of comments shows that ChatGPT intensified ideological polarization: liberal-leaning authors posted increasingly liberal comments, while conservative-leaning authors posted increasingly conservative comments. Multiple falsification tests suggest that these findings are unlikely to be driven by contemporaneous events, such as the 2022 U.S. midterm elections, or by broader platformwide trends in political polarization. Mechanism tests show that this shift does not stem from the creation of more persuasive or ideologically extreme original content using LLM. Instead, it originates from the tendency of LLM-assisted comments to echo and reinforce the original post's viewpoint, a pattern consistent with algorithmic sycophancy. Yet, despite growing ideological divides, affective polarization, measured by hostility and toxicity, declined. These findings reveal that LLMs can simultaneously deepen ideological separation and foster more civil exchanges, challenging the long-standing assumption in literature that extremity and incivility necessarily move together.

title: Software Innovation Engineering: Institutionalizing Exploration in Software Engineering for Digital Transformation

detail.title: Software Innovation Engineering: Institutionalizing Exploration in Software Engineering for Digital Transformation
detail.abstract: Digitally transforming organizations require software engineering functions not only to operate existing digital capabilities and execute committed initiatives, but also to systematically explore technological possibilities whose suitability is uncertain. The Exploitation-Execution-Exploration (EEE) problem explains why this third mode is particularly vulnerable: exploitation is protected by operational necessity, execution by formal delivery commitments, while exploration is frequently embedded within projects, performed ad hoc, or crowded out. This research note proposes Software Innovation Engineering (SIE) as a distinct engineering function and the Software Innovation Engineer as an occupational role for institutionalizing such exploration. SIE is defined by purpose rather than exclusive activities: it systematically identifies, investigates, contextualizes, adapts, integrates, invents where necessary, validates, and matures software technologies and engineering possibilities into organization-specific capabilities and value, subject to organizational vision, strategy, context, and constraints. The role bridges engineering research and science with organizational software engineering and innovation, while remaining distinct in primary purpose from Software Research Engineering, Software Development Engineering, and Software Operations Engineering. SIE may support engineering-directed, project-directed, and business-directed exploration. The paper argues that SIE provides a partial structural response to the EEE problem by giving systematic exploration explicit ownership, capability, resourcing, governance, and pathways into execution and exploitation.

title: Multimodal EHR Fusion Models: A Dual-Encoder Architecture for Unified ICU Patient Representation and Downstream Transfer Learning

detail.title: Multimodal EHR Fusion Models: A Dual-Encoder Architecture for Unified ICU Patient Representation and Downstream Transfer Learning

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study was a secondary analysis of the publicly available MIMIC-III database. The establishment of MIMIC-III and collection of patient data were previously approved by the Institutional Review Boards of the Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, with a waiver of individual patient consent. Because the data are fully de-identified and publicly accessible under a PhysioNet Data Use Agreement and certification that the author was approved for, further ethical approval from a local IRB was exempt / not required.
declarations.funderStatement: Graduate project at UT Austin (self-funded).

detail.abstract: Electronic Health Records (EHR) contain a wealth of multimodal data. Traditional clinical machine learning often relies on single-task models trained on unimodal data, which is computationally inefficient and fails to capture the holistic patient state. This study proposes a Multimodal EHR Fusion Model utilizing a dual-encoder architecture built upon a Feature Store generated from the MIMIC-III database. By fusing statistically aggregated structured features with unstructured clinical note embeddings generated via a ModernBERT model, we construct a unified, reusable representation of a patient's first 24 hours in the Intensive Care Unit (ICU). We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach by applying transfer learning across multiple downstream clinical tasks, spanning acute interventions and chronic phenotyping. Interpretability analysis using latent space (Z) and Integrated Gradients (IG) confirm cross-modal generalization, proving that multimodal fusion enhances explainability and aligns with sound clinical reasoning.

title: Toward Decentralized Carbon Trading in Indonesia: A Public-blockchain Architecture for Tokenized Real-world Assets
affiliations: , Otoritas Jasa Keuangan and Western Sydney University

detail.title: Toward Decentralized Carbon Trading in Indonesia: A Public-blockchain Architecture for Tokenized Real-world Assets
detail.abstract:
Indonesia has established a regulated carbon market supported by national registry infrastructure and the IDXCarbon exchange. Carbon units can be issued, recorded, traded, and retired within this framework. IDXCarbon currently uses a private blockchain for its trading infrastructure. This creates an opportunity to examine how Indonesian carbon credits could also be represented and traded through public blockchain infrastructure. 
     This study proposes an architecture for tokenizing Indonesian carbon credits as real-world assets (RWAs), with particular focus on Sertifikat Pengurangan Emisi Gas Rumah Kaca (SPE-GRK). The proposed architecture retains the Sistem Registri Unit Karbon (SRUK) as the authoritative source of carbon-unit status. It introduces a public-blockchain layer for token representation and programmable transactions. The architecture is designed to support lifecycle management, token-based asset representation, public observability of token activity, interoperability, wallet-based transactions, and programmable settlement. 
     The architecture consists of four layers: the authoritative carbon layer, the registry interoperability and tokenization layer, the public-blockchain RWA layer, and the market and application layer. Access to the tokenized carbon assets remains regulated. Token issuance and transfers are linked to participant eligibility and registry status. Retirement also remains dependent on the authoritative carbon registry. The proposed architecture provides a framework for introducing public-blockchain RWA infrastructure into Indonesia's existing carbon market while maintaining SRUK authority and existing market-integrity controls.

title: The Institutional Window: Occupation-and Jurisdiction-Specific Calibration of Liability Signaling for Preserved Human Fallback Capability

detail.title: The Institutional Window: Occupation-and Jurisdiction-Specific Calibration of Liability Signaling for Preserved Human Fallback Capability
detail.abstract: Problem definition. When generative AI produces expert artifacts that clients cannot distinguish from those of a competent provider, the classical cost-based quality signal collapses and only outcome-contingent commitments can separate types. Prior work establishes that such a commitment certifies an endogenous and perishable asset: the human fallback capability a firm builds by keeping staff engaged with cases the AI handles, eroding otherwise. That work is silent on where the mechanism holds. We ask where, across occupations and liability institutions, it remains informative-and what becomes of the capability stock where it does not. Methodology/results. We introduce an institutional wedge between the liability cap a firm posts and the retained exposure that carries information, generated by four legal primitives: the cost-allocation rule, the enforceability of penalty clauses, the displacement of private liability by state liability or pooled indemnity, and mandatory limits on contractual liability. The wedge compresses the separating type space into an institutional signaling window [s, s] bounded above by solvency and the penalty doctrine, and below where standard-terms control voids liability caps beneath a required threshold, truncating the enforceable message space. We calibrate five occupations and seven jurisdictions on published error-rate, deskilling and enforcement evidence. Three results follow. In the calibrated common-law agreed-damages channels the provability gross-up is unavailable whenever verifiability falls below 1/m, converting a contracting problem into an operational one. Verifiability investment widens the window where the ceiling binds but narrows it where the cap floor binds. In an agent-based market, within the tested policy class, every empty-window cell converges to zero engagement and fallback-skill collapse. Managerial implications. Liability institutions are a workforce-capability instrument, not merely a risk-allocation device. Firms should target the binding margin in each jurisdiction; regulators should recognize that cap floors and pooled indemnity each suppress the signal sustaining fallback capacity. * Aegis Compliance and Strategies OÜ, Vienna. This paper builds on two companion working papers by the author, Bauer [2026a] and Bauer [2026b]; Section 3.4 states the provenance of every model component. Simulation and calibration code, together with an interactive simulator, are provided in the Electronic Companion.

title: Beyond Exploration-Exploitation: The Exploitation-Execution-Exploration Problem in Software Engineering for Digital Transformation

detail.title: Beyond Exploration-Exploitation: The Exploitation-Execution-Exploration Problem in Software Engineering for Digital Transformation
detail.abstract: Digital transformation has expanded the mandate of organizational software engineering. Engineering teams are increasingly expected to operate and improve existing digital capabilities, rapidly execute growing portfolios of transformation initiatives, and simultaneously investigate unfamiliar technologies and uncertain solution possibilities. Organizational learning theory has traditionally framed the tension between using established knowledge and searching for new possibilities through March's exploration-exploitation framework. This research note argues that, although execution belongs within March's broad conception of exploitation, the binary becomes insufficiently granular when the software engineering function in digitally transforming organizations is the level of analysis. It proposes the Exploitation-Execution-Exploration (EEE) Problem: the persistent three-way tension that arises when finite engineering resources must simultaneously support the exploitation of operational software, execution of committed transformation initiatives, and exploration of uncertain technological problems and possibilities. The paper theorizes EEE as generating a three-way engineering resourcing problem, characterized by capacity contention, cognitive-mode switching demand, and capability diversity demand, which in turn creates a digital transformation performance tension among execution quality and speed, operational stability and sustainability, and innovation and competitiveness. It further identifies exploration as particularly vulnerable to becoming implicit within project execution and distinguishes engineering-directed, project-directed, and business-directed exploration. The note develops the EEE construct as a dynamic, coupled system and frames a focused research agenda for the Business and Information Systems Engineering, Software Engineering Management, Digital Transformation, Innovation Management, and Organization Design communities.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Rotman School of Management Working Paper Forthcoming

detail.abstract: A software firm that red-teams a product chooses how a confidential finding will guide remediation, post-release defence and defence placement. Following the report seems natural, but it can be wrong. Remediation changes the composition of residual risk: a missed attack class may become more dangerous than the class that was reported and repaired. Testing, therefore, affects defence through both risk removal and risk allocation. Holding remediation fixed, greater test precision raises optimal coverage only when precision is sufficiently high and attacker reconnaissance sufficiently weak; otherwise it weakly lowers coverage. Holding precision fixed, greater remediation weakly lowers coverage. A report-contingent defence can also reveal the report to an attacker that fingerprints its location. When recognition neutralises the defence and reconnaissance is fixed, the firm either adapts placement fully or pools across reports. When the attacker chooses reconnaissance effort, partial adaptation emerges. The analysis distinguishes requirements to test, remediate, deploy, condition placement on a finding and disclose technical detail. Conditional on the other portfolio choices, requiring defence to follow the finding can protect the wrong attack surface or induce additional reconnaissance.

title: Tokenized Collectibles: Digital Claims, Fractionalization, and the Financialization of Sports and Trading Cards
affiliations: Marquette University

detail.title: Tokenized Collectibles: Digital Claims, Fractionalization, and the Financialization of Sports and Trading Cards
detail.abstract: The tokenization of physical collectibles is creating a new digital layer within established markets for sports cards and trading card games. Rather than replacing the underlying physical asset, tokenized platforms can create blockchain-based digital claims associated with cards that remain in professional custody. This paper examines the emerging market structure surrounding tokenized collectibles, including professional grading, online secondary markets, vaulting, blockchain-based digital representations, and collector demand. Particular attention is given to the distinction between one-to-one tokenization, in which a digital token is associated with an identified physical collectible, and fractionalization, in which economic interests in a collectible are divided among multiple holders. The paper evaluates the economic benefits and limitations of these models, including potential reductions in transaction, shipping, and storage frictions, while emphasizing the continuing importance of authentication, grading, custody, insurance, enforceable redemption rights, and market liquidity. It also considers the securities-law, tax, and contractual questions that may arise when collectible ownership is represented or divided through digital assets. The analysis suggests that tokenization should be understood not as a replacement for the institutions supporting collectible markets, but as a technology-enabled layer that changes how claims to physical assets can be recorded, transferred, and potentially financialized. The durability of these markets will depend less on blockchain technology itself than on the legal and institutional arrangements supporting the underlying physical collectibles.

title: Allowed to Make, Not to Sell: The Binding Constraint and Unequal Incidence of Monetization Governance in the Generative-AI Creative Economy

detail.title: Allowed to Make, Not to Sell: The Binding Constraint and Unequal Incidence of Monetization Governance in the Generative-AI Creative Economy
detail.abstract: Generative AI has sharply lowered the cost of producing creative work, yet whether cheaper production expands creative supply depends on a margin the literature has largely left implicit: not whether creators can make AI work, but whether platforms let them sell it. We study a natural experiment that isolates this margin-the synchronized May-2023 ban on monetizing generative-AI content across Japan's largest creator-economy platforms, enacted while the free pixiv gallery continued to allow AI posting. A triple-difference (AI × paid-channel × post), using the still-permissive free gallery to net out the concurrent anti-AI backlash, shows that removing monetization permission cut prolific creators' paid-AI supply by roughly two-thirds (-63.5%)production capability untouched-and that banned creators stayed rather than exiting, with suggestive reallocation toward human-style work. We then take the question to the population: from an independent 16.3-million-work corpus we reconstruct the full treated population (5,344 creators); rebuilt at the original design's cells with the corpus supplying the free-gallery arm, the headline estimate replicates (-64.7%) and is invariant to how AI work is labeled. An entrycohort design that aligns the boom-era entrants public search never surfaced reveals a steep incidence gradient in paid posting volume-roughly-70% for established monetizers versus-41% for boom entrants (stack-alone-39%, banded [-25%, ≈-53%], its principal measured biases pointing deeper; pure AI-content withdrawal-58%)-with the loss concentrated where monetized volume lived: the typical casual creator's posting probability did not fall, and demonetization caused no differential exit. Multihoming onto off-platform paid channels predicted measurably better retention and a markedly shallower collapse through the shock; and in the aftermath AI works were removed from the gallery at far higher rates than human work while the attention dilution associated with AI's arrival faded to near zero. Monetization governance is a distinct, binding instrument of platform control-and its incidence is selective, pruning monetization-dependent boom entry while committed creators adapt.

title: How Did the COVID-19 Pandemic Affect the Adoption and Performance of E-Commerce Across Large and Small Firms, and to What Extent Did the Industry Coherence and Policy Support Influence Their Ability to Adapt?

detail.title: How Did the COVID-19 Pandemic Affect the Adoption and Performance of E-Commerce Across Large and Small Firms, and to What Extent Did the Industry Coherence and Policy Support Influence Their Ability to Adapt?
detail.abstract: This paper examines the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on e-commerce adoption and performance across large and small firms. Drawing on industry coherence and population ecology frameworks, it explores how large firms, with established resources and policy support, adapted more successfully to the shift towards digital platforms. In contrast, small firms faced significant challenges due to limited financial flexibility and technological infrastructure. By analyzing these disparities, the paper highlights the role of policy and digital readiness in ensuring business resilience and sustainability in a post-pandemic ecommerce driven economy.

detail.abstract: We compare the relative informativeness of SPX implied volatility measured at 3:45 PM versus the conventional 4:00 PM close. The comparison is motivated by the rise of 0DTE options, which makes the close both the standard valuation timestamp and the expiration boundary for same-day contracts. Using matched option-chain snapshots, we show that the two volatility surfaces has become less aligned in shape as 0DTE trading has expanded. We find that using liquid at-the-money short-maturity options, the 3:45 PM data (as opposed to the 4:00 PM close data) is a better predictor of next-day realized variance. It also improves GARCH/EGARCH volatility models. Next, we construct raw volatility surfaces and train Convoluted Neural Networks (CNN) for out-of-sample forecasting, using the entire surface. The 3:45 PM surface outperforms the 4:00 PM surface as a standalone input. But, combining the two surfaces is even better.  Forecasts using the entire surface significantly outperform traditional at-the-money based forecasts. They are comparable to conditional volatility models.

title: From Seoul to Bharat: A Digital Content Strategy Study for HYBE India's Audience Building Among Indian Gen Z

detail.title: From Seoul to Bharat: A Digital Content Strategy Study for HYBE India's Audience Building Among Indian Gen Z

declarations.ethicsApproval: Participation in the survey was voluntary and anonymous. Respondents were informed of the study's academic purpose before completing the questionnaire, and no personally identifiable information was collected. As this study did not involve vulnerable populations, sensitive personal data, or physical/psychological risk, formal institutional ethics board approval was not sought, consistent with standard practice for undergraduate survey-based consumer research.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was self-conducted as part of the author's undergraduate coursework.

detail.abstract: HYBE Corporation formally launched HYBE India as its fifth global headquarters in Mumbai in September 2025-the first Korean entertainment company to establish a physical subsidiary in India. This study presents the first primary empirical research examining Indian consumer readiness for HYBE India's market entry. Through a structured survey of 100 Indian respondents spanning K-culture consumers and nonconsumers across Tier 1, 2, and 3 cities, combined with a 58-post Instagram brand audit and competitor analysis, this research maps consumer behaviour, platform preferences, cultural affinity, and engagement barriers relevant to HYBE India's digital content strategy. Key findings reveal that 65% of respondents were already aware of HYBE India prior to this survey, excitement about Indian artist development averages 3.95 out of 5, and 93% expressed willingness to attend a HYBE India event (47% confirmed Yes, 46% Maybe). Critically, poor social media execution (56%) ranks as the top engagement barrier-above the absence of Indian artists in HYBE's roster (47%). A brand audit of @hybeindia reveals an engagement rate declining from 21.9% in its launch phase to 3.9% by August 2026, indicating an audition-bubble effect that requires urgent strategic diversification. This research synthesises both datasets into actionable content strategy recommendations for HYBE India's audience-building among Indian Gen Z.

title: How Innovation Takes Shape: Organizations, Ecosystems, and Technological Futures
affiliations: National Research University Higher School of Economics (Moscow), Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications (BUPT), Universidade Estadual de Campinas (UNICAMP) - School of Applied Sciences, Universidade Estadual de Campinas (UNICAMP) - School of Applied Sciences, Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, , Tsinghua University - School of Public Policy and Management and Tsinghua University

detail.title: How Innovation Takes Shape: Organizations, Ecosystems, and Technological Futures
detail.abstract:
The last decades witnessed a never-ending debate about the generation of innovations under different circumstances and, to a lesser extent, on adoption. With a dedicated focus on technologies, the topic of adoption and diffusion emerged only a little. However, this focus is on technologies, expressed in Technology Acceptance Models and Technology Diffusion Models, which cover only parts of the overall spectrum of innovation types. Innovation Diffusion Models similarly highlight innovation adoption but pay less attention to implementation. The challenge, however, lies more with the implementation of innovation than with initial adoption. This is especially the case for organizational innovation, which causes considerable change inside organizations. Changes inside organizations aren’t always welcome and supported by people, which resulted in the change management paradigm.

The working paper highlights these general thoughts. It comes in two parts. The first focuses on Organizations, Ecosystems, and Institutional Power, and the second on Saturation and the Limits of Adoption.

detail.abstract: Modern software development faces exploding code volumes and AI-generated changes, yet risk assessment remains largely qualitative. This paper presents ChangeShield, a deterministic tool for quantitative change risk management. ChangeShield computes entity-level structural and dependency risks using static and dynamic analysis and equilibrium flow dynamics, delivers userprofile-specific risk scores, and automatically generates targeted entity-to-test mappings for efficient mitigation. Evaluated on various Enterprise standard technologies : (JVM, CLR .NET, JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, PHP), ChangeShield enables data-driven change request workflows, reduces running full regression suites via targeted testing, and supports architecture governance. Results demonstrate significant improvements in risk visibility compared to traditional linting and review practices. ChangeShield advances software engineering by making risks assessments in change management measurable and actionable.

title: Requisite Variety and Observability: Value-Creation-Chain Tokenization and Artificial Intelligence in the Architecture of Financial Regulation
affiliations: Republic of Kazakhstan

detail.title: Requisite Variety and Observability: Value-Creation-Chain Tokenization and Artificial Intelligence in the Architecture of Financial Regulation
detail.abstract: This paper continues the author's research program on the tokenization of the value creation chain based on the SDA (Structured Digital Assets) methodology: Korabayev (2026a) introduced the formal methodology and the five-level trust architecture, while Korabayev (2026b) demonstrated its systemic effects empirically on a three-module simulationincluding an increase in the transparency of the entire processing chain. The author provides this empirically established transparency effect with a rigorous theoretical foundation. The difficulty of contemporary financial regulation is interpreted not as a crisis of a particular monetary model but as a structural requisite-variety gap between the complexity of the real production-and-logistics sector and the observational-and-computational capacity of the supervisory apparatus. The gap is formalized through W. R. Ashby's Law of Requisite Variety and the Touchette-Lloyd information-theoretic limit of control; it is stated explicitly that this is a heuristic transposition of the principle into entropic language, not a proven theorem for economic systems. It is argued that tokenization combined with artificial intelligence forms a two-sided mechanism for closing the gap: tokenization and technical oracles raise observability (the mutual information between the controlled system and the regulator), while AI raises the computational capacity of the regulator, which by the Conant-Ashby theorem must embody a model of the controlled system. A two-level anchor-modular architecture is proposed. The limits of the approach are stated honestly: the oracle problem is not eliminated but compressed to a smaller, more costly, and more observable residue; requisite variety is a necessary but not a sufficient condition.

title: Institutional Ownership and Biodiversity Risk

detail.title: Institutional Ownership and Biodiversity Risk
detail.abstract: I examine how institutional investors respond to biodiversity risk and how ownership patterns relate to corporate biodiversity disclosure. Using industry-level biodiversity rankings and firm-level 10-K disclosure measures over 2010-2023, I document a robust negative within-industry relationship: a one standard deviation increase in biodiversity risk is associated with a 6.7 percentage point decline in institutional ownership, intensifying when biodiversity concerns receive greater media attention. At the firm level, lower institutional ownership associates with increased biodiversity disclosure, consistent with a governance gap rather than enhanced monitoring. Non-blockholding institutions drive portfolio reallocation, whilst blockholders maintain stable positions and relate primarily to disclosure sentiment.

title: Greening EU Intellectual Property Law through the Human Right to a Healthy Environment: An Operative Methodology for Constitutional Interpretation

detail.title: Greening EU Intellectual Property Law through the Human Right to a Healthy Environment: An Operative Methodology for Constitutional Interpretation

keywords: Human Right to a Healthy Environment

detail.abstract: Can the human right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment (HR2HE) reshape the interpretation of EU intellectual property (IP) law? This chapter argues that the question is no longer whether environmental protection should influence IP law, but how it should do so. Drawing on international environmental law, United Nations practice, regional human rights jurisprudence and EU constitutional law, it reconstructs an operative methodology for translating the constitutional relevance of environmental protection into concrete legal reasoning. The resulting three-stage framework distinguishes three questions: why environmental protection is constitutionally relevant to the interpretation of IP law; whether and to what extent the activity at issue genuinely advances constitutionally protected environmental objectives; and how those objectives should be reconciled with the legitimate purposes of the IP regime concerned through the interpretation of its existing doctrines. The chapter illustrates the methodology through the recent Hermès upcycling litigation before the Paris Judicial Court. It argues that the HR2HE need not operate primarily through new environmental exceptions or defences, but can function as an internal constitutional consideration informing the interpretation of open-textured IP doctrines wherever they leave room for judicial choice.

title: Modular Open Systems beyond Defense: Reducing Structural Dependency and Expanding Economic Participation

detail.title: Modular Open Systems beyond Defense: Reducing Structural Dependency and Expanding Economic Participation
detail.abstract:
This study examines whether the architectural logic of the Modular Open Systems Approach (MOSA), developed in defense procurement to reduce single-vendor dependency through modularity, open interfaces, interface standardization and verified conformance, can transfer to civilian technology ecosystems. The study distinguishes MOSA's technical mechanisms from the defense-specific governance conditions under which they operate and tests their relevance across major global technology ecosystems.

A purposive sample of 50 technology companies across enterprise software, cloud infrastructure, artificial intelligence, consumer technology, search and social media, commerce, fintech, telecommunications, cybersecurity, and semiconductors is examined to identify concentrated dependencies, candidate modules, separation barriers and practical replaceability. 

The study applies the resulting analytical framework to India, examining existing MOSA-like architectures including UPI, Aadhaar, Account Aggregator and ONDC, and mapping critical dependencies in areas including cloud infrastructure, AI compute and semiconductor capability. An economic feasibility layer considers human capital, wages, financing, taxation and official government baselines to assess whether expanded modular participation is economically viable.

The study finds that technical interfaces can transfer beyond defense, but interoperability alone does not guarantee replaceability. Effective governance and conformance mechanisms are necessary to prevent open architectures from reproducing concentration. India's public digital architectures provide evidence that neutral protocol or network stewards can perform part of this governance function. The study therefore frames modularity primarily as an architecture for reducing structural dependency and expanding participation, rather than as a mechanism for reducing cost.

title: Geoeconomics of Development Finance: Competing Financial Spheres (US, EU, China, Gulf) and their Influence on EMDE Development Pathways

detail.title: Geoeconomics of Development Finance: Competing Financial Spheres (US, EU, China, Gulf) and their Influence on EMDE Development Pathways
detail.abstract:
Development finance has shifted from a Washington‑anchored, aid‑centric system into a multipolar field shaped by four competing financial spheres — the United States, the European Union, China, and the Gulf states. Each sphere deploys distinct instruments, norms, and monetary infrastructures that increasingly determine the development pathways available to emerging‑market and developing economies (EMDEs). As the report notes, “the terms on which capital reaches a poor country increasingly determine whether that capital builds durable institutions or simply accumulates debt.”

The American sphere leverages institutional power — the IMF/World Bank veto, the dollar’s dominance, and a strategically retooled DFC — even as the 2025 dismantling of USAID shrinks its concessional footprint. The European sphere commands the largest global aid budget and uses governance, environmental, and human‑rights conditionality to define “quality” infrastructure. China has transformed development finance by scaling non‑concessional, policy‑bank lending through the Belt and Road Initiative, creating both rapid infrastructure delivery and a rising debt‑distress burden; “China’s share of developing‑country bilateral debt climbed from about 2 percent to about 16 percent within a decade.” The Gulf sphere, backed by ~$5 trillion in sovereign wealth and Islamic finance instruments, acts as a non‑aligned capital intermediary, financing infrastructure, logistics, and energy transitions across Africa and Asia.

The report argues that EMDE agency is now the decisive variable. Countries able to arbitrage across spheres — combining Chinese credit, Western conditionality, and Gulf equity — gain policy space, while those locked into a single patron face heightened debt and governance risks. The emerging order is not a binary contest but a competitive, three‑dimensional system in which development finance has become an arena of geoeconomic strategy, and its rules are still being written.

title: Motivation Concentration Theory: When Motivating the Most Motivated Reduces Total Effort
affiliations: and Utah State University USA

detail.title: Motivation Concentration Theory: When Motivating the Most Motivated Reduces Total Effort
detail.abstract:
Competitive incentive systems are often evaluated by asking whether they increase motivation on average. Motivation Concentration Theory (MCT) explains why that question can be misleading. Organizations can direct favorable feedback, developmental opportunities, and other motivationally consequential resources toward participants who already occupy advantaged positions. The result is motivation concentration: an effort-producing motivational state becomes disproportionately concentrated among a subset of participants while deteriorating among others. When additional increases in that state produce diminishing increases in effort, concentrating motivation among the already highly motivated can reduce the group’s total effort—even when average motivation rises. 

MCT develops this argument in competitive, position-based systems through effort attainability (EA): a participant’s judgment that their own continued effort can still bring a valued competitive outcome within reach from their current position relative to others. EA is not proposed as a new general theory of motivation or as a replacement for established concepts of expectancy or attainability. It serves a narrower function: it names the effort-contingent, position-sensitive judgment whose distribution MCT theorizes. The theoretical contribution lies in explaining how organizational practices can systematically concentrate this motivational advantage among stronger contenders while weakening it among others. 

The theory links the organizational production of motivation concentration to its collective consequence. Practices such as relative-performance feedback and rank-contingent allocation of mentoring, visibility, stretch assignments, and sponsorship can systematically raise EA among participants who already occupy stronger positions while lowering or failing to sustain EA among those who fall behind. If effort increases with EA at a decreasing rate, the incremental effort gained by making high-EA participants still more motivated can be smaller than the effort lost when lower-EA participants become discouraged. Total effort can therefore fall as motivation becomes more concentrated. 

MCT’s central contribution is to explain how organizational practices can endogenously concentrate motivational advantage among already advantaged participants and why that concentration can reduce aggregate effort. The theory identifies a recursive organizational mechanism: position-contingent feedback and opportunities reshape the distribution of an effort-producing motivational judgment; diminishing behavioral returns make that distribution consequential; and resulting effort and position can feed back into subsequent information and opportunity allocation. The central prediction is counterintuitive: a system can increase average perceived attainability while simultaneously concentrating motivational advantage and reducing total effort.

title: Dual-State Recovery Theory: When Motivation and Work Diverge
affiliations: and Utah State University USA

detail.title: Dual-State Recovery Theory: When Motivation and Work Diverge
detail.abstract:
Organizations use temporary systems-such as sales contests, promotion tournaments, innovation competitions, employee rankings, internal grants, and competitive stretch assignments-to concentrate attention and effort on a focal objective for a limited period. These systems are typically evaluated by what happens while the focal demand is active: whether employees become more motivated, exert greater effort, or improve performance. Yet what happens after the system ends may depend on something different. Dual-State Recovery Theory (DSRT) proposes that recovery of the actor and recovery of the work system are not necessarily the same process. An employee's motivation may recover quickly once the focal demand ends, while the Regular Work to which the employee returns may remain impaired by resources and supports diverted during the focal pursuit. Post-intervention performance therefore depends not only on the employee's current motivation, but also on the inherited condition of the incumbent work to which the employee returns. 

DSRT suggests that post-intervention performance reflects two states that may follow very different recovery trajectories: the actor's current motivation and W(t), the state of Regular Work inherited from prior focal pursuit. Under DSRT, Regular Work refers to the actor's incumbent responsibilities, while W(t) captures how ready those responsibilities are to proceed given the supporting configuration of plans, cues, coordination, active work, and ownership. When focal pursuit competes with continuing responsibilities for these shared supports, it creates Work Diversion: incumbent work is reduced, deferred, or disrupted as attention and capacity are redirected toward the focal pursuit. When the focal demand ends, motivation may normalize even though Regular Work remains impaired. DSRT calls this temporal separation Recovery Divergence. The impairment accumulated in Regular Work during focal pursuit creates Maintenance Debt: the gap between the actual state of Regular Work and the state it would have reached had its normal maintenance trajectory continued. When motivation has recovered but this Maintenance Debt remains, the actor may perform below the level that would be expected from current motivation alone; DSRT calls this performance shortfall the Recovery Deficit. Finally, when Maintenance Debt is not fully resolved before another focal-demand cycle begins, its effects can carry forward and accumulate across cycles. DSRT describes this path-dependent persistence as hysteresis: current performance depends not only on current conditions, but also on the unresolved consequences of prior focal pursuits. 

The central contribution of Dual-State Recovery Theory is therefore not the familiar observation that neglected work can remain unfinished after attention shifts elsewhere. It is the identification of a theoretically consequential second state in post-intervention recovery. An actor's motivation can be fully recovered while the work system to which that actor returns is not. In sum, DSRT explains why recovery of the actor can diverge from the recovery of the work system, and why that divergence can persist and reproduce itself across cycles.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes a phased virtual currency (VC) framework that enables coalitions of nations to reduce dependence on a target reserve currency while preserving macroeconomic stability and long-run monetary sovereignty. A jointly governed Coalition Reserve Entity (CRE) accepts deposits of the target currency, issues a blockchain-based asset-backed VC, and phases out reserves through a multi-step exponential decay schedule whose parameters are set collectively via on-chain governance and informed by policy signals such as VC velocity. The framework supports multi-currency settlement excluding the target currency using atomic on-chain FX conversion at CRE oracle rates, while a redemption firewall prevents leakage back to the phased-out currency. Stability is reinforced through diversified reserve management, volatility-sensitive buffer reserves, and optional stake-transfer auctions, with a lightweight coalition marketplace available as an optional coordination layer. Once the phaseout is complete, VC is redeemed for CRE-managed assets, the VC supply is extinguished, and the CRE itself dissolves, preventing the emergence of a permanent supranational currency or authority. A stylized BRICS case study illustrates how these mechanisms collectively enable orderly reserve diversification, resilient settlement flows, and stable coalition markets.

detail.title: Beyond Interchange Caps Domestic and Cross-border Payments in an Era of Open Banking, Account-to-Account Payments, and Tokenised Money
detail.abstract:
Interchange fee regulation has a coherent economic rationale. Card networks are two-sided
platforms; merchants may be unable to refuse widely held cards; collectively set default fees
are opaque; and high merchant charges can create transfers from users of low-cost payment
instruments to rewards-card users. Yet an interchange cap regulates only one price in a layered
system that can reprice through issuer account fees, rewards, acquiring margins, scheme and
processing fees, foreign-exchange spreads, or the terms on which new payment providers enter.
The paper’s new empirical anchor is Chemla et al. (2026), which studies two opposite
regulatory shocks at the same European issuer: a Swiss domestic cap imposed in November 2025
and the post-Brexit removal of European caps from UK–EEA card-not-present transactions in
October 2021. The targeted issuer price moves sharply in both directions and respects the legal
boundary of the intervention. The Swiss cap reduces the effective domestic rate by about 10.75
basis points and does not reprice adjacent corridors. The Brexit shock raises blended issuer
yield by about 55 percent at UK corridor exposure. Consumer incidence is not symmetric: the
Swiss revenue loss is followed by contraction of the free plan and migration toward paid plans,
while the Brexit gain produces no detectable change in spending per user, transactions per user,
or ticket size; aggregate acquisition remains too imprecisely estimated to resolve. A successful
regulatory first stage is therefore not a sufficient-statistic for consumer welfare.
The paper proposes a Payment Cost and Contestability Framework. Its core elements are
mandatory full-stack and corridor-level fee disclosure; rail-neutral access, steering, routing, and
data-portability rules; sustainable and consumer-protective account-to-account payment design;
direct instruments for financial inclusion; interoperable domestic and cross-border standards;
and functionally equivalent safeguards for tokenised deposits, stablecoins, and tokenised central-
bank settlement. A price cap remains available as a backstop, but only after a market-power,
pass-through, alternatives, incidence, and scope test, with anti-circumvention rules and review
tied to market contestability and the adjustment speed of the relevant margins.

title: "Can I Talk to a Human?": Queue Design to Influence Channel Choice in Customer-Service Interactions
affiliations: Tsinghua University - Tsinghua University School of Economics and Management, University of Texas at Dallas - Naveen Jindal School of Management and University of Texas at Dallas - Naveen Jindal School of Management

detail.title: "Can I Talk to a Human?": Queue Design to Influence Channel Choice in Customer-Service Interactions
detail.abstract: Many customer service systems now operate both AI and human channels. We study such a dual-channel service system, in which customers receive private, noisy signals about their request type (simple or complex) and choose a channel. Truly complex requests attempted by AI eventually fail and must transfer to the human channel. The service provider's objective function is average sojourn time; ideally, it would route simple-signal requests to AI to avoid congesting the human channel, and complex-signal requests to the human channel to avoid the higher chance of wasted time on AI failure. However, the provider does not know customers' signals. Nevertheless, it can use queue design to influence customers' self-interested channel choices toward socially preferable outcomes. To that end, we propose the prioritize-transfer, delay-direct mechanism, an easily implementable queue design that rewards customers who try AI. Post-AI-failure transfers to the human channel are with some probability placed in a priority queue. Direct-to-human customers are placed in the lower-priority queue and also experience a fixed amount of extra delay beyond the necessary queueing time. We show that there always exists a prioritize-transfer, delay-direct mechanism that optimally solves the provider's problem. Moreover, under intermediate AI failure time, we show that the prioritize-transfer mechanism (the special case without extra direct-to-human delay) even manages to achieve the first-best outcome, i.e., the minimum sojourn time achievable by a provider who knows all customer signals and controls routing. We also obtain insights on the increase in average sojourn time caused by customer choice and private information.

detail.abstract: Little work has been done to potentially explain relations between funding rates of perpetual futures in the centralized exchange (CEX) and the broader DeFi leverage cycle. We construct a new funding rate-derived metric called “Sign-Aware Time to Zero Funding” (SATZeF) as a candidate for an off-chain regime indicator of onchain leverage, proxied by liquidation volumes. Through empirical observations of lending activity on Aave v3 Mainnet and funding rate time-series on Kraken (CEX), we show that the SATZeF serves as a reliable off-chain regime indicator of the DeFi ecosystem’s current state with respect to the leverage cycle, while daily funding rates can better explain granular movements in on-chain liquidation volumes. From a macro-policy standpoint, this paves the way for greater insight into potentially enforcing leverage requirements on CEXs as a means of indirectly affecting funding conditions in DeFi lending pools.

detail.abstract: The review examines S. Vijay Kumar’s The Idol Thief as a lens through which to assess India’s legal and institutional response to the illicit trafficking and restitution of cultural antiquities. It situates Kumar’s account of the Subhash Kapoor network within the broader intersection of property law, provenance, international cultural-property regimes, and the global antiquities market. The review evaluates the limitations of India’s existing framework, particularly the Antiquities and Art Treasures Act, 1972, highlighting weaknesses in registration, provenance verification, enforcement capacity, and international coordination. It further considers the tension between cultural nationalism and cultural internationalism and the ethical responsibilities of museums, auction houses, collectors, and intermediary institutions. Against this backdrop, the review examines recent Indian efforts towards repatriation, digitised heritage documentation, bilateral cooperation, and the growing role of civil-society initiatives such as the India Pride Project. It argues that restitution cannot remain a predominantly reactive, diplomatic exercise and calls for a more comprehensive framework combining stronger domestic enforcement, mandatory provenance due diligence, technological tracking, international cooperation, and meaningful reintegration of recovered artefacts into their cultural communities. Ultimately, the review frames cultural restitution not merely as the recovery of objects, but as a question of sovereignty, identity, cultural memory, and justice.

detail.abstract: This theoretical study examines sustained strategic cognitive commitment: a settled intention, orientation, or plan capable of being channelled through communication, organization, doctrine, technology, or action. It does not claim that ordinary thought is statistically more lethal than physical weapons. Its narrower claim is that deliberate strategic cognition can precede, organize, and outlast material instruments of conflict. Through conceptual analysis and qualified comparative readings of traditions associated with Kautilya/Chanakya and Shakuni, the study advances an eleven-property taxonomy, an antecedent-to-channelization heuristic, a lifecycle distinction between the transformation ('recycling') and recurrence ('resurfacing') of unresolved destructive intention, and testable propositions for later comparative research. It also places destructive cognition within a balanced generative account: thought, when converted into collective commitment and action, may construct, transform, destroy, or restore institutions and historical trajectories. The proposed contribution is the specific synthesis and application of these elements, not a claim that their underlying ideas lack precedent. The author-proposed, non-clinical remedy architecture matches preventive, corrective, and restorative interventions to the stage, theatre, and pathway of externalized intention, with safeguards against coercive forgiveness, victim-blaming, censorship, and punishment of private thought. The analysis yields conceptual findings and propositions rather than empirical effect estimates; systematic prior-art review and comparative or empirical validation remain necessary before stronger causal or effectiveness claims can be made.

title: How AI Changes What we can do with English: Surface Fluency and Silent Cultural Adjustment in Multilingual Communication

detail.title: How AI Changes What we can do with English: Surface Fluency and Silent Cultural Adjustment in Multilingual Communication

detail.abstract:
For those who use English as an additional language, generative AI is changing the relationship between the English they have personally acquired and the English they can produce and use in communication. Multilingual users can now move ideas across languages and express them in fluent, professionally valued English with unprecedented speed and autonomy. This change may widen access to English-dominant academic, professional, and social spaces. It also creates less visible communicative risks.

This article proposes two concepts for understanding these risks: surface fluency and silent cultural adjustment. Surface fluency arises when the linguistic performance displayed by an AI-assisted message exceeds what the user can adequately understand, assess, explain, or carry forward as their own communication. Silent cultural adjustment arises when AI changes the stance, certainty, commitment, authority, relational positioning, or expected action expressed by a message without the user recognising and consciously choosing that shift. To address these risks, the article proposes user-centred calibration of AI-assisted messages, guided by three criteria: users should be able to Understand, Own, and Explain the messages they use as their own communication.

detail.abstract: Why do otherwise similar firms differ in their ability to convert technological opportunities into innovation? This paper studies whether one explanation lies in CEO prior exposure to innovation at other firms where they previously served on boards. Linking BoardEx employment histories to USPTO AI patents, we construct grant-based measures of CEO external AI innovation exposure. Firms led by CEO with greater external AI innovation exposure subsequently produce more AI Innovation, robust to firm, CEO and industry-year controls, and the relation is specific to AI rather than general patenting. Event studies around CEO turnover, comparing firms with similar pre-turnover innovation potential, show that the arrival of exposed CEO is followed by increases in both AI Innovation Filings and AI Innovation, with no evidence of pre-existing filing trends. The effect is stronger in firms with greater absorptive capacity, and exposed insider and outsider CEO transitions have similar effects. Exposed CEO are also associated with the reallocation of AI inventors to the firm, including from firms on whose boards they previously served, and give rise to first-time AI inventors at the firm. The findings show that technology-specific CEO exposure is a form of managerial human capital that helps firms transform frontier technological opportunities into realized innovation.

title: Do You Have My Size In Stock? Assortment and Inventory Optimization Under the Consider-Fit-Then-Choose Choice Model
affiliations: , , UCLA Anderson School of Management and Washington University in St. Louis - John M. Olin Business School

detail.title: Do You Have My Size In Stock? Assortment and Inventory Optimization Under the Consider-Fit-Then-Choose Choice Model
detail.abstract:
In apparel retail and other applications, when a customer's preferred size is unavailable, demand may shift to nearby sizes. This substitution creates new assortment and inventory optimization challenges because product availability---and, consequently, demand---becomes coupled across sizes. To address these challenges, we introduce the consider-fit-then-choose (CFTC) model, a simple yet rich framework for capturing size-dependent choice behavior. The model applies to settings in which each product may be offered in multiple sizes and the set of available sizes directly affects both customer preferences and consideration sets through a notion of fit, measured by the distance between an available size and the customer's ideal size. Under this model, we study both assortment optimization and the show-all inventory selection problem, in which the retailer chooses initial inventory levels before the selling horizon and subsequently offers every in-stock product to each arriving customer.

We first show that assortment optimization under the CFTC model is NP-hard and develop a polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS) when customers are willing to deviate by at most $O(1)$ sizes from their ideal size. Combined with the recent black-box framework of Fu et al. (2026), this result yields a nearly 0.272-approximation for the corresponding show-all inventory selection problem. We then ask whether stronger guarantees can be obtained by exploiting the specific choice dynamics of the CFTC model. Our approach to both the fluid and stochastic versions of the inventory problem begins by stocking only every other size, thereby decoupling demand across the stocked sizes. Under this restriction, the CFTC model reduces to a special class of mixed multinomial logit models, which we prove satisfies the convex chain decomposition (CCD) property introduced by Goyal et al. (2023). This property allows us to translate solutions to a classical choice-based linear program into feasible show-all inventory policies.

Building on this structure, for the fluid problem we develop a polynomial-time (1/2-ε)-approximation algorithm under adjacent-size substitution and a mild condition on the preference weights. For the stochastic problem, we establish an asymptotic 1/2-approximation guarantee using a new coupling argument that connects the stochastic inventory process to its fluid counterpart. Numerical experiments on instances calibrated using footwear data demonstrate that our inventory solutions achieve small optimality gaps across a broad range of substitution patterns and problem settings.

detail.abstract: Medical device recalls often pose significant risks to patient safety, operational continuity, and financial sustainability. Managing these events at the intersection of Cost, Quality, and Outcomes (CQO) requires rapid reactive response and structured proactive risk assessment. Although alerts/recalls platforms are widely adopted, recall management remains largely fragmented, causing administrative latency, delayed item tracing, inconsistent patient impact assessment, and prolonged exposure to affected products. This paper introduces a scalable, data-driven framework transitioning healthcare operations from unstructured crisis response to a hybrid resilience model that balances effective reactive protocols with proactive risk-mitigation pathways. The framework is designed to integrate structural recall intake with Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) and Electronic Medical Record (EMR) data using the Unique Device Identifier (UDI) to enable rapid item-and lot-level tracing, and patient-level visibility. Concurrently, it introduces a quantitative risk-scoring methodology-incorporating clinical severity, historical recall patterns and traceability-to identify high-risk products proactively, prioritize active recalls, and drive supply chain strategy. Furthermore, we explore the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in automating recall data extraction, normalizing product identifiers, strengthening data governance, and enhancing dashboarding capabilities. Existing literature correlates recall response efficiency with clinical outcomes-including Length of Stay (LOS) and revision rates-and financial metrics such as recoverable asset value and uncompensated procedural costs. By enhancing response efficiency and enabling proactive mitigation, this framework provides a scalable blueprint for strengthening compliance with evolving federal quality mandates while reducing the national burden associated with recalled medical products and supply chain disruptions.

title: Trade Diversion through the Eurasian Economic Union: Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan as Conduits for Sanctioned Russian Trade

detail.title: Trade Diversion through the Eurasian Economic Union: Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan as Conduits for Sanctioned Russian Trade
detail.abstract: In February 2022, the Russian invasion of Ukraine triggered one of the biggest sanctions campaigns in modern history. The measures were designed to isolate Russia from foreign technology and finance, but in the two Central Asian countries most closely linked to the Russian economy, trade increased. This paper seeks to assess the extent to which a re-export boom affected these two economies, and the extent to which it simply transferred them from trade reliance on Russia to reliance on China. This paper, based on published statistics and existing research, concludes that the longer-lasting impact was a deepening of Chinese economic influence that neither government fully chose. The gains were not maintained after Russia closed the tariff loopholes in 2024, when Kyrgyz vehicle re-exports dropped by about 85 percent. Kazakhstan, with Western energy investment to protect, has strengthened export restrictions. In contrast, Kyrgyzstan, which has no such limitation, maximised the trade.

title: Drivers of Green Supply Chain Management Adoption in Egyptian Manufacturing: A Reproducible Synthetic-Data Validation Study

detail.title: Drivers of Green Supply Chain Management Adoption in Egyptian Manufacturing: A Reproducible Synthetic-Data Validation Study
detail.abstract: This computational research article evaluates an integrated model of green supply chain management (GSCM) adoption using a reproducible synthetic dataset of 450 firm-level cases calibrated to an Egyptian manufacturing research context. Six antecedents-external pressure, organizational readiness, human capability, digital readiness, supplier collaboration, and logistics-ecosystem readiness-were generated from a correlated latent structure and linked to GSCM adoption and three performance outcomes. Reliability estimates ranged from 0.78 to 0.82. The adoption model explained 51.5% of variance; all six drivers were positive and statistically distinguishable from zero in the synthetic benchmark. GSCM adoption was strongly associated with environmental performance (β=0.57), operational performance (β=0.49), and resilience (β=0.46). The results demonstrate model identifiability, expected-sign recovery, and the feasibility of a future empirical test. They do not constitute evidence about actual Egyptian manufacturers.

title: Cyclical Fiscal Multipliers: Policy Mix and Financial Friction Puzzle
affiliations: and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Cyclical Fiscal Multipliers: Policy Mix and Financial Friction Puzzle
detail.abstract: We show that the widely accepted view that fiscal multipliers are larger during recessions is not a structural feature of the economy, but a consequence of the prevailing fiscal–monetary policy regime. Using a Time-Varying Parameter Vector Autoregression (TVP-VAR) estimated on U.S. data, we find that the relationship between fiscal multipliers and business cycles changed fundamentally after the 1980s. Before the Volcker disinflation, government spending multipliers increased during recessions, whereas under the subsequent monetary-led policy regime they became substantially smaller and, in some episodes, declined during downturns. These results indicate that fiscal multiplier dynamics are driven primarily by changes in the fiscal–monetary policy mix rather than by recessions themselves. We further document a new empirical puzzle: financial frictions, which historically amplified fiscal multipliers, appear to dampen them in the post-2000 period, particularly during the Global Financial Crisis. The findings imply that recession-based fiscal policy rules of thumb can be systematically misleading unless conditioned on the prevailing policy regime.​

title: Searching for the Right Ingredients: A Recipe for Matching U.S. Labor Market Volatility
affiliations: Amherst College and Amherst College

detail.title: Searching for the Right Ingredients: A Recipe for Matching U.S. Labor Market Volatility
detail.abstract: Both job finding and job separation rates contribute substantially to unemployment rate volatility in the U.S., yet standard search and matching models of the labor market have difficulty matching both. Exogenous-separation models miss the volatility of inflows into unemployment entirely, while those with endogenous separations tend to understate the importance of the job finding rate. We present a framework with three ingredients that are sufficient to match both margins. Matches form with heterogeneous quality; initial productivity is near the bottom of the distribution, generating a tight fundamental surplus; and subsequent shocks to match quality can either lower or raise productivity. The model is able to match the volatilities of unemployment, labor market tightness, finding and separation rates, the autocorrelation of separations, the Beveridge curve, and the decomposition of unemployment fluctuations into contributions from each flow margin---all without resorting to wage rigidity or on-the-job search.

title: Automation, Income Incidence, and Capital Accumulation in Incomplete Markets
affiliations: University of Michigan at Ann Arbor - Department of Mathematics

detail.title: Automation, Income Incidence, and Capital Accumulation in Incomplete Markets
detail.abstract: This paper studies how automation changes the stationary distribution of income, consumption, and wealth in an incomplete-market economy. An automating sector trades off productivity gains and labor-cost savings against adoption costs. Households differ by skill and wealth, save in a capital/equity claim, and face uninsurable skill risk. Competitive factor prices and aggregate capital clear jointly with household Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equations and the stationary Kolmogorov forward equation. Automation affects consumption through labor-income incidence, precautionary saving, skill mobility, ownership of automation rents, and the stationary capital stock. In an adverseincidence scenario with high exposure, adverse reskilling, capital obsolescence, and concentrated ownership, decentralized automation lowers stationary consumption and capital relative to the no-automation allocation. With stronger productivity and complementarity, lower obsolescence, and broader ownership, automation raises output, consumption, and capital. Reversing the assumed skillmobility response also raises consumption, output, and capital substantially at a fixed automation intensity. A proxy diagnostic combining U.S. evidence on AI adoption, investment, labor-income pass-through, equity ownership, and marginal propensities to consume places the current economy near the boundary between the two scenarios. The model provides a quantitative framework for separating automation’s aggregate gains from its distributional incidence.

detail.abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) can fit an aggregate partial differential equation (PDE) objective while retaining errors concentrated in one physical variable, residual channel, or part of the domain. We introduce Variable-Aware Regional Adaptation for physics-informed neural networks (VARA-PINN), a channel-region adaptation framework whose guarded controller instantiations diagnose this structure and reallocate a fixed PINN training budget. A channel-by-region severity tensor proposes changes to collocation density and local loss weight; guarded variants screen proposals for gradient conflict, test them against matched neutral probes, and restore state when reference-free guard metrics deteriorate beyond tolerance. Tests combine guarded analytical and transient studies with sparse-data lid-driven cavity reconstruction and Reynolds-number continuation using the same channel-region allocation principle. Across five seeds, VARA reduces Kovasznay errors by 33–46%, while the sparse-CFD cavity instantiation reduces full-field velocity error by 9.1% and sparse-velocity mean-square error by 26.2%. It wins 29/35 paired Allen–Cahn comparisons and 21/21 advection–diffusion comparisons, with mean normalized reductions of 35.1% and 58.6%, respectively. Five-seed mechanism and sensitivity studies identify regional allocation as the principal scalar-PDE mechanism and show stability under moderate controller perturbations. A complementary single-seed sweep improves the reference-free cavity aggregate at 14 of 15 Reynolds numbers from 100 to 10,000. Under these protocols, VARA-PINN improves field reconstruction and localized error correction without requiring dense reference access during training; it does not imply that every residual channel improves in every run.
