title: Cyclical Fiscal Multipliers: Policy Mix and Financial Friction Puzzle
affiliations: and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Cyclical Fiscal Multipliers: Policy Mix and Financial Friction Puzzle
detail.abstract: We show that the widely accepted view that fiscal multipliers are larger during recessions is not a structural feature of the economy, but a consequence of the prevailing fiscal–monetary policy regime. Using a Time-Varying Parameter Vector Autoregression (TVP-VAR) estimated on U.S. data, we find that the relationship between fiscal multipliers and business cycles changed fundamentally after the 1980s. Before the Volcker disinflation, government spending multipliers increased during recessions, whereas under the subsequent monetary-led policy regime they became substantially smaller and, in some episodes, declined during downturns. These results indicate that fiscal multiplier dynamics are driven primarily by changes in the fiscal–monetary policy mix rather than by recessions themselves. We further document a new empirical puzzle: financial frictions, which historically amplified fiscal multipliers, appear to dampen them in the post-2000 period, particularly during the Global Financial Crisis. The findings imply that recession-based fiscal policy rules of thumb can be systematically misleading unless conditioned on the prevailing policy regime.​

title: The Six Syndromes of Pakistan's Political Economy: A Mathematical Theory of Socialized Costs, Institutional Learning, and Macroeconomic Fragility
affiliations: Independent and Quaid-i-Azam University

detail.title: The Six Syndromes of Pakistan's Political Economy: A Mathematical Theory of Socialized Costs, Institutional Learning, and Macroeconomic Fragility
detail.abstract: Pakistan's recurrent episodes of fiscal stress, expensive credit, power-sector arrears, stateowned-enterprise losses, regulatory fragmentation, subsidy dependence, and commodity-market interventions are generally examined as separate policy failures. This paper develops a unified political-economy framework in which these phenomena are interpreted as six mutually reinforcing economic syndromes: the Interest Rate Syndrome, Independent Power Producers (IPPs) Syndrome, State-Owned Enterprises (SOEs) Syndrome, Governance Syndrome, Subsidiaries Syndrome and the Commodities Inverted Import and Export Syndrome. The central mechanism is a cost-socialization trap: concentrated groups can retain identifiable benefits while significant portions of the associated fiscal, quasi-fiscal, regulatory, financing, or price costs are transmitted to diffuse households, taxpayers, firms, bank borrowers, and future public budgets. The paper develops a micro-founded political-economy model of distortion persistence, a fiscal-banking model of interest-rate amplification and sovereign crowding out, a capacity-transmission model of electricity tariffs, a softbudget-constraint model of SOEs, a multi-agency rent-extraction model of governance, a distributional model of subsidy capture, and a DeGroot social-learning model of information aggregation and policy error. The framework yields ten analytical propositions. Among them, monetary tightening is shown to have larger real effects when sovereign refinancing exposure and banking-sector government exposure are high; generation expansion can raise electricity tariffs without increasing deliverable electricity when transmission constraints bind; fragmented regulatory extraction produces a larger aggregate burden than coordinated extraction; soft budget constraints reduce managerial effort; untargeted quantity subsidies reproduce underlying asset concentration; and influential biased signals in policy networks increase the probability of erroneous commodity export decisions followed by costly import reversals. Pakistan provides an institutionally revealing setting for these mechanisms. Official FY2025-26 data report markup payments equivalent to 5.5 percent of GDP; scheduled-bank budgetary lending to government of Rs2.79 trillion during July-March compared with Rs934.1 billion of private-sector credit; installed electricity capacity of 49,651 MW amid continuing capacity, network, and circular-debt reforms; and substantial fiscal exposure to SOEs. These facts do not, by themselves, establish causality, but they motivate a falsifiable empirical agenda using monetary shocks, firm and bank exposure, plant-grid data, SOE reforms, administrative digitalization, household microdata, and commodity-level policy events. The paper's contribution is therefore to show analytically how sector-specific distortions can become endogenously interconnected through fiscal socialization, institutional networks, trust, and privatesector incentives, generating a persistent low-investment and low-productivity equilibrium.

title: Monetary Policy Transmission by Securitising Banks
affiliations: Banque de France and

detail.title: Monetary Policy Transmission by Securitising Banks
detail.abstract: This paper studies whether securitisation affects monetary policy transmission via banks. Using granular loan-level data from the euro area, we show that banks actively engaged in securitisation adjust credit supply more strongly in response to monetary policy shocks than a matched sample of non-securitising banks. This is because securitisation expands banks' lending capacity, but by increasing reliance on investors whose required returns and risk appetite are more sensitive to monetary policy conditions. Following a monetary tightening, these investors demand higher compensation and reduce their exposure to securitised assets, leading securitising banks to contract lending more than other banks. Effects are stronger for loans more likely to be securitised-i.e., to safer borrowers with longer maturities-and are primarily driven by synthetic securitisations, which provide additional capital relief through Significant Risk Transfers. Firms exposed to securitising banks cannot fully substitute tighter loan supply through existing or new bank relationships.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a model of revolving doors in which a regulator designs policy signals that affect a regulated firm’s capital structure while holding an implicit career option to leave public service and join the regulated firm or its advisers. The model has three linked mechanisms. First, regulatory signals alter the firm’s admissible pricing and leverage choices by changing the tradeoff between consumer surplus and firm profit. Second, because the regulator’s outside payoff is convex in the value of the regulated firm, the value of the regulator’s career option increases with firm value, leverage, and signal-induced volatility. Third, when signal-induced volatility raises the option vega of firm equity, the same mechanism can increase tail risk and lower distance to default. A proof-of-concept calibration illustrates the model’s leverage-vega warning regions and shows how a regulator-induced signal can move a firm from a go-leverage region into an early-warning or crash-risk region. The calibration is extended with maturity comparisons, a sensitivity grid overcompensation convexity and initial leverage, a bank-like parameter anchor, stochastic signal simulations, and a stopping-horizon diagnostic. External evidence from federal payroll data on post-employment restrictions supports the model’s career option primitive, while the exercises also organize historical regulatory failures: Lehman Brothers as a regulatory-vacuum case, Silicon Valley Bank as a distorted-signal and weak-supervision case, and Signature Bank as a converted-signal case in which post-public-service incentives and lighter oversight coincided with rapid growth, uninsured-deposit exposure, and tail risk. The model does not predict collapse dates; it helps explain and predict when regulatory forbearance, weak debt penalties, and career-option incentives can delay binding oversight until firms cross a leverage-vega warning threshold.

detail.abstract: This study examines the relationship between exchange rate movements and consumer price inflation in Pakistan over the period January 2020 to June 2025. The analysis uses 66 monthly observations of the USD/PKR exchange rate obtained from the State Bank of Pakistan and CPI-based inflation data obtained from the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics. Descriptive statistics, monthly trend analysis, and Pearson's product-moment correlation coefficient are employed to examine the co-movement between exchange rates and consumer price inflation. The results indicate a moderate positive correlation between the USD/PKR exchange rate and inflation, with a Pearson correlation coefficient of r = 0.423 . The period from 2022 to 2023 is characterized by pronounced exchange-rate depreciation alongside elevated inflation, while both indicators show comparatively lower inflationary momentum during the subsequent period. The observed positive association is consistent with the theoretical view that exchange-rate depreciation can contribute to domestic price pressures through higher import costs and production expenses. However, the bivariate correlation does not establish a causal relationship, and other factors, including commodity prices, monetary conditions, energy costs, fiscal developments, and supply-side disruptions, may also have influenced inflation during the study period. The findings provide descriptive evidence on exchange-rate and inflation dynamics in Pakistan and provide a basis for future research using multivariate and time-series econometric methods.

title: Multipolar Currency System: Prerequisites, Risks and Mechanisms of Formation

detail.title: Multipolar Currency System: Prerequisites, Risks and Mechanisms of Formation
detail.abstract: The article examines the prerequisites for the formation of a multipolar monetary system as a more distributed model of the international monetary architecture, within which several centers of liquidity, settlements and reserves compete and coexist. It is shown that the modern transformation of the global monetary system is determined not only by the redistribution of the role of individual currencies, but also by the development of payment infrastructure, regional financial institutions, currency swaps and digital instruments. A typology of scenarios for the formation of a new monetary architecture is proposed, including soft multipolarity, regional multipolarity and a fragmented multi-contour system.

detail.title: Property in Information: A Formal Analysis of Forty-Five Works

Part One treats the thirty works the case against intellectual property cites, contests or relies upon, among them.

detail.abstract: I study the effect of terrorist attacks on people’s trust in their families and diverse in–group and out–group social groups, exploiting the quasi–random overlap between the Global Terrorism Database and the World Values Survey at the regional level across 20 countries. I use a sharp regression discontinuity design as identification strategy. The coefficient of interest captures the effect on people’s trust level when exposed to a terrorist attack. This research contributes to three literatures, emphasizing its international perspective: i. It analyzes the differential impact of terrorism on trust across different social groups; ii. It contributes with a methodology that moves away from experimental designs to assess the effects of terrorism on people’s trust; and iii. It studies low–intensity terrorism at a regional level with a worldwide perspective, going beyond the major terrorist attacks. The main finding is that trust toward unknown people declines by 0.47–0.61 Likert–scale units (approximately 25–32% of the mean), an effect that is robust to data–driven bandwidth selection (Calonico, Cattaneo & Titiunik, 2014), leave–one–out country exclusions, and placebo cutoff tests. Evidence of effects on trust toward people of other nationalities is suggestive but sensitive to specification. No robust effects are found on trust toward people of other religions. Changes in trust toward known people are not statistically different from zero. Heterogeneous effects are explored by region, country, and individual characteristics, which reinforce the hypothesis that social reconstruction mechanisms operate with greater speed and effectiveness in contexts where prior social capital density is high.

title: Air Pollution and Labor Productivity: Evidence From a Global Panel

detail.title: Air Pollution and Labor Productivity: Evidence From a Global Panel
detail.abstract: I estimate the effect of ambient air pollution on labor productivity at the macroeconomic level, using an unbalanced panel of 94 countries over 2011-2021. The panel combines WHO pollutant data (PM2.5, PM10, NO₂) with ILO productivity series, Penn World Tables controls, and WHO health expenditure data. I anchor the estimating equation in a semi-endogenous growth model extending Jones (1995) with a pollutionimpairment channel that delivers three testable predictions: a negative balanced-growth-path semi-elasticity of output per worker with respect to steady-state pollution (Proposition 1), independence of the long-run growth rate from pollution concentration (Proposition 2), and full comparative statics that nest the augmented Solow model while adding an orthogonal pollution term (Proposition 3). The preferred firstdifference estimator yields β̂ =-0.00037 (p = 0.048), implying that a 10 μg/m³ increase in annual mean PM2.5 reduces GDP per worker by 0.37 percent, approximately $248 per worker per year at the sample mean of $67,900. The system-GMM estimator, which corrects for the attenuation bias induced by reverse causality between productivity and pollution abatement, shifts the estimate to β̂ =-0.00179 (p = 0.039). Dynamic fixed-effects specifications recover long-run BGP semi-elasticities of β_LR =-0.00042 to-0.00057 across lag structures of one, three, and five years, consistent with pollution operating as a permanent level drag. PM10 yields a consistent negative coefficient across first-difference specifications; NO₂ does not, reflecting within-country confounding between nitrogen dioxide and economic activity that the panel cannot resolve. Placebo regressions using GDP per capita, TFP, and hours worked yield null results, isolating the mechanism to within-worker impairment. The growth-rate specification confirms Proposition 2: pollution has no statistically significant effect on labor productivity growth in any specification, establishing that the benefit of abatement is a permanent upward shift in the balanced growth path, not a transitional gain. If all 94 sample countries achieved the WHO annual PM2.5 guideline of 5 μg/m³, the aggregate productivity gain would range from 0.68 to 3.32 percent per worker annually. Environmental regulation, in this framework, functions as a productivity investment whose returns compound as long as lower concentrations are maintained. The estimation sample, constrained by monitoring coverage to predominantly high-income economies, implies that these figures are a lower bound on the true global average.

detail.abstract: This is the technical and research companion to Wisdomism: Toward the First Wisdom Revolution. It presupposes the founding paper and develops the computational architecture, mathematical formalisation, and research frontiers that the founding paper introduces but does not fully develop. The companion presents the expanded transformation grammar Y = G · A · X and the H = G · A decomposition; the network formulation of Dynamic Prophecy (D_global) with its inter-cluster influence matrix; the causal graph underlying spillover and the conditions under which entanglement between actors is structurally possible; an information-theoretic grounding of Dynamic Prophecy in which D is the expected signed information gain from wise action, the Amber matrix is mutual information and the Graphene matrix is conditional mutual information; a Win-Wiser Win-Wiser equilibrium theorem establishing existence, positive surplus, and convergence under stated assumptions, with its relationship to Nash equilibrium and its open problems; the LWM developmental progression (LLM → LOM → LIM → LWM) toward Artificial General Wisdom; and privacy-preserving proof primitives for verification without surveillance. title: Pricing Access to the Himalayas: Evidence from Mountaineering Royalty Reforms

detail.title: Pricing Access to the Himalayas: Evidence from Mountaineering Royalty Reforms
detail.abstract: Access fees are commonly used to ration entry to congested natural places on the assumption that visitors respond to prices and that higher fees reduce participation. To test this assumption, I study Nepal's mountaineering royalty reforms that have been restructured repeatedly since 1993 and eliminated entirely in one region for a decade. I employ a rich expedition-level archive covering 11,425 expeditions and roughly 89,000 climbers, in conjunction with royalty schedules recovered from Nepali government publications, to evaluate the impact of access prices on the demand for Himalayan mountaineering. First, I find that a complete ten-yearlong elimination of the royalty in the mid-and far-western regions resulted in no significant increase in expedition counts. Second, I show that a graduated schedule introduced in 2008 that cut the price faced by teams of fewer than seven raised the share of small expeditions on the Nepalese side of Mount Everest by 8.8 percentage points relative to the Tibetan side of the same mountain. These results indicate that access pricing does not appear to ration entry, but it does shape participation. I show that the schedule's thresholds did not generate any bunching, and find evidence of cross-border substitution through an examination of both Nepal-side and Tibet-side expeditions. Together, these findings highlight that fixed participation costs and binding capacity constraints limit the responsiveness of entry to access prices, while variable team-level costs generate a more elastic intensive margin, particularly when nearby alternatives provide close substitutes.

title: Transformation of the Global Monetary System as a Reflection of a New Scientific Paradigm

detail.title: Transformation of the Global Monetary System as a Reflection of a New Scientific Paradigm
detail.abstract: The article examines the transformation of the global monetary system in the context of structural changes in the global economy, digitalization of international settlements and increasing multipolarity. It is proved that the modern world monetary system should be analyzed not only as a financial mechanism, but also as an institutional and scientific-methodological object. It is concluded that the new paradigm manifests itself primarily in changing the principles, relationships, and mechanisms of the system's functioning.

title: The Missing Market: Diagnosing Institutional Absence in Investment Ecosystems
affiliations: Stanford University and Stanford University

detail.title: The Missing Market: Diagnosing Institutional Absence in Investment Ecosystems
detail.abstract: Why do pension funds not invest in nature? Why is human capital not an investable asset class? Why is AI 'compute' not yet a financialized commodity market? We examine why seemingly attractive investment opportunities, where the supply and demand forces are validated and underlying economics are well-understood, still fail to become recognizable, mature financial geographies. Existing scholarship on path dependence, institutional change, and evolutionary economic geography offers powerful explanations for why change does or does not occur within historically structured trajectories. However, these frameworks are less well suited to explaining "nothingness": cases in which financial markets, exchanges, or ecosystems do not emerge despite expectations that they will. This paper develops a methodological framework for studying 'nothingness'; that is, a framework for diagnosing asset-class non-consolidation within institutional investment ecosystems. The framework organizes diagnosis across three analytically distinct levels (macro-level institutions and regulation, meso-level market formation, and micro-level firm organization) and introduces porosities and blocks as the mechanisms through which practices, claims, and knowledge either translate successfully across level boundaries or fail to gain recognition and traction. Building on this framework, the paper proposes a diagnostic instrument that classifies conditions across the three levels at a given point in time, generating twenty-seven possible configurations, each linked to a recommended course of action ranging from active adoption to withdrawal. A five-step empirical protocol operationalizes the framework for practical application. The instrument offers a snapshot diagnostic: a structured way for researchers, regulators, and market actors to identify whether non-emergence is rooted in macro-level constraints, meso-level market dynamics, micro-level organizational capacity, or insufficient translation between levels, and help to determine where targeted intervention would be most effective. We illustrate the framework and instrument through a case study of US climate infrastructure.

title: Loss Aversion in Strategy Switching: Evidence on Dynamic Collective Behavior in Financial Markets
affiliations: National Taipei University and Tamkang University

detail.title: Loss Aversion in Strategy Switching: Evidence on Dynamic Collective Behavior in Financial Markets
detail.abstract: This study reexamines loss aversion in financial markets within an interactive agentbased framework, recasting loss aversion from a fixed individual preference into a dynamic, market-level selection mechanism. Collective loss aversion is defined as an endogenous force governing strategy switching across heterogeneous agents. Using simulation calibrated to major global equity markets, results show that collective loss aversion exhibits a neutral level under normal conditions, implying symmetric responses to gains and losses. Significant deviations arise primarily in less-developed markets, where elevated loss aversion accelerates strategy adjustments and mitigates speculative inefficiencies. Two stabilization channels are identified: arbitrage by risktolerant fundamentalists and endogenous corrections driven by collective loss aversion. However, our empirical results indicate that fundamentalists may be the driven force to correct mispricing given the disappearance of collective loss aversion in welldeveloped financial markets.

title: Circular Economy Policy, Industrial Behavior, and Firm Performance

detail.title: Circular Economy Policy, Industrial Behavior, and Firm Performance
detail.abstract: This paper asks whether circular economy policy shifted industrial firms toward circular practices in a developing economy, using as a case study Colombia, and whether it did so at the cost of economic performance. I exploit regional variation in the intensity of policy implementation to estimate three difference-indifferences specifications on an unbalanced panel of 5,488 manufacturing establishments drawn from the Environmental Industrial Survey and the Annual Manufacturing Survey for 2012-2022 (26,832 establishment-year observations, excluding 2019 as a transition year). The preferred two-way fixed-effects estimator interacts a post-ENEC indicator with a standardized measure of regional implementation intensity and absorbs establishment and year fixed effects, with standard errors clustered at the establishment level. I find that value added rose by approximately 6.1 percent (p < 0.01) in high-intensity regions relative to low-intensity ones, a result that survives a battery of robustness checks including a placebo treatment at 2016, a balanced-panel restriction, alternative treatment definitions, and firm-size controls. Environmental fines fell in high-intensity regions, consistent with proactive compliance through normative isomorphism rather than reactive penalty avoidance. A multi-industry decomposition reveals that the aggregate value-added effect concentrates in metals and metal products (21.8 percent) and wood and paper (11.1 percent), sectors where material recovery generates the largest cost savings. An intra-sectoral triple-interaction test confirms that the treatment effect is significantly larger in the ENEC's priority sectors (9.1 percent) than in nonpriority ones (1.4 percent, interaction p = 0.07), validating the policy's flow-based prioritization design.

title: The Right to Remain Silent in Finance: Why Nonresponse Alone Should Not Be Treated as Risk

detail.title: The Right to Remain Silent in Finance: Why Nonresponse Alone Should Not Be Treated as Risk

detail.abstract:
Financial institutions increasingly observe pauses, incomplete interactions, unanswered messages, unused offers, delayed confirmations, and other forms of nonresponse. This article examines when observed nonresponse may legitimately support an adverse financial inference. Using a structured conceptual synthesis of peer-reviewed research on missingness, nonresponse, choice deferral, administrative burden, and automated decision-making, together with primary legal and regulatory materials from the United States, European Union, and United Kingdom, the paper separates four states often collapsed in practice: missing data, unqualified silence, qualified omission, and objective financial events. 

The analysis develops a rebuttable presumption of governed ambiguity: institutions may record nonresponse, but nonresponse alone should not determine materially adverse treatment unless the assigned interpretation is supported by independent, decision-relevant evidence proportionate to the consequence. The proposed "right to remain silent in finance" is a normative governance principle, not an asserted constitutional, statutory, or contractual entitlement. It does not erase payment duties, verification requirements, deadlines, or other independently observed events. 

The paper contributes an adverse-inference constraint, eight linked governance principles, an illustrative cross-context decision analysis, and seven falsifiable propositions for future research. Applied to credit, servicing, collections, fraud controls, investing, and financial marketing, the analysis shows why observation, interpretation, and permissible use should be treated as separate questions. The central conclusion is that silence may justify inquiry, verification, or reversible safeguards, but does not identify its own cause and should not, by itself, be treated as evidence of intent, character, emotion, capacity, willingness, or financial risk.

title: Navigating The Postassad Transition:  Update on Syria Sanctions and Export Controls (May 2025 – December 2025)

detail.title: Navigating The Postassad Transition:  Update on Syria Sanctions and Export Controls (May 2025 – December 2025)
detail.abstract: This research paper analyses the definitive shift in international economic statecraft regarding Syria from May 2025 through December 8, 2025. Following the collapse of the Bashar al-Assad regime, the United States, United Kingdom, European Union, and United Nations executed a coordinated dismantling of the comprehensive sanctions architecture that had isolated the country for over a decade. The study details the revocation of key U.S. Executive Orders, the legislative repeal of the Caesar Act, and the regulatory amendments in London and Brussels that unlocked Syria's energy and financial sectors. It examines the critical legal manoeuvres required to de-list President Ahmed al-Sharaa and the governing apparatus from global terrorist lists, legitimizing the transitional government. Finally, the paper evaluates the emerging compliance landscape, arguing that while the legal barriers to trade have fallen, a "bankability gap" persists, requiring firms to adopt adaptive, trajectory-based risk frameworks to navigate the residual targeted sanctions and "snapback" mechanisms that define this new era of conditional engagement.

detail.abstract: This paper points to a loophole in the tax code. Deductions for in-kind donations depend on a cost basis and a valuation that the firm can substantially inflate. This makes certain pharmaceutical donations more profitable than selling, and the tax code subsidizes the transfer of expired or unusable products. I document this mechanism in the United States and show that major pharmaceutical firms almost exclusively donate in kind, many approaching or hitting the regulatory cap on the maximum allowed deduction. The same vulnerability appears in 11 of 25 other countries surveyed. A remedy is to cap deductions at the direct production cost, replace inflated price metrics with the actual market price, and cap further when a cheaper equally effective option exists.

title: Navigating U.S. Sanctions and Export Controls on Syria: Overview of Restrictions, Impact, and Pathways to Relief

detail.abstract:
This paper provides an analysis of U.S. sanctions and export control regime targeting Syria. It details the historical evolution of these restrictions, the primary U.S. government agencies involved in their administration (OFAC, BIS, and the Department of State), and the complex legal foundations upon which they are built. 

There are several legal pillars underpinning the web of restrictions currently in place by the US that impact Syria’s access to financial system as well as the country’s ability to import key items, goods, services and technologies necessary to start its reconstruction efforts. Paramount is Syria's longstanding designation as a State Sponsor of Terrorism (SST) in place since 1979 as well as numerous Executive Orders imposing a wide range of prohibitions, and significant Congressionally mandated sanctions such as the Syria Accountability Act (SAA), the Iran Threat Reduction and Syria Human Rights Act (ITRSHRA), and the impactful Caesar Syria Civilian Protection Act of 2019. These sanctions’ framework are supplemented with stringent export controls administered by BIS under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR), which impose a general policy of denial for most exports and reexports to Syria. 

Following the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024, this sanctions landscape has been evolving across multiple dimensions. This includes the issuance of General License 24 by OFAC in January 2025, which offers temporary and conditional authorizations for certain transactions with new "governing institutions" and in specific sectors like energy and personal remittances. The recent announcement by President Trump in May 2025 regarding his intention to lift U.S. sanctions on Syria reflects the most significant shift in U.S Government stance and intent towards the country although details of how this relaxation/lifting will be implanted in practice remain scarce and noting that the complex web of existing sanctions means this will not be a simple or immediate process. Despite these recent developments, Syria remains one of the most comprehensively sanctioned countries in the world. The renewal of the Caesar Act and the continued SST designation signal that substantial and sustained sanctions relief will likely depend on demonstrable, broad behavioural changes by the new Syrian authorities that address deep-rooted U.S. concerns regarding governance, regional stability, terrorism, and WMD proliferation. 

The environment for businesses and humanitarian actors engaging with Syria remains challenging and the "chilling effect" of sanctions is expected to persist until clearer U.S. policy shifts or more fundamental changes to the sanctions architecture occur. Navigating this landscape requires thorough due diligence, compliance with both OFAC and BIS regulations, and often direct engagement with U.S. government agencies for licensing or guidance. However, while this challenging environment persist, the positive intent signalled in recent days should work as a catalyst for firms, companies and other operators to revisit their own long-held stance on restricting/denying permissible/licensable business activities in the country as well as start the long process of assessing the level of due diligence that would be appropriate to ensure safe engagement with local partners, businesses and NGOs.  Current estimates today suggest that the Syria reconstruction cost will be USD400-600bn in core sectors such as energy, utilities, health, education to name a few. This level of investment will require a robust finance, payment and banking infrastructure that can support this growth while also ensuring that adequate, compliance, resilience, Money laundering and Terrorist Finance risks are properly managed.  

After 46 years of isolation culminating with 14 years of civil war and displacement of 50% of the population, this will be both a challenge and an opportunity to support the rebuild of a modern, fair and prosperous Syria.

title: Reconstructing Worker Protections in the Wake of Humphrey's Executor
affiliations: and Harvard Law School

detail.title: Reconstructing Worker Protections in the Wake of Humphrey's Executor
detail.abstract:
The Supreme Court has gutted independent agencies – a form of governance that has been a fixture in our country for more than a century. The Court ruled that President Trump could fire Democratic commissioner Rebecca Slaughter from the Federal Trade Commission (FTC), overruling Humphrey’s Executor v. United States (1935), where the Court held that a president may remove an FTC commissioner only for cause. The decision  definitively resolves questions about the President’s authority to dismiss members of bipartisan commissions or boards in contravention of statutory constraints that he may remove them only for cause.

Congress created independent agencies to have unique expertise and protect core functions from political interference. This commitment to the long-term public good comes from the very features that define independent agencies: the need for members to discuss decisions with colleagues who likely have a different perspective; the goal of freeing incumbents to rely on their best informed judgment in making decisions that are insulated from the political desires of the president; and the enhanced expertise that comes from sitting on a board or commission for a term longer than that usually enjoyed by political appointees.  

This Article examines the implications that the overturning of Humphrey’s Executor will have for workers’ labor and employment rights, with a particular focuses on the ramifications for the National Labor Relations Board (“NLRB”) and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (“EEOC”). 

We suggest mechanisms for Congress to respond to the Court’s upheaval of the protections provided by independent agencies, including enacting a private right of action in the NLRA, removing federal preemption of labor law, relocating the NLRB’s adjudicatory functions, and other options for merging and restructuring the agencies. The Court’s actions undermine the commitment that Congress made to the public that important rights and protections will be enforced by experts free from the front lines of politics. Congress can amend these agencies’ enacting laws to ensure that those protected by these agencies do not have their ability to get a fair hearing of their interests captured by a President’s political whims.

title: Magnesium Fertilization Affects Carotenoid and Mineral Element Accumulation in Three Kale (Brassica oleracea var. acephala) Cultivars Grown Hydroponically

detail.title: Magnesium Fertilization Affects Carotenoid and Mineral Element Accumulation in Three Kale (Brassica oleracea var. acephala) Cultivars Grown Hydroponically
detail.abstract: Kale (Brassica oleracea L. var. acephala) is a nutrient-dense, leafy vegetable characterized by its high content of health-promoting phytonutrients, particularly carotenoids, which contribute to its nutritional value. Magnesium (Mg) is an essential mineral element for plants, playing a significant role in physiological and biochemical processes. Despite its importance, the optimal Mg rate in nutrient solutions remains largely underexplored in terms of its impact on crop yield and nutritional quality in hydroponic culture. We evaluated the effect of different Mg concentrations (12.3, 24.6, 36.9, and 49.2 mg•L-1) in nutrient solutions on shoot biomass, elemental nutrient composition, and carotenoid accumulation in three hydroponically grown kale cultivars: Darkibor, Mamba, and Red Russian. The experiment was a split-plot design, with Mg concentration as the main plot and kale cultivars as the subplots. Results showed a decreasing quadratic relationship between Mg rates and shoot biomass (fresh and dry). Increasing Mg concentration improved the accumulation of Mg and iron in leaf tissues across all kale cultivars, but decreased significantly the uptake of potassium, phosphorus, calcium, and sulfur. A quadratic increase was observed in the case of zinc. Moreover, total carotenoids and b-carotene contents in the leaf tissues of the kale cultivars increased significantly at an optimum Mg concentration of 36.9 and 24.6 mg•L-1 , respectively, before declining at high Mg concentrations. This suggests that optimizing carotenoid biosynthesis in kale can be achieved within the Mg range of 24.6 to 36.9 mg•L-1 , but its interaction with other ions in nutrient solutions must be managed carefully to avoid potential antagonistic effects on the uptake of other essential elements.

detail.abstract: We find Flammer's (2021) reported positive market response to the announcement of issuance of corporate green bonds is not replicable in a data set designed to mimic her own. In our closest replication, on her 16-day event window, the t-statistic is not +2.03, but +1.10. The largest positive daily mean return occurs 9 days after the announcement. Furthermore, the three-day response around the announcement day is-0.012% (using the country-specific market model benchmark) and statistically insignificant. Also, we do an out-of-sample test of whether the reported effect (in the 2013 to 2018 period) exists in a later period (2019 to 2025); we find no such effect in the latter period. Finally, during 2019 to 2025 (which has almost ten times the sample than during 2013 to 2018), the 16-day announcement return is negative and Flammer's estimate lies outside the 95% confidence interval.

title: The Pricing of Cyber Catastrophe Bonds: Evidence from the First Market Cycle, 2023-2026

detail.title: The Pricing of Cyber Catastrophe Bonds: Evidence from the First Market Cycle, 2023-2026
detail.abstract: Cyber risk reached the catastrophe bond market in November 2023. This paper assembles a census of all Rule 144A cyber catastrophe bonds issued to mid-2026 (eight transactions, ten priced tranches) and asks how the market has priced them. Benchmarked against the average multiple of expected loss across all catastrophe bond issuance in the quarter of issue, cyber tranches paid a mean premium ratio of 2.3: roughly twice the spread per unit of modelled expected loss carried by contemporaneous natural-catastrophe issues. Every tranche priced above its sameexpected-loss benchmark (exact binomial p = 0.002). Nominal cyber spreads fell by roughly a third between 2023 and 2025, but the market-wide multiple fell as fast: benchmark-adjusted, the cyber premium shows no decay, and point estimates rise. Sponsors gained instead on composition margins: deal size, guidance execution and structure. Persistence is consistent with ambiguity about cyber tail models rather than a transient novelty load.

title: Optimal Insurance Design under Government-subsidized Public-Private Partnership
affiliations: The University of Hong Kong, The University of Hong Kong and Southern University of Science and Technology

detail.title: Optimal Insurance Design under Government-subsidized Public-Private Partnership
detail.abstract: Public-private partnerships can extend insurance coverage to risks that exceed private market capacity. Their design requires balancing policyholder protection, insurer profitability, and public expenditure. This paper studies the joint design of proportional insurance policies under premium subsidies within a social welfare framework that accounts for policyholders' risk reduction, the insurance industry's profit, and the government's subsidy expenditure. For a single policy, we characterize optimal insurance coverage and participation. Under certain mild conditions, more subsidies and greater risk exposure raise social welfare, whereas higher expected losses and greater emphasis on fiscal cost reduce it. Market composition can trigger discrete changes in coverage. For a two-policy menu, we establish monotonic sorting, partially characterize interior solutions, and employ a constrained Differential Evolution algorithm to identify the optimal menu. Numerical comparative statics examine how the safety loading, subsidy ratio, and welfare weights affect the optimal menu and policyholder sorting.

title: A Non-Equilibrium Interactive Agent-Based Model in Financial Markets: Fundamentalists, Positive-Feedback Trading, and Regime Transitions

detail.title: A Non-Equilibrium Interactive Agent-Based Model in Financial Markets: Fundamentalists, Positive-Feedback Trading, and Regime Transitions
detail.abstract: This mini review examines a non-equilibrium interactive agent-based model for financial markets, focusing on the roles of fundamentalists, positive-feedback traders, and noise traders. The reviewed studies show that trader heterogeneity, risk tolerance, funding constraints, and excess-demand price adjustment can generate bubbles, crashes, fat-tailed returns, volatility clustering, and regime transitions. The framework is also applied to trading signals and cryptocurrency markets, showing its usefulness for interpreting both traditional and digital asset dynamics. Overall, the non-equilibrium agent-based approach provides a flexible mathematical and statistical framework for linking individual trading behavior to market instability.

title: Tail and Ruin Estimates for the Common Poisson Shock Model

detail.title: Tail and Ruin Estimates for the Common Poisson Shock Model
detail.abstract: We consider the Common Poisson Shock model in the context of insurance loss modeling, as introduced in [10], and study the effect of the dependence between severities on the tail of the aggregated loss and on the ruin probability. We obtain asymptotic formulas for both quantities in terms of the spectral measure arising in the context of multivariate extreme value theory [6, 9]. Although the proofs of the results are straightforward, as soon as one realizes the link between our subject and the results in [2, 9, 13], to the author's knowledge, no such studies involving the Common Poisson Shock model have been addressed in the literature, and the consequences seem to be interesting by themselves.

detail.title: Technical Analysis of Fama and French international 25 Size and Book to Market Portfolios
detail.abstract: We test a momentum strategy based on moving averages applied to the Fama and French internaGonal 25 (FF25) porLolios for the U.S., Japan, Europe, Asia Pacific ex-Japan, and Developed ex-U.S. markets. Our analysis reveals that small stocks deliver the strongest returns in the U.S. and Europe, while large stocks yield the highest returns in Japan, Asia Pacific ex-Japan, and Developed markets. We develop a strategy to buy internaGonal FF25 porLolios when the S&P 500 is above its moving average, indicaGng posiGve momentum. We compare the returns with and without this moving average strategy. Our results show that both the U.S. and Japan benefit from using the moving average, with higher returns across all 25 porLolios. However, results are mixed for the remaining markets. We use the Fama and French fivefactor model to explain the excess returns cross-secGonally. The U.S. and Japan exhibit some posiGve and staGsGcally significant excess returns. When applying a 10-period moving average, both porLolios show enhanced performance, with all U.S. porLolios demonstraGng strong and staGsGcally significant results. In contrast, the other markets do not exhibit posiGve and significant excess returns.

detail.abstract:
A payment instrument is an instrument – usually transferrable – which embodies a claim for money of some form on some person, and whose purpose is to be delivered in final settlement of a money obligation. This is the function performed by stablecoins. However, the status of payment instruments within the existing regulatry system is unclear, and this lack of clarity causes difficultes for regulatrs seeking to apply exiting securities and payment regulatory paradigms to cryptoassets generally.

The difference between payment instruments and debt securities is not always immediately apparent – both embody a promise by a person to pay an amount and which is potentially transferrable. These instruments therefore sit in the liminal space between securities and payment regulation. It is fair to say that both securities and payment regulation largely deal with them by ignoring them.  However, the development of crypto stable coins, which are deliberately designed to function as payment instruments, raises a set of policy issues sufficiently important to require a closer examination of this area. This paper examines some of the issues which arise in seeking to fit stablecoins into existing regulatory paradigms. It concludes that attempting to apply the existing securities regulatory model to stablecoins may severely reduce their utility.

title: The Arguments We Stop Making

detail.title: The Arguments We Stop Making
detail.abstract: The legal profession has spent three years worrying about the wrong problem. The fabricated citation is loud, binary, and already policed by the duty of candor; the sanctions docket proves the existing rules work. This Article is about the failure those rules cannot see. Randomized trials across cognitive science, education, and humancomputer interaction keep landing in the same place: large language models steer the people who use them. Users offload thinking and lose skill without feeling the loss. The tools agree too readily, out-persuade expert humans, and nudge different users toward the same output. Every commercial legal AI product runs on a base model tuned by the training step that research implicates. If the profession routes its reasoning through the same three or four tools, the body of legal argument will compress in ways no individual lawyer can detect. Briefs converge, the adversarial clash softens, and the raw material of common-law change (the odd distinction, the losing argument that later wins) thins out. The same tools now draft bills, comment letters, and testimony, so the compression reaches the lawmaking process itself, while price consolidates the market onto the cheapest base models, wherever they come from. The mechanism is established across disciplines; the legal-corpus evidence has not been gathered. This Article maps the research onto the tools lawyers use every day, tests it against the strongest objections on productivity and access to justice, and lays out the empirical study that would settle the question. The danger worth watching is not the argument the machine makes up. It is the argument that quietly stops getting made.

detail.abstract: Farmland has long been both an agricultural resource and a financial asset, yet recent decades have seen new actors and investment logics reshape U.S. farmland markets. Drawing on interviews with landowners, appraisers, farm managers, lenders, and brokers in Iowa, this study examines how stakeholders interpret farmland as an investment. Findings highlight five themes: land's stability and tangibility, evolving return expectations, investor diversity, rental market dynamics, and the role of technology. Results reveal heterogeneity in motivations and practices and suggest implications not only for market behavior but also for extension programming that supports diverse landowners and investors.

title: The Human Signal: Reader-Facing AI Detection, the Disclosure Field, and the Tax on Assisted Authorship

detail.title: The Human Signal: Reader-Facing AI Detection, the Disclosure Field, and the Tax on Assisted Authorship

keywords: New York City Human Rights Law

detail.abstract: In July 2026, Substack integrated a commercial AI detector into its reading surface, letting any reader scan any newly published post and receive an estimate of how much of the text a machine produced, displayed as a percentage beside the author's name. Announcing a funding round the following week, the detection company's chief executive stated the mission in a sentence: "If we do not actively discriminate in favor of human content, then we're just gonna see more and more AI, and it's just gonna drown out any human signal that we have." This Article takes the sentence at its word and asks the question it leaves open: who counts as human when authorship runs through assistive technology. The instrument examined here is the third of its kind, after the invisible watermark and the crowdsourced authenticity flag, and it perfects what the first two began, because it ships with the remedy attached. Beside the detection badge sits a voluntary disclosure field where the author may explain how the work is made. The Article's central claim is that the pairing converts the field into a tax assessed by disability. A nondisabled writer clears an adverse badge with a style preference; a writer whose work runs through dictation software and a language model clears it only by publishing a diagnosis. The exculpatory answer is priced differently for the two populations, silence becomes an answer once the field exists, and rising detector accuracy raises the tax rather than curing it, because the harm was never the error rate. The harm is a taxonomy with no category for assisted authorship, enforced by an increasingly reliable instrument. The Article then shows that every accommodation-shaped repair fails a one-sentence test, since a badge, an exemption tag, or a visible opt-out that permits any inference of disability is itself the disclosure, and it specifies the universal-design remedies that pass. It closes with the doctrine: the screen-out and methods-of-administration provisions of ADA Title III, and the New York City Human Rights Law, which reaches the detection company where it lives.

title: Product Market Power as a Labor Distortion: the Case of Home Production Substitutes
affiliations: ,  and University of North Carolina (UNC) at Chapel Hill

detail.title: Product Market Power as a Labor Distortion: the Case of Home Production Substitutes
detail.abstract: We introduce monopolistic competition in markets for home production substitutes into a model of household time allocation and study the implications for female labor supply. Households in our model consume market goods and home-produced goods; the latter are produced using a combination of the wife's time and home inputs, where the market for home inputs is monopolistically competitive. The resulting markups on home inputs are endogenous and depend on both the elasticity of substitution between products and the home production technology. Markups directly raise the price of outsourcing housework and thereby reduce female labor supply; we show theoretically that markups can also amplify or dampen the effect of other economic forces, such as the cost of home inputs and the gender wage gap. We estimate our model using a combination of time allocation, expenditure, and markup data. Our estimates imply that endogenous markups amplify the labor supply effects of technological progress in housework substitutes by approximately 12%. The framework identifies a distinct channel through which product market power shapes female labor supply, operating through household time allocation.

title: The Latency Frontier: Mapping the Limits of Financial Observability
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Latency Frontier: Mapping the Limits of Financial Observability

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or non-financial interests. This research was conducted independently, without institutional affiliation, external funding, or corporate sponsorship that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This research did not involve human participants, animal subjects, or confidential/personally identifiable data. All empirical analysis was conducted using publicly available financial market data, corporate filings, and aggregate statistics. Therefore, formal ethics approval by an Institutional Review Board (IRB) or equivalent ethics committee was not required.

detail.abstract:
The non-bank financial intermediation sector reached $256.8 trillion in assets in 2024 — 51.0 percent of global financial assets — with private credit alone approaching $2 trillion globally, much of it outside the disclosure regimes governing public markets. Private credit and private equity funds typically report valuations quarterly, on a model-derived basis, rather than continuously. The canonical contagion framework, Eisenberg and Noe (2001), assumes a network's obligations and asset values are fully observable. Mark-to-model reporting violates that assumption structurally: a fund can be insolvent in fact while solvent in every observable record until its next scheduled valuation. This paper formalises that condition as a zombie node, and the interval of non-disclosure as a latency wedge, δᵢ(t).

This paper develops the Granger-Augmented Latency Estimator (GALE), an extension of the Eisenberg-Noe clearing framework: the same fixed-point clearing map evaluated at a corrected input, not a separate procedure placed beside it. GALE estimates the unobservable latency wedge from market behaviour in publicly traded instruments linked to a private fund — BDC equity, regional bank CDS, short-interest and borrow-fee data — without requiring compelled disclosure of private fund positions.

Five subordinate modules extend the baseline estimator, each with an explicit point where it stops working: GALE-K (a state-space filter for delayed or obscured proxy data), GALE-N (a cross-dealer test for exposure fragmentation and circular evergreening), GALE-CB (a covariance-bridging estimator for cases lacking historical depth), GALE-V (Implied Synthetic Volatility, reversing mark-to-model smoothing via liquid credit proxies), and GALE-P (projecting the estimate forward into probability, timing, magnitude, and systemic footprint of a future breach).

The mechanism is examined against six cases: two historical episodes where a public proxy signal preceded official recognition of distress (Wirecard, 2016–2020; First Brands and Tricolor, 2025); one, Archegos (2021), where proxy estimation reaches a rank-deficient identification limit; one live, unresolved case — AI-infrastructure private-credit financing, flagged by the BIS in June 2026 — extending the framework prospectively; and two executable numerical tests, the March 2020 Ares Capital contraction (a full-information baseline) and the March 2023 SVB collapse (testing the state-space extension under degraded data). A panel VAR specification, policy recommendations scoped to existing legal authority, and a comparative survey of four regulatory regimes complete the analysis.

title: Unsealing the Settlements: An Empirical Investigation of Patent litigation and Bargaining

detail.title: Unsealing the Settlements: An Empirical Investigation of Patent litigation and Bargaining
detail.abstract: Out of court settlements are ubiquitous in patent litigation because trials are costly and outcomes uncertain. This is believed to encourage "frivolous" litigation, however the secretive nature of settlement agreements poses a challenge to evaluating the quality of cases filed, and the cost they impose on innovators. I develop a dynamic model of litigation in which the defendant screens out plaintiffs through a series of sequential out-of-court settlement offers, exploiting heterogeneity in the likelihood that cases are dismissed or succeed. Using a newly constructed dataset combining granular information on all U.S. patent infringement cases filed from 2007 to 2022 with data on the parties involved, I estimate my model. This allows me to recover (i) the ex-ante distribution of plaintiffs' probabilities of victory, (ii) the unobserved distribution of settlement amounts and (iii) the relative bias of courts toward plaintiffs versus defendants. I find that patent litigation costs listed defendants over $48.8 billion annually, of which $19.4 billion reflects settlement transfers. Cases brought by patent assertion entities are smaller, lower quality, and more likely to settle for smaller amounts. I then consider two counterfactuals. First, I consider several fee-shifting rules, finding that conditional feeshifting is effective in discouraging frivolous litigation, however it can induce costly delays before settlements. Second, I examine forum shopping and find that limiting plaintiffs' discretion in venue choice would sharply reduce incentives to file low-quality cases, especially in the Eastern District of Texas.

title: Institutions, Technology and Migration: A Case Study of the Early Diffusion of Tractors in Türkiye's Agricultural Sector and Interprovincial Migration

detail.title: Institutions, Technology and Migration: A Case Study of the Early Diffusion of Tractors in Türkiye's Agricultural Sector and Interprovincial Migration
detail.abstract: I exploit differences in land tenure to estimate the effect of the early diffusion of tractors in the Turkish rural sector on interprovincial migration. Ottoman economic institutions persisted into the 1950s, shaping the organization of production. Cultivation in small plots by free peasant households under the Ottoman land regime evolved into the cultivation of larger landholdings under a 50-50 sharecropping system in 20th-century Türkiye. This institutional persistence weakened with distance from the center of the Empire, resulting in regional variation in land tenure. In regions where sharecropping was widespread, tractor adoption was incentivized by the opportunity to substitute costly labor with cheaper automation technology. Thus, farm mechanization transformed the historical organization of production, reducing the labor share in the process, creating a push factor for migration. Exploiting these differences in land tenure, I find large effects of tractor adoption on migration from the least mechanized provinces to more mechanized ones.

title: Quantile Restrictions, Revealed Rankings, and the Limits of Multinomial Choice

detail.title: Quantile Restrictions, Revealed Rankings, and the Limits of Multinomial Choice
detail.abstract:
This paper analyzes when choice probabilities reveal rankings of deterministic utility indices in semiparametric discrete choice models. It begins with binary choice, where quantile thresholds guarantee ranking recovery, and shows that such thresholds can arise either from behavioral departures from utility maximization (e.g., limited attention) under exchangeable unobservables, or from non-exchangeable unobservables under standard utility maximization. These behavioral and distributional routes are then extended to multinomial choice. Under limited attention, balance restrictions on attention probabilities yield global linear ranking partitions which are robust to the distribution of unobservables and, given sufficiently rich joint variation in the differences of utility indices, are also necessary.  Absent the required attention restrictions, opposite rankings can produce overlapping probability images. Under non-exchangeable unobservables, a comparable distribution-uniform partition generally need not exist. 

Holding the distribution fixed, however, ranking recovery remains possible via an injective  nonlinear map from normalized utility differences to choice probabilities under both behavioral and distributional extensions. Together, the results distinguish distribution-robust global ranking partitions from ranking recovery with a fixed distribution of unobservables  and clarify the limits of extending binary quantile restrictions to multinomial choice.

title: Steam Gasification of Poultry Feathers: Syngas Quality Assessment and Process Optimization
affiliations: Robert Gordon University,  FUTEC Engineering Limited,  FUTEC Engineering Limited and  FUTEC Engineering Limited

detail.title: Steam Gasification of Poultry Feathers: Syngas Quality Assessment and Process Optimization
detail.abstract: Poultry feather waste is an abundant protein-rich resource with strong potential for thermochemical conversion into value-added gaseous fuels. In this study, the steam gasification of turkey feathers was investigated using an Aspen Plus equilibrium model to evaluate syngas quality and identify favorable operating conditions. Pine woodchips were simulated as a reference lignocellulosic biomass for comparative assessment. The process model, was validated against published experimental data for pine woodchips gasification, showing good agreement for major syngas species, particularly carbon dioxide (CO2), hydrogen (H2), and carbon monoxide (CO), although methane (CH4) was underpredicted due to equilibrium-model limitations. A total of 6000 simulations were performed over a gasifier temperature range of 700-1100 0C and steam-to-biomass ratio (SBR) range of 0.4-3.0. Results indicate that hydrogen production is mainly controlled by SBR, whereas temperature strongly influences CO formation, methane reforming, and overall enrichment of synthesis-active gases. Increasing SBR enhances H2 production but also increases CO2 formation through the water-gas shift reaction, leading to syngas dilution. Higher temperatures increase the useful syngas fraction (H2 + CO), raise the CO/CO2 ratio, and suppress CH4 formation. Compared with pine woodchips, turkey feathers produced higher fractions of H2 and CO and lower CO2, indicating a more synthesis-rich gas, although higher sulfur species (mainly, hydrogen sulfide) were observed. Optimal operating conditions were identified at approximately 900-1050 0C and SBR of 1.0-2.4, where favorable H2/CO ratios, high useful syngas fractions, and improved CO/CO2 ratios were achieved. These findings demonstrate the potential of poultry feathers as a promising feedstock for hydrogen-rich syngas production.

title: The Global Relay: A Hierarchical Structure of International Information Transmission Originating from the New York Close An Empirical Study on the Asymmetry of Hierarchical Market Efficiency

detail.title: The Global Relay: A Hierarchical Structure of International Information Transmission Originating from the New York Close An Empirical Study on the Asymmetry of Hierarchical Market Efficiency
detail.abstract: A companion pair of papers (Kinoshita, 2026a, 2026b) showed that information available at the New York market's close can predict the direction of the next day's opening move in Asia-Pacific markets. Three things stood out. A simple statistical model, trained only on data available before each Asian market opens, calls next-day direction noticeably more often than a coin flip, and this edge disappears within about a trading day. The information driving it comes from New York's ordinary daytime session, not the overnight move. And across markets and sectors, predictability tracks a target's sensitivity to U.S. stock-market risk-its "beta"-a pattern we call the beta law. This paper asks whether these results are specific to the New York-Asia link, or part of something larger. We find two things. First, the beta law is not a Japan-specific coincidence: it reappears independently in U.S. and European sector data, though it disappears when comparing whole countries rather than sectors within a country-a real boundary on its reach. Second, and more strikingly, when we connect New York, Asia-Pacific, and Europe into a single loop, only one link carries no information once each destination's own recent trend is controlled for: the link running back into New York. Every other link stays clearly alive, including the reverse direction from Europe to Asia. This asymmetry holds regardless of which market anchors the loop, survives standard-error corrections for markets appearing more than once in the data, and reappears in a separate test built on energy-linked stocks and ETFs rather than broad indices. Taken together, these results suggest international stock markets are not simply chained together with information leaking out at each step. Instead, New York behaves like a hub: it originates information for the rest of the world while absorbing almost everything that flows back to it.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Asian Journal of Biotechnology and Bioresource Technology, volume 12, issue 3, 2026[10.9734/ajb2t/2026/v12i3322]

detail.abstract: The selection of an appropriate growing medium is a key factor influencing seed germination, seedlinggrowth, and transplant quality in chilli (Capsicum annuum L.) nurseries. The present study was conductedduring July to September 2020 at Chikka Madhure, Doddaballapur Taluk, Karnataka, India, to evaluate theeffect of different growing media on nursery performance of chilli hybrid 'Devsena-88'. Nine treatmentscomprising different combinations of cocopeat, soil, vermicompost, sand, perlite, and field soil (control) wereevaluated. Observations on days to germination, germination percentage, days to first true leaf appearance, seedling height, stem girth, number of leaves, root length, shoot fresh weight, root fresh weight, and seedlingsurvival were recorded and analysed using an analysis of variance (ANOVA). Significant differences wereobserved among the treatments for all growth parameters. The growing medium consisting of cocopeat:vermicompost: perlite (3:1:1, v/v/v) (T₇) produced the earliest germination (5.8 days), highest germinationpercentage (98%), earliest true leaf emergence (12 days), maximum seedling height (14.5 cm at 28 DAG),greatest stem girth (0.48 cm), highest leaf number (15 leaves plant⁻¹), longest root length (11.5 cm),maximum shoot fresh weight (2.84 g) and root fresh weight (0.78 g), and the highest seedling survival (99%).In contrast, seedlings raised in field soil alone exhibited delayed germination, reduced growth, lower biomassaccumulation, and poor survival. The superior performance of T₇ was attributed to improved aeration,moisture retention, nutrient availability, and enhanced root-zone conditions provided by the combinedsubstrate components. The results indicate that cocopeat: vermicompost: perlite (3:1:1, v/v/v) is an effectivegrowing medium for producing healthy, vigorous, and uniform chilli seedlings suitable for commercialnursery production.

title: The Collective Victim Problem in African Reparatory Justice: Who Holds the Right to Reparation for Historical Wrongs?

detail.title: The Collective Victim Problem in African Reparatory Justice: Who Holds the Right to Reparation for Historical Wrongs?

keywords: African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights

detail.abstract: African reparations discourse has focused largely on whether slavery, colonialism and related historical wrongs generate reparatory obligations under international law. This article addresses a prior and less examined problem: who, in law, is entitled to reparation when the original victims, their communities, contemporary African States, descendants and the African diaspora do not coincide. It develops the concept of the Collective Victim Problem to identify this structural gap and examines whether international law provides a coherent basis for a corresponding Collective Reparatory Entitlement. Drawing on treaty interpretation, the law of State responsibility and African regional human rights jurisprudence, the article identifies doctrinal foundations including Article 21(2) of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights, the collective character of certain protected interests, the doctrine of continuing wrongful acts, and jurisprudence recognising peoples as holders of collective rights and remedies. It concludes that international law does not yet furnish a general concept of the collective historical victim, yet these elements support a differentiated approach where the affected community is historically identifiable and legally cognisable. The African Union's emerging reparations architecture has likewise not resolved questions of entitlement and representation. The article therefore proposes, as a lex ferenda contribution, an African framework linking collective victimhood, reparatory entitlement, representative authority, remedial measures, beneficiary structures and accountability. Its central claim is that the future of African reparatory justice depends not only on establishing historical responsibility, but on constructing a legally determinate relationship between the wrong, the collective entitled to reparation, and the mechanisms through which reparation is delivered.

title: Money Under the Two Constraint States: Monetary Neutrality Reconsidered, the Puzzle of Missing Inflation, and the Macroeconomic Role of Finance

detail.title: Money Under the Two Constraint States: Monetary Neutrality Reconsidered, the Puzzle of Missing Inflation, and the Macroeconomic Role of Finance
detail.abstract: Monetary economics is burdened by a set of puzzles that mainstream theory has been unable to resolve: whether money is neutral, why the massive monetary expansion after 2008 failed to produce the inflation that quantity theory predicted, and why finance-whose centrality the 2008 crisis made undeniable-remains external to the core apparatus of macroeconomic analysis. This paper argues that these are not three separate problems but three manifestations of a single error: mainstream monetary theory mistakes the behavior of money under supply constraint for a universal law. Once the constraint state is identified, the puzzles dissolve. Under supply constraint, new money flows into the production system, manifests as general price inflation, and is approximately neutral in the long run-the world of the quantity theory. Under demand constraint, where productive investment cannot absorb available savings, new money flows instead into the asset system, inflating asset prices without general inflation, and becomes structurally non-neutral-reshaping wealth distribution, cost structures, and the form of crises. The distinction between the production system and the asset system, developed here, gives finance the structural place in macroeconomic analysis that mainstream models have lacked. Money is not a veil over the real economy, nor an autonomous first cause; it is a mirror of the constraint state, and its effects are state-dependent.

title: Cryptocurrency Taxation Policies: International Experiences and Recommendations for Vietnam

detail.title: Cryptocurrency Taxation Policies: International Experiences and Recommendations for Vietnam
detail.abstract: This article examines how Vietnam should tax cryptocurrency and crypto-asset transactions while preserving administrability, legal coherence, and market neutrality. It builds on a Vietnamese-language article published in 2025 and reassesses its comparative recommendations after major changes in Vietnamese law during 2025–2026. The new framework recognizes crypto-assets within the digital-asset taxonomy, establishes a pilot licensed market, excludes core crypto-asset transfers from value-added tax during the pilot, and introduces distinct corporate and individual tax rules supported by platform withholding and transaction reporting. Comparing Vietnam with approaches in the United States, United Kingdom, Australia, Singapore, India, and emerging international reporting standards, the article argues that Vietnam has largely solved the earlier threshold problem of legal recognition but still faces second-generation design questions. These include the incidence of a gross-basis transaction levy, cost-basis and loss recognition, the treatment of staking, mining, airdrops and decentralized finance, and offshore activity. The article recommends retaining compliance-by-design and structured reporting while using pilot data to determine whether the current 0.1 percent levy should remain permanent or evolve toward a more gain-sensitive system.

title: Generative Bayesian Computation: A Proper Scoring Rule Alternative to DCGAN
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and George Mason University

detail.title: Generative Bayesian Computation: A Proper Scoring Rule Alternative to DCGAN
detail.abstract: The deep convolutional generative adversarial network of Radford et al. (2016) fixed a set of architectural conventions that remain in use: strided convolutions in place of pooling, fractionally strided convolutions for upsampling, batch normalisation in both networks, and no fully connected hidden layers. These conventions concern the architecture. The learning signal is a separate object, and it is the learning signal that carries the known pathologies of adversarial training, namely mode dropping, absent uncertainty quantification and sensitivity to the random seed. We show that Radford's generator can be retained verbatim while the discriminator is replaced by a strictly proper scoring rule, which is the Generative Bayesian Computation (GBC) construction of Polson and Sokolov (2023). The resulting estimator is Fisher consistent for the conditional quantile function, admits a Knothe-Rosenblatt transport interpretation, and cannot drop mass without incurring an excess risk that we bound below. In four studies, GBC attains lower calibration error at equal mode coverage on an eight component mixture; on amortised posterior inference with exact ground truth it is roughly seven times closer in W 1 and nominally calibrated, where a conditional GAN covers 58% at nominal 90%; and on a miniature but architecturally faithful DCGAN, holding the generator fixed and varying only the learning signal, the unmodified adversarial arm recovers 4.0 ± 1.6 of eight modes while GBC recovers 8.0 ± 0.0 and halves the energy distance. That advantage does not survive stabilisation: adding spectral normalisation restores full mode coverage to the adversarial arm and gives it both a smaller energy distance and sharper samples than GBC, leaving GBC ahead only on seed to seed variance, by a factor of five to ten. A hybrid arm that adds a critic supplied sharpness term to the score recovers most of the fidelity gap while retaining the best mode balance of any arm. A fourth study isolates a design rule for the quantile path that mattered more than network width. We are explicit about scale: the image study is 16 × 16, and the sharpness deficit of scoring rule training is real and unresolved.

detail.abstract: We investigate the role of information about dividends in expectation formation and price dynamics. We introduce a novel experimental design within the learning-toforecast framework that combines predictions about dividends, modelled as an exogenous stationary variable, with predictions about prices endogenously determined by a positive feedback mechanism. We vary the salience of the dividend across the treatments, with participants able to observe its mean value only, its realized series, or required to forecast it. Our results suggest that the way dividend information is presented shapes whether market prices remain anchored to fundamentals or depart from them. Increasing the salience of the information about dividends significantly changes market dynamics: large and persistent bubbles shrink substantially and prices remain surprisingly stable around the fundamental.

title: Gender, Power, and Technology-Facilitated Gender-Based Violence in Jamaica

detail.title: Gender, Power, and Technology-Facilitated Gender-Based Violence in Jamaica

declarations.ethicsApproval: Secondary data was used.

detail.abstract: This article examines technology-facilitated gender-based violence (TFGBV) in Jamaica as an extension of entrenched gender inequalities and a broader continuum of violence across the life course. Drawing on national data and preliminary findings from a World Bank-commissioned regional study, it explores how online harassment, cyberstalking, non-consensual sharing of intimate images, sextortion, and other digital harms affect women, young people, and LGBTQ+ communities. Particular attention is given to the layered vulnerabilities of lesbian, bisexual, and queer women, whose exposure to digital and offline violence is compounded by discriminatory laws, heteronormative assumptions, and limited access to protection and support. Although Jamaica’s 2026 amendments to the Cybercrimes Act represent important progress, significant legal and institutional gaps remain, including the absence of specific provisions addressing sextortion and threats to publish intimate content, limited platform accountability, inadequate digital forensic capacity, and fragmented survivor-support systems. The article argues that TFGBV is fundamentally a question of power, participation, and justice. An effective response therefore requires gender-responsive and LGBTQ+-inclusive legal reform, stronger institutional coordination, accessible trauma-informed services, improved capacity among justice-sector actors, and early interventions addressing harmful gender norms and violence among young people

declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is a theoretical survey paper that does not involve human subjects, animal research, or any primary data collection requiring ethics approval.
