title: Trump v. Biden Judges - Is the Gap Closing?
affiliations: New York University School of Law and University of Virginia School of Law

detail.title: Trump v. Biden Judges - Is the Gap Closing?

publicationDetails.detailsText: European Corporate Governance Institute – Finance Working Paper Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: European Corporate Governance Institute (ECGI) - Finance Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Curious about the merits of judges Donald Trump appointed in his first term as president, two prior studies examined the performance of his appointees against those of other presidents. On a predetermined set of three measures, the Trump judges performed as well as, if not better than, judges appointed by Presidents Obama and Bush, while President Biden's appointees lagged behind. However, Biden's judicial selections were new to the bench during those initial studies. This paper is a standalone follow-up. It evaluates the 2024-2025 period to answer a lingering question: Would the Biden judges begin to close the gap as they gained seasoning? Preliminary results suggest the gap is closing in key areas, particularly in terms of writing influential opinions. When it comes to writing dissents and concurrences, however, the Trump judges lead by a wide margin.

title: Reinventing The Wheel? Innovation and Borrowing in The New Hungarian Legislation on The Suspension of Citizenship
affiliations: University of Turku

detail.title: Reinventing The Wheel? Innovation and Borrowing in The New Hungarian Legislation on The Suspension of Citizenship
detail.abstract: There has been widespread concern about the recent introduction of the suspension of citizenship in Hungarian law. The new institution has been seen as worrying both from the perspective of the rule of law and the security of rights protections afforded by Hungarian citizenship, and with regard to the general coherence and intelligibility of the concept of suspending citizenship. This article intervenes in the debate on the suspension of citizenship in four ways. First, it describes the new rules on suspension in the context of Hungarian citizenship law. Second, it argues that 'suspension' is best understood as a type of citizenship revocation: both the novelty and the unintelligibility of the concept are strongly overstated. Viewed against the backdrop of a still-expanding European legislative push for denationalization and citizenship revocation, Hungarian laws are, in fact, quite humane and respectful of the right to a nationality. Third, it argues that the new Hungarian laws are nevertheless badly conceived and drafted, resulting in obvious conflicts with EU law on EU citizenship. Finally, the article considers the ways in which suspension interacts with the temporal, spatial and other structural institutions around citizenship.

title: The Effect of Populism on Electoral Promises

detail.title: The Effect of Populism on Electoral Promises
detail.abstract: This study examines whether populist politicians are more likely to fulfill their electoral promises compared to non-populists. Focusing on members of the U.S. House of Representatives from 2016-2020, I develop a novel measure of semantic similarity between electoral platforms and approved laws using various text analysis techniques. Employing a regression discontinuity design to address endogeneity concerns, I analyze 633 electoral platforms and 743 approved laws across three Congresses. My findings suggest a positive and significant correlation between populist rhetoric and promise fulfillment, particularly during Republican-majority sessions. The effect is robust across multiple text vectorization methods, with populist platforms showing 2-3% higher similarity to approved laws. However, this relationship flips when considering only co-sponsored laws, indicating a complex dynamic between populist rhetoric and legislative outcomes. These results are preliminary and need to be corroborated with a wider dataset of platforms and new vectorization techniques in my future research.

title: Crisis and Elite Communication Networks: Evidence from Telegraphs in Late Qing China
affiliations: Wuhan University - Hongyi Honor College

detail.title: Crisis and Elite Communication Networks: Evidence from Telegraphs in Late Qing China
detail.abstract: When do political crises activate communication across elite groups? I study telegrams and letters centered on Li Hongzhang from 1880 to 1901. A triple-difference design compares medium use across political ties and crisis periods within the same communication network. Cross-faction telegram use falls by 2.931 messages per dyad-month during the Sino-Japanese War, when defeat concentrated responsibility around identifiable officials, but rises by 2.968 messages during the Boxer crisis, when provincial decisions became interdependent. The first response coincides with a shift toward same-faction telegrams. The second is concentrated in cross-regional and brokered ties and in more secretive, bargaining-oriented messages. The estimates capture the allocation of realized communication across ties and media, not total interaction among all potential dyads. The findings separate the formation of elite relationships from their use: crises activate ties when the coordination value of speed outweighs the political cost of observable association.

title: Incentive Fragility in Optimistic Resolution Mechanisms
affiliations: Nanyang Technological University, Singapore, Nanyang Technological University (NTU) - Division of Economics,  and Nanyang Technological University (NTU)

detail.title: Incentive Fragility in Optimistic Resolution Mechanisms
detail.abstract: This paper studies the incentive fragility of the report-disputeadjudication oracle architecture adopted by decentralized applications. We formalize such designs into optimistic resolution mechanisms (ORMs) and model settlement as a strategic game between a proposer and potential disputers who face costly verification. Disputers may free-ride, producing a no-challenge equilibrium in which incorrect reports finalize. Adjudication noise further weakens deterrence by lowering the expected return to disputing. We model adjudication as token-weighted voting and derive a concentration-sensitive Hoeffding bound that motivates an empirical Adjudication Risk Index (ARI). Using UMA voting and staking data from 2020-2026, we estimate daily voting correctness and construct event-level and daily ARIs, documenting pronounced time variation and spikes that coincide with periods of increased voting-power concentration. We then show that dynamically subsidizing disputers based on live concentration metrics can restore strict incentive compatibility during high-risk periods.

title: Minimum Effective Scale in Unconventional Monetary Policy: Threshold Effects in the Transmission of Central Bank Balance Sheet Expansion to Banking System Stability

detail.title: Minimum Effective Scale in Unconventional Monetary Policy: Threshold Effects in the Transmission of Central Bank Balance Sheet Expansion to Banking System Stability
detail.abstract: To date, the crosscountry evidence on whether central bank balance sheet expansion strengthens the health of the banking system is still mixed. We argue that this is due to misspecification, rather than weak fundamental effects. Assuming that accommodation needs to penetrate the minimum effective scale before it significantly changes bank funding costs and collateral values, as well as loss-absorption capacity; in such a case, linear estimators will mix inert and active regimes and return attenuated and sample-dependent coefficients. Based on a balanced panel of 33 advanced and emerging economies over 2012-2020, we estimate a fixedeffects panel threshold model following Hansen (1999), with the existence of the threshold assessed through country-clustered wild bootstrap. The threshold is estimated at central bank assets of 4.4 percent of GDP (95 percent confidence region 2.6 to 5.6 percent). Below that scale, accommodation has no detectable effect on bank Z-scores (β = 0.009, p = 0.743), while above that the effect is positive and significant (β = 0.068, p = 0.006), and the Wald test for regime equality is rejected with confidence (χ² = 12.37, p = 0.0004). The threshold existence test is conservative in its design: with 33 clusters, the power of the country-clustered wild bootstrap is quite limited, and it returns p = 0.087 compared to p = 0.020 for the i.i.d. residual bootstrap in the original formulation. We retain the clustered procedure as the main statement, while the comparison is reported as a sensitivity result. The linear and quadratic specifications fail to capture this structure. The Lind-Mehlum test also rejects the interior extremum underlying the inverted-U interpretation. This contrast between regimes persists in the advanced economy sub-sample only, ruling out country-composition confounding, and it does not disappear when Japan or 2020 are excluded. The data suggest that sub-critical purchase programs are unlikely to yield any measurable banking-stability dividends.

title: Enterprise Architecture Frameworks for Cross-Jurisdictional Energy Infrastructure Security Transferability of Regulatory Models Between UK and U.S. Critical Infrastructure Protection
affiliations: University of Liverpool

detail.title: Enterprise Architecture Frameworks for Cross-Jurisdictional Energy Infrastructure Security Transferability of Regulatory Models Between UK and U.S. Critical Infrastructure Protection

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is employed within the UK energy regulatory sector. This research was conducted independently, in a personal capacity, and does not represent the views or position of any employer. The analysis is based entirely on publicly available documents.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: This paper presents a comparative documentary analysis of UK and U.S. energy infrastructure governance, examining published regulatory frameworks, cybersecurity compliance structures, and data governance approaches from Ofgem, FERC, and NERC. The analysis is structured across five dimensions: regulatory structure, enterprise architecture governance, cybersecurity compliance, data sharing mechanisms, and workforce capability. Findings indicate that both jurisdictions published major updates to energy infrastructure governance within months of each other during 2025 and 2026, arriving at similar conclusions independently. The UK’s domain coordinator model and the U.S. standards-based compliance framework each contain transferable elements the other currently lacks. Significant workforce capability gaps inhibit cross-jurisdictional knowledge exchange, particularly in enterprise architecture roles that bridge regulatory expertise with technical infrastructure design. The paper identifies specific transferability pathways and argues that structured programmes of cross-jurisdictional knowledge exchange would strengthen grid security in both countries.

title: Manipulation by Design: Performance Incentives and Adverse Selection in Bureaucracy
affiliations: and Duke University

detail.title: Manipulation by Design: Performance Incentives and Adverse Selection in Bureaucracy
detail.abstract: Performance-based promotion is often seen as meritocratic. We show it can do the opposite. When principals value the effort that promotion incentives elicit over the quality of the bureaucrats they elevate, it becomes rational to tolerate bureaucrats' manipulation of performance metrics. Manipulation drives both weaker and stronger candidates to compete harder, raising aggregate effort while corrupting selection. We formalize this logic and test it in the Chinese bureaucracy, developing a method that recalibrates city-level GDP growth to separate actual performance from manipulation. We find that reported growth predicts promotion but recalibrated growth does not. Instead, promotion is positively associated with overreporting: the system rewarded officials not for capability but for cheating. These findings position manipulation in authoritarian bureaucracies as a feature of incentive design rather than a symptom of weak oversight, and suggest how autocracies can grow without compromising loyalty: by eliciting effort rather than identifying the ablest.

title: Does Digital Registration Formalise or Merely "Platformise" India's Informal Labour Market? A Quasi-Experimental Study of the e-Shram Portal's Impact on Gig Worker Welfare and Labour Mobility

detail.title: Does Digital Registration Formalise or Merely "Platformise" India's Informal Labour Market? A Quasi-Experimental Study of the e-Shram Portal's Impact on Gig Worker Welfare and Labour Mobility
detail.abstract: India's rapidly expanding gig economy has created a policy challenge: workers can be economically active while remaining outside conventional systems of employment protection and social security. This paper investigates whether the e-Shram portal, launched nationally in August 2021 to create a database of unorganised workers, generated substantive improvements in gig-worker welfare or primarily produced a narrower form of administrative formalisation. Using a simulated balanced panel of 400 Indian districts observed annually from 2018 to 2023, the paper exploits cross-district variation in e-Shram registration intensity and estimates continuous-treatment difference-indifferences models with district and year fixed effects. The simulated results indicate statistically significant gains in average daily wages, social-security registration, and platform mobility following higher-intensity registration, but only a small increase in access to formal credit. The estimated effects are approximately 4.8 percent for wages, 4.1 percentage points for social-security registration, and 3.0 points on the mobility index. The credit effect is approximately 1.4 percentage points. The results suggest that digital registration improves administrative visibility and may reduce some information frictions, but registration alone does not generate comprehensive economic security. The policy implication is that e-Shram should be treated as institutional infrastructure that must be connected to portable social-security contributions, financial inclusion, and platform-level obligations rather than as a complete formalisation policy.

title: Macroeconomic Shocks and Dynamics of Labor Markets in Korea
affiliations: Ajou University and Dongduk Women's University

detail.title: Macroeconomic Shocks and Dynamics of Labor Markets in Korea
detail.abstract: A New Keynesian model with labor friction, in which involuntary unemployment can be endogenized, is estimated with the Korean macroeconomic data using a Bayesian estimation approach. The model is extended by specifying a small open economy with tradable and nontradable goods sectors to characterize the Korean labor market empirically. Results of empirical analyses based on the estimated model can be summarized as follows. First, the sectoral reallocation of labor plays an important role in the adjustment of the Korean labor market, which responds to macroeconomic shocks, particularly foreign shocks. Second, the historical decomposition analysis demonstrates that the cyclical fluctuations of unemployment in Korea are explained by key domestic shocks, such as domestic productivity shocks and preference shocks. A relatively small contribution of foreign shocks to aggregate labor market variables is partly caused by the sectoral shift of employment rather than extensive changes in aggregate employment and labor force.

title: Short (Critical) Memo on the Decision of the Maryland Tax Court on the Maryland Digital Advertising Tax
affiliations: University of California, Davis - School of Law

detail.title: Short (Critical) Memo on the Decision of the Maryland Tax Court on the Maryland Digital Advertising Tax
detail.abstract:
This short memo relates to a recent decision of the Maryland tax court striking down Maryland’s digital advertising tax.

I was not involved in drafting the tax nor in the case to defend it, but I have argued that it should be upheld and so the decision is disappointing.  In the press, opponents of the tax have enjoyed chortling about how this decision will undermine similar efforts around the country.  And of course they say that, but I do not think that it is likely true.  As a matter of law, this opinion will only matter in other states if it is persuasive on matters at issue in those states.  (It will not even matter in Maryland if it does not persuade higher courts.). However, this opinion hardly addresses, much less persuasively, the main issues raised by Maryland’s tax, much less the taxes being challenged in Illinois, Utah or Washington.

In this short memo, I will explain why I think this is so by providing my initial abbreviated analysis of the Maryland decision, subject to later revision and expansion.

detail.title: Urban and Rural Differences in Consumer Payments
detail.abstract: Using survey data on consumer payments in the United States, the paper analyzes rural and urban differences in consumer ownership and use of payment methods. Both in-person and remote (not in-person) payments are analyzed. Relative to urban consumers, rural consumers are less likely to own debit and credit cards. The shares of cash and debit card payments made in-person by rural consumers are larger than those of urban consumers. The share of credit card payments is lower. To make remote payments, rural consumers use credit cards less and write more checks relative to urban consumers. Regression and machine learning random forest analyses indicate that differences in consumer use of payment methods are influenced by transaction-specific and individual-specific variables in addition to rural and urban differences.

detail.abstract: We ask whether the optimal size of a city depends on which government's welfare criterion is applied, using 324 Indonesian kabupaten/kota. The agglomeration elasticity is 0.155 for cities and 0.000 for regencies; pooled it is-0.059, because administrative population does not measure urban scale. detail.abstract: Short-horizon reversal and intermediate-horizon momentum are established empirical regularities, but the geometry of the transition between them is not. This paper studies whether return persistence is organized in a joint spectral-state-horizon space even when it cannot be reduced to one universal numerical threshold. For each asset, date, return definition, and horizon, I construct a causal horizon-matched spectral persistence coordinate inspired by the frequency-domain representation of Sepp and Lucic (2026), together with a continuous past-future phase product. Positive conditional phase products denote persistence; negative values denote reversal. Flexible time-out-of-sample spline models reveal horizon-dependent topology but only weak observationlevel discrimination. In raw returns, the exploratory spectral-state-horizon interaction improves mean datewise out-of-sample AUC by 0.00401 relative to an additive spline, with a moving-blockbootstrap 95% interval of [0.000285, 0.007581]. A stronger discovery claim-a common critical horizon beyond which the full spectral domain becomes reversal-only-fails under a frozen disjointuniverse validation, and a read-only forensic audit classifies the result as statistical non-replication rather than implementation failure. The research program then narrows the transported object. The final v10 protocol prospectively freezes a percentile-normalized upper spectral tail, q Ψ ≥ 0.85, a Huber-clipped phase response, dependent-data inference, and a market-specific critical onset. On a previously unseen, pre-bound Nikkei 225 universe, the endpoint passes in both return modes: h c = 96 sessions for local-market-residual returns and h c = 147 for raw returns. The evidence rejects the tested universal scalar-boundary formulations and independently confirms a robust spectral reversal region whose onset varies by market and return definition. The results are consistent with a low-complexity spectral-horizon geometry, but do not claim a formally identified intrinsic dimension for the global phase surface.

title:
Thermodynamic-freezing via Fixed-point Erasure: 

A Mathematical Paradigm for Bypassing Landauer's Limit
affiliations: Universal Standard Axiom Corp

detail.title:
Thermodynamic-freezing via Fixed-point Erasure: 

A Mathematical Paradigm for Bypassing Landauer's Limit
detail.abstract:
This paper introduces Thermodynamic-Freezing via Fixed-Point Erasure, a novel computational paradigm that bypasses Landauer's limit by eliminating information erasure as a computational primitive. Conventional computing architectures dissipate energy at every bit operation, fundamentally bounded by Landauer's Principle (k_B T \ln 2). While emerging analog thermodynamic computing approaches this limit to within \sim 100 k_B T per bit, and reversible computing attempts to bypass it through temporal symmetry (uncomputation), these approaches face severe limitations including storage overhead, quantum time-reversal ambiguities, and geometry-dependent optimal transport constraints.

​By operating on WAD-18 fixed-point arithmetic (W = 10^{18}), the Lambda Optimization Engine structures state transitions as invariant fixed-point mappings rather than destructive boolean logic gates. Non-compliant states are geometrically excluded rather than actively calculated and deleted, achieving logical reversibility without traditional overhead. Convergence is formally proven via the Banach fixed-point theorem as a contraction mapping (\alpha = 0.85), turning NP-hard optimization into deterministic geometric convergence. This mechanism constitutes computational thermodynamic freezing—the system consumes orders of magnitude less energy because it never overwrites data, converging to an invariant equilibrium state with zero steady-state dissipation. This work establishes a foundational shift in computational thermodynamics, providing both a theoretical framework and immediate implementation pathways for classical, neuromorphic, and hardware architectures.

title: U.S. Paris Agreement Exit and Emission Strategy Adjustments
affiliations: VinUniversity

detail.title: U.S. Paris Agreement Exit and Emission Strategy Adjustments
detail.abstract: This paper examines how the 2017 U.S. withdrawal from the Paris Agreement affected corporate emission strategies and the capital-market pricing of climate risk. Using a difference-in-differences (DID) framework that compares U.S. firms to firms in countries that remained committed, I find that the withdrawal significantly reduced Paris alignment among U.S. firms, an effect that builds gradually over three years and is driven by a deceleration of abatement effort rather than higher emissions. The response is strategic: firms relax effort on less visible supply-chain margins while maintaining directly regulated emission performance and avoiding environmental controversies. These effects are more pronounced in capital-intensive, high-salience sectors and are partially offset by domestic institutional ownership. In capital markets, the rewards to alignment are state-dependent: the ESG-rating, accounting-performance, and cost-of-capital benefits of alignment weaken or disappear after the withdrawal, and sustained alignment switches from a return-reducing hedge to a positive return premium. The 2021 re-entry produces no detectable realignment once pandemic effects are removed, indicating that the credibility damage is not readily reversible. Our results enrich the climate-finance literature by isolating the policy-credibility channel from intrinsic firm risk and by documenting the asymmetry between the destruction and restoration of climate-policy credibility.

title: Liability of Banks in Online Banking Fraud: Need for a Stronger Consumer Protection in India
affiliations: and CHRIST ( deemed to be) University

detail.title: Liability of Banks in Online Banking Fraud: Need for a Stronger Consumer Protection in India
detail.abstract:
With the advent of digital banking in India, driven by technologies such as Unified Payments Interface (UPI), mobile banking, and internet-based financial services has led to significant transformation in the Indian banking landscape. Although, these developments have enhanced convenience, accessibility and financial inclusion, but it has also led to a sharp increase in banking fraud. Cases of phishing, vishing, malware attacks and unauthorized transactions have highlighted concerns about the security and reliability of digital payment platforms. One of the key challenges in this context is the uncertainty over liability in online banking services. The determination of whether the financial burden should fall on banks or customers remains a complex legal and regulatory issue. Although the Reserve Bank of India has introduced guidelines in 2017 on capping the consumer liability but practical difficulties persist in their implementation, particularly in determining the negligence of the customer and effective redressal of complaints.

 This paper aims to critically examine the legal framework governing bank liability in India by analyzing statutory provisions and judicial precedents to evaluate the adequacy of existing consumer protection mechanisms, as the current framework provides for a foundational structure for addressing digital fraud, but there still remains a significant gap in enforcement, consumer awareness and inconsistency in the determination of liabilities. In order to comprehend the complexities which surrounds the UPI-related fraud by closely examining the nature of the risks it poses. It critically evaluates whether the existing regulatory safeguards are sufficient to protect customers and proposes practical solutions to address this by highlighting the need for strong measures and more effective implementations of existing safeguards.

title: Structural Financial Counterfactual Explanations for AI-driven Portfolio Allocation
affiliations: T A Pai Management Institute

detail.title: Structural Financial Counterfactual Explanations for AI-driven Portfolio Allocation
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence has become increasingly important in quantitative portfolio management, enabling deep learning models to capture complex nonlinear relationships between macroeconomic conditions and asset allocation decisions. Despite their predictive capability, these models often operate as black boxes, limiting transparency and reducing practitioner trust in high-stakes financial decision-making. Counterfactual explanations provide an attractive mechanism for explaining model behavior by identifying minimal input modifications that alter model predictions. However, existing counterfactual generation methods typically optimize over unrestricted feature spaces, frequently producing economically implausible market scenarios that lack practical value for institutional portfolio management. This paper proposes a financially constrained counterfactual explanation framework for AI-driven portfolio allocation. Counterfactual generation is formulated as a constrained optimization problem over economically actionable macro-financial variables while enforcing historical feasibility throughout the optimization process. Unlike unconstrained optimization, the proposed framework restricts interventions to the Federal Funds Rate, Yield Curve Slope, and market volatility, generating economically meaningful explanations that remain consistent with historically observed market behavior. Experiments conducted on 934 out-of-sample historical market observations demonstrate that the proposed framework substantially reduces intervention dimensionality relative to unconstrained counterfactual generation. Compared with an unconstrained gradientbased optimizer, the proposed approach reduces the average number of modified variables from 9.73 to 3.00, while the counterfactual success rate decreases from 57.17% to 19.27%. An ablation study further demonstrates that jointly optimizing multiple macro-financial variables substantially improves feasible recourse relative to singlevariable interventions. The results highlight the trade-off between optimization flexibility and financial realism and demonstrate the importance of incorporating domain constraints into counterfactual explanations for quantitative portfolio management.

title: Speed of Intervention in Algorithmic Markets: Controlling Collusion and Stability
affiliations: , University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and Imperial College Business School

detail.title: Speed of Intervention in Algorithmic Markets: Controlling Collusion and Stability
detail.abstract: Algorithmic pricing is prevalent in online marketplaces, raising concerns that learning algorithms may sustain supracompetitive outcomes. We study two sellers in a repeated Prisoner's Dilemma who delegate decisions to memoryless value-based learning algorithms. A platform steers demand toward sellers choosing the more competitive action. Using a fluid approximation, we characterize how intervention intensity, learning architecture, and implementation speed determine market dynamics. Stronger intervention lowers cooperation levels at the fixed point. Algorithmic responsiveness determines the location of stationary outcomes, while action-dependent learning rates determine their local stability. As intervention intensifies, the fixed point can lose stability through a Hopf bifurcation and its local basin of attraction shrinks as the stability threshold is approached. Consequently, an abrupt intervention may leave inherited Q-values outside the target's local basin of attraction and lead to persistent oscillations, whereas gradual intervention leads to a stable market outcome. We also derive local bounds on implementation speed and rollout time. Our results show that platform regulation of algorithmic collusion may require choosing not only how much to intervene, but also how quickly to implement the intervention relative to the algorithms' learning dynamics.

title: Economic Interpretation of Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors in S&P 500 Correlation Matrix via Marchenko-Pastur Law

detail.title: Economic Interpretation of Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors in S&P 500 Correlation Matrix via Marchenko-Pastur Law
detail.abstract: By applying the Marchenko-Pastur law from Random Matrix Theory to the Pearson correlation matrix of daily logarithmic returns for 474 S&P 500 stocks from 2013-2018, groups of correlated stocks can be distinguished from random fluctuations. With N = 474 assets over T = 1,258 time periods (Q ≈ 0.377), the eigenvalues of the correlation matrix should fall in the range of [0.15, 2.60] for a random matrix. The correlation matrix yielded 15 eigenvalues exceeding the upper Marchenko-Pastur bound, 3.2% of total eigenvalues, accounting for ≈ 50% of the total eigenvalue sum, versus an expected 0% under randomness. All eigenpairs can be interpreted as an eigenportfolio with each stock's weight determined by its eigenvector component. Because the eigenvalue equals the eigenportfolio's variance, larger eigenvalues should correspond to stronger co-movement and therefore higher magnitudes of correlation among the top-loading stocks. The largest eigenvalue (λ_0 = 141.07, 29.8% of total eigenvalue sum) is interpreted as a broad market factor, with top-loading stocks spanning diversified companies, suggesting correlation driven by macroeconomic moves. A large proportion of significant eigenvalues correspond to industry clustering (utilities, regional banks, airlines), while the remainder likely reflect event-driven correlation or economic linking between business models that causes correlation. These results demonstrate that a physics-derived theorem provides a null hypothesis for matrix randomness and an approximate quantitative threshold for separating correlation from noise in financial markets. Significant eigenpairs identified by the Marchenko-Pastur threshold correspond to economically coherent groups of correlated stocks, bridging the Marchenko-Pastur law with observable market fundamentals over the 2013-2018 period.

title: Banking on Supply Chain Decarbonisation: A Case Study on Scope 3 Emissions Management in Purchased Goods and Services at BNY

It does not represent the views or positions of BNY or its Sustainability teams. The research drew on interviews with BNY subject matter experts and on data approved for external use. While the report endeavoured to maintain objectivity and minimise bias, the author’s employment relationship with the case study institution is acknowledged as a source of potential bias, and readers should weigh the findings accordingly.

detail.abstract: Carbon accounting methods for purchased goods and services were designed around supply chains that produce physical things. Financial institutions do not have such supply chains, and the resulting mismatch has left Scope 3 Category 1 among the least consistently reported categories in the sector, despite Scope 3 accounting for the substantial majority of financial sector emissions. This paper examines Category 1, Purchased Goods and Services (PG&S), through a case study of BNY, a global custodian bank whose supply chain is composed almost entirely of purchased services. Benchmarking across a peer group of custodians and universal banks establishes that PG&S disclosure is fragmented and that BNY does not currently carry the category into its primary sustainability reporting. Publicly disclosed expenditure indicates that its purchased inputs are concentrated in technology and professional services, with technology both the largest and the fastest growing component. A comparative review of greenhouse gas standards identifies the GHG Protocol, PCAF, and TCFD as the most relevant frameworks for the sector, though none is designed for service- heavy institutions. Drawing on a high-level internal review of BNY’s calculation approach and supplier data landscape, the paper argues that of the four calculation methodologies the GHG Protocol specifies for this category, the hybrid approach offers the most workable balance between accuracy and data availability, that location-based emission factors provide a defensible baseline where spend-based estimation is unavoidable, and that market-based factors should be applied only selectively and under stated conditions. Supplier maturity emerges as the variable governing which methods are available in practice. Supplier engagement, procurement design, and contractual mechanisms are assessed as levers, while the evidence base for supply chain mapping is found to derive predominantly from goods-heavy sectors and to transfer only selectively to service supply chains. The paper concludes that effective management of PG&S emissions depends less on any single framework or technology than on combining pragmatic data solutions with supplier partnerships, procurement choices, and sustained institutional commitment.

title: A Structured Framework for Improving Digital Transformation Maturity in Food Supply Chains
affiliations: Cranfield University - School of Management, Cranfield University and Cranfield University

detail.title: A Structured Framework for Improving Digital Transformation Maturity in Food Supply Chains
detail.abstract: Purpose: Digital transformation is the transition from traditional to digital supply chains, enabled by emerging technologies. A digital transformation maturity assessment is necessary to manage this transition effectively. However, existing maturity frameworks for digital transformation in supply chains lack a structured process with detailed actions guiding maturity improvement. This research, therefore, develops a digital transformation maturity improvement framework with evidence from food supply chains (FSCs). Design/methodology/approach: In-depth case studies conducted in two food companies were used to gain insights into the digital transformation journey. Adopting Diffusion of Innovation (DOI) theory, a seven-step maturity improvement process was established, taking into account context-specific influences. Insights obtained from 32 FSC practitioners through a workshop were used to confirm the framework and identify additional improvement actions. Findings: The developed prescriptive digital transformation maturity improvement framework presents a circular improvement process, beginning with an evaluation of the current digital transformation status and progressing through the seven steps (initiation planning, alignment, preparation, configuration, pilot testing, scaling, and sustaining), followed by re-evaluation to support continuous improvement. The identified internal and external contextual influences highlight their relevance to FSCs. Step-specific actions are provided for advancing digital transformation maturity. Originality/value: This study extends the application of DOI theory to develop a maturity improvement process for digital transformation in FSCs. It enriches the understanding of DOI by emphasising the 'sustaining' step, which aims to maintain achieved maturity levels and accommodate the evolving nature of digital supply chains.

title: Institutional Protection and Organizational Resilience under Chinese Competition

detail.title: Institutional Protection and Organizational Resilience under Chinese Competition
detail.abstract: The United States and the European Union answered the rise of subsidized Chinese competition in electric vehicles with markedly different policy architectures. The central claim of this paper is that protection differs not only in strength but in the mechanism through which it shapes firms' adaptive capabilities. The paper argues that the familiar framing (stronger versus weaker) obscures the variable that governs long-run resilience: whether a protection regime preserves the selective pressure that forces organizations to adapt. Drawing on the MRRM model and the concept of organizational entropy, it builds a typology of protection regimes by mechanism (passive, adaptive and capability-building) and applies it to the 2024-2025 responses of the United States and the European Union. The American trajectory shifted from the capability-building logic of the Inflation Reduction Act toward a more isolating posture of prohibitive tariffs and withdrawn demand support; the European Union combined calibrated, rules-based countervailing duties with continued openness to inbound Chinese investment. The paper advances a falsifiable hypothesis requiring testing: regimes that remove external pressure without relocating it internally accelerate the accumulation of organizational entropy among protected incumbents. The effect is illustrated downstream through the case of the US dealer sector. Explicit falsification tests and practical implications close the paper.

title: Simulating Stress Laws under Extremal Dependence: Characterizing What Generative Models Must Preserve
affiliations: Indian Institute of Management Bangalore and Indian Institute of Management (IIMB), Bangalore

detail.title: Simulating Stress Laws under Extremal Dependence: Characterizing What Generative Models Must Preserve
detail.abstract: We study stress-scenario generation for systems driven by multivariate heavy-tailed risk factors. Within regions where several financial losses are simultaneously extreme, stress analysis concerns both the conditional law of the risk factors and the most plausible configurations producing those losses. We show that both are governed by the same limiting tail law. Preserving its measure recovers rare-event probabilities and scaled conditional stress laws, while misspecifying extremal dependence distorts some regular joint-stress probability. Its density governs reverse-stress optimization, whose maximizers identify the most plausible stress configurations. To exploit this common structure in finite samples, we develop SSGEN (Self-Similar Generative Estimation), which learns extremal dependence from intermediate exceedances and extrapolates to rarer levels using a Pareto radial component. Even when the target event is absent from the sample, we establish convergence rates for the generated conditional law, and data-driven reverse-stress solutions.

title: After the Apocalypse? Preterism, Alexandrian Eschatology, and the Future of Coptic Orthodox Theology

detail.title: After the Apocalypse? Preterism, Alexandrian Eschatology, and the Future of Coptic Orthodox Theology
detail.abstract: New Testament apocalyptic discourse repeatedly announces imminent fulfillment, yet the Coptic Orthodox Church continues to confess a future resurrection, judgment, and Parousia. Partial Preterism resolves this tension by locating much of that discourse, including substantial portions of the Olivet Discourse, within the first-century horizon of Jerusalem's destruction, while leaving final consummation future. This article argues that Coptic Orthodox theology need not adopt Preterism to answer the exegetical problem it identifies, because the Alexandrian tradition already possesses the hermeneutical resources to do so. Reading Origen, Athanasius, and Cyril of Alexandria alongside the Coptic Church's creedal and liturgical eschatology, the article constructively develops a model termed Alexandrian realized-futurist eschatology, in which historical fulfillment, christological-ecclesial realization, and eschatological consummation are held together rather than treated as competing alternatives. The article's contribution is this constructive retrieval: a distinctly Coptic grammar for confessing that, in Christ, the end has begun without claiming that it is exhausted.

title: A Multidimensional Framework for Assessing Territorial Vulnerability to Gender-Based Violence in the Ecuadorian Amazon
affiliations: Universidad Católica del Ecuador

detail.title: A Multidimensional Framework for Assessing Territorial Vulnerability to Gender-Based Violence in the Ecuadorian Amazon
detail.abstract: Gender-based violence (GBV) is a multidimensional phenomenon shaped by socioeconomic inequalities, territorial conditions, gender norms, institutional capacity, and exposure to environmental and social stressors. This study aimed to develop and empirically assess a multidimensional framework for measuring territorial vulnerability to GBV in Gonzalo Pizarro Canton, Ecuadorian Amazon. A quantitative, cross-sectional analytical study was conducted using 299 valid questionnaires. Territorial vulnerability was operationalized through three dimensions: territorial risk perception (TRP), structural vulnerability (SV), and territorial protection capacity (TPC). Indicators were normalized to a 0-1 scale and aggregated using equal weighting to construct the Territorial Vulnerability Index for Gender-Based Violence (TVI-GBV). Internal consistency, confirmatory factor analysis, distributional diagnostics, between-group comparisons, effect sizes, and robustness across parametric and non-parametric procedures were examined. The instrument demonstrated high internal consistency (Cronbach's α = 0.918; McDonald's ω = 0.926). Significant sex-based differences were identified across TRP, SV, and TPC, with the strongest effect for TRP (d = 0.744), followed by SV (d = 0.424) and TPC (d = 0.285). Governance (d = 0.878), inequality (d = 0.674), and economic conditions (d = 0.641) showed substantial differentiation. Findings remained robust across Student's t, Welch's t, and Mann-Whitney U tests. The framework provides a promising basis for territorially targeted, gender-responsive prevention and governance strategies.

title: From Innovation Drivers to Regional Patterns: A Hybrid Econometric and Machine Learning Framework
affiliations: Dyrecta Lab - Istituto di Ricerca, eCampus University and Lum University Giuseppe Degennaro - Lum Enterprise s.r.l.

detail.title: From Innovation Drivers to Regional Patterns: A Hybrid Econometric and Machine Learning Framework
detail.abstract: This study develops an integrated Explain–Predict–Classify framework to investigate the determinants, territorial heterogeneity, and predictability of regional innovation performance. Using Regional Innovation Scoreboard data for 246 regional units across 31 European countries over 2016–2023, the analysis combines panel-data econometrics, unsupervised clustering, and supervised machine-learning regression. The Summary Innovation Index (SII) is examined alongside indicators capturing scientific collaboration, non-R&D innovation expenditure, SME product and process innovation, collaborative networks, design applications, innovative sales, and environmental conditions. Econometric results show positive and statistically significant associations across all selected innovation dimensions. The Hausman test favors fixed effects over random effects, while the dynamic specification indicates significant persistence in regional innovation performance, although instrument-validity diagnostics require caution. The clustering analysis compares six algorithms using multiple internal validation criteria. K-Means provides the strongest overall solution, with R² = 0.6301, a Calinski–Harabasz index of 370.60, and relatively balanced cluster sizes, revealing ten heterogeneous and partially overlapping regional innovation profiles. The predictive analysis compares seven regression algorithms. K-Nearest Neighbors achieves the strongest test performance (R² = 0.9482; RMSE = 7.90; MAE = 4.793), followed by Random Forest (R² = 0.9289). Permutation importance identifies international scientific co-publications, design applications, and SME collaboration as the most influential KNN predictors. Overall, the findings demonstrate that regional innovation combines common systematic relationships with heterogeneous territorial configurations and nonlinear predictive structures. Integrating econometrics, clustering, and machine learning therefore provides a richer empirical basis for understanding regional innovation and designing differentiated, place-sensitive innovation policies.

title: Robustness Over Efficiency: A Design Principle for Climate Policy Coalitions

detail.title: Robustness Over Efficiency: A Design Principle for Climate Policy Coalitions
detail.abstract:
International climate cooperation has failed to build coalitions that include both energy importers and exporters because existing instruments offer exporters only exit, not adaptation. The failure is architectural rather than political: existing instruments rest on assumptions about institutional stability that international climate cooperation does not satisfy. Climate policy thus faces a design choice between maximizing allocative efficiency under idealized institutional conditions and accepting efficiency losses in exchange for robustness under fragile conditions. The paper develops the resulting trade-off as an explicit design axis between allocative efficiency and institutional robustness. Against the most sophisticated alternative at the efficiency end (the clean-up certificates of Lessmann, Gruner, Kalkuhl, and Edenhofer), it argues that current institutional conditions favour the robust instrument proposed here: a carbon currency system in which units of currency are required at the points where fossil carbon enters the economic system (upstream capture), are extinguished upon surrender rather than re-traded (destruction principle), and are governed as quantities rather than processes (technology-neutral regulation), opening an adaptation pathway also for petroleum-exporting states. Enforcement operates through market price differentials, and governance is disaggregated across four specialized institutions complemented by an intergenerational future damages reserve. The efficiency–robustness axis applies beyond climate policy since the design principle is general. AI disclosure: This article was prepared with the assistance of an AI system
(Anthropic Claude), used under the author's direction as an interactive research and drafting tool; the author takes full responsibility for the
content.

title: A Survey of Simulation in Finance: Data, Methods, Applications, and Evaluation
affiliations: , Fudan University, Wuhan University, Wuhan University, Nanjing University, Wuhan University, Wuhan University, Wuhan University, Wuhan University, Wuhan University, Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence, McGill University, Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence, Wuhan University, Wuhan University and The University of Manchester

detail.title: A Survey of Simulation in Finance: Data, Methods, Applications, and Evaluation
detail.abstract: Simulation has long been an important tool in finance, from Monte Carlo pricing and risk analysis to artificial markets and agent-based models. Recent advances in high-frequency data, reinforcement learning, deep generative models, and large language model (LLM) agents have substantially expanded the scope of financial simulation. Contemporary studies no longer use simulation only to approximate price paths or evaluate portfolios; they increasingly construct interactive market environments, synthetic limit order books, heterogeneous trading populations, user simulators, and multi-agent financial decision systems. This survey reviews the emerging literature on simulation in finance through four dimensions: the financial problems being simulated, the datasets and environments used to support simulation, the methodological paradigms adopted by existing studies, and the evaluation protocols used to assess realism and performance. Based on a structured review table covering market simulators, agent-based models, LLM-based financial agents, reinforcement-learning environments, and generative market models, we propose a taxonomy of financial simulation research and identify major open challenges, including benchmark fragmentation, limited data availability, simulation-to-reality gaps, and the difficulty of evaluating agent behavior in complex financial systems.

title: Resource-Adaptive Primal-Dual Learning for One-Warehouse Multi-Store Systems with Censored Demand

detail.title: Resource-Adaptive Primal-Dual Learning for One-Warehouse Multi-Store Systems with Censored Demand
detail.abstract: The one-warehouse multi-store (OWMS) system is a fundamental inventory network in which a nonreplenishable warehouse allocates shared stock across multiple stores over time. Existing OWMS learning policies are built around a fixed target calibrated to the initial average resource rate, but such a fixed-target architecture cannot re-center after realized sales change the remaining resource available per future period. We develop Resource-Adaptive Primal-Dual Learning, a new learning framework that tracks the primal-dual resolving path with censored demand as the remaining-resource state evolves. In each period, the current resource rate indexes the target store allocations and dual variable, while censored sales provide gradient estimates for updating both. The analysis combines expected-sales geometry with a moving-target argument to yield logarithmic expected regret, improving on the state-of-the-art square-root-order guarantees of existing OWMS learning policies. The underlying design and analytical ideas may inform other online learning problems with depleting shared resources. Numerical experiments further demonstrate good finite-horizon performance of a practical variant across different horizon lengths and inventory regimes.

title: Kingdom, Government, Glory: Leadership as Apparatus

detail.title: Kingdom, Government, Glory: Leadership as Apparatus

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that she has no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this article.

detail.abstract: Leadership research has not converged on a stable object. This article treats that nonconvergence as a philosophical problem concerning the kind of thing leadership is. Drawing on Agamben's distinct analyses of auctoritas and potestas and of Kingdom, Government, and Glory, it reconstructs leadership as an apparatus composed of three heterogeneous organizational functions: a position that represents organizational unity, distributed conduct through which the organization operates, and an attribution function through which accomplishment becomes legible and is gathered around the represented center. The reconstruction brings otherwise competing leadership literatures into relation as accounts of different functions. It also distinguishes recognition, misrecognition, and non-registration. Non-registration occurs when the organizational account generates no relation between a contributor and a contribution and therefore cannot be remedied by reassigning an existing record. The apparatus renders organizational action legible through position, conduct, and attribution, but it does not exhaust the situated actor's continuing relation to what is at stake. Arendt's account of beginning, carrying through, bearing, and executing recovers a vocabulary for this limit. Leadership emerges not as a single object awaiting a better definition, but as the name given to a machine whose coordinated functions have been studied separately.

title: Institutional Knowledge and Learning: Preserving Reasoning across Generations

detail.title: Institutional Knowledge and Learning: Preserving Reasoning across Generations

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This conceptual paper did not involve human participants, animals, or identifiable personal data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Institutions preserve extensive records of transactions, ownership, authority, contracts and formal decisions. They are less capable of preserving the reasoning through which those records became institutionally meaningful. Minutes may show what was approved without explaining which assumptions supported the decision, which alternatives were rejected, which trade-offs were accepted or which future conditions were expected to trigger reconsideration. As office-holders, advisers, providers and technologies change, the formal structure may survive while the knowledge required to understand and govern it gradually disappears. This paper develops a distinction among institutional data, records, knowledge, reasoning and learning. Data identifies facts. Institutional knowledge explains how structures operate and why they exist. 

Institutional reasoning applies that knowledge to proposed action under changing conditions. Institutional learning occurs only when experience changes the framework through which future decisions are evaluated. The paper introduces institutional forgetting as a structural process rather than a simple failure of storage. Forgetting may occur through succession, outsourcing, technological migration, procedural ritualisation, selective documentation and loss of the questions that originally made institutional information meaningful. The deepest form of forgetting arises where records remain accessible but can no longer be interpreted competently. To address this problem, the paper proposes the Institutional Reasoning Record, or IRR. It is designed to support succession, post-execution review and cumulative institutional learning without allowing historical reasoning to become binding authority. Technology and artificial intelligence may support retrieval, comparison and reconstruction. They cannot determine institutional purpose, decide which inherited assumptions remain legitimate or replace the responsibility of lawful successors. The paper's contribution is to define institutional learning as an architectural capability through which preserved reasoning informs, but does not control, future judgment.

title: The BEVRA Framework: A Proposed Conceptual Framework for Employee Belonging, Empowerment, Value, Retention, and Advancement toward Sustainable Organizational Performance

detail.title: The BEVRA Framework: A Proposed Conceptual Framework for Employee Belonging, Empowerment, Value, Retention, and Advancement toward Sustainable Organizational Performance
detail.abstract: Employee retention is an increasingly important concern for organizations seeking to maintain workforce continuity, organizational capability, employee well-being, and sustainable performance. Existing research provides substantial insight into individual factors associated with employees' workplace experiences and decisions to remain, including organizational belonging, psychological empowerment, perceived organizational support, organizational commitment, career development, and workrelated well-being. However, these constructs are frequently examined through separate theoretical perspectives, creating an opportunity for a more integrated approach to understanding sustainable organizational membership. This conceptual paper introduces the BEVRA Framework, a proposed people-centered framework comprising five interconnected dimensions: Belonging, Empowerment, Value, Retention, and Advancement. The framework further positions employee wellbeing and work-life balance as foundational conditions supporting sustainable participation in organizational life. BEVRA proposes that employees' experiences across these dimensions may contribute to retention orientation, workforce continuity, and, under appropriate organizational conditions, sustainable organizational performance. The framework is intended to provide a structured foundation for future research and potential organizational application. At its present stage, BEVRA is conceptual and has not yet been empirically tested or validated. The researcher and creator of the framework intends to conduct subsequent empirical and practical studies involving employees, HR specialists, HR managers, senior HR professionals, and other relevant HR practitioners who work directly with employees. These studies will test the framework's measurement properties, dimensional structure, proposed relationships, predictive capacity, and practical applicability. Consequently, the present paper establishes the theoretical foundation for a continuing program of empirical testing, practical evaluation, evidencebased refinement, and subsequent independent validation

title: Intelligence as Loop Performance
affiliations: Astrala Advisory Services Ltd

detail.title: Intelligence as Loop Performance
detail.abstract: Intelligence, in the richer practical sense, is the observable pattern by which a person sustains control loops between accepted aims and environment under conditions of disturbance, including the higher-order capacity to revise aims when outcomes persistently disconfirm them. The essay distinguishes this loopperformance account from the psychometric conception of intelligence as a battery of measurable dispositions, while granting the statistical reality and practical utility of constructs such as g. Three axes of critique are developed. Methodologically, factor analysis summarises covariation among selected tests and cannot, by extraction alone, observe temporal control under disturbance. Historically, modern testing matured within industrial-modernist sorting problems and privileged cognitive operations suited to bureaucratic and technical labour. Culturally, what counts as intelligent competence is relational to the forms of life a community values, as comparative and cultural work on intelligence indicates, without collapsing the phenomenon into mere social attribution. Theoretical warrant is drawn from Perceptual Control Theory, MacIntyre's account of practical rationality, Global Workspace Theory as a possible neural-level account of discrepancy broadcast, and Layered Intelligence Theory as an integrative architectural layer. Implications for measurement favour disciplined biographical reconstruction alongside, rather than instead of, psychometric evidence. Section 8 examines the developmental possibility opened when artificial systems redistribute g-loaded cognitive labour, and the architectural distinction between scaffold and substitute. The domain claim is that intelligence is a real observable phenomenon, describable in control-theoretic terms: neither a hidden universal capacity read directly from a score, nor a mere social attribution conferred at will.

title: Knowing When to Disagree with AI: Override Selectivity as a Strategic Decision Capability

detail.title: Knowing When to Disagree with AI: Override Selectivity as a Strategic Decision Capability

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study reanalyzes previously released anonymized research datasets. No new human participants were recruited for the present study. MSOD v1.0 contains no collected participant responses. Accordingly, no new human-participant data collection was conducted as part of this research.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Human oversight of artificial intelligence (AI) is often evaluated by how much people rely on algorithms. That framing misses a more difficult strategic question: whether disagreement occurs when it should. We develop override selectivity as the capacity to allocate human resistance to cases in which the human has an observed comparative advantage while permitting AI correction when AI has the advantage. The behavioral diagnostic is the Override Selectivity Index (OSI), the difference between override rates in these two conflict states. We ground the upstream representation boundary in Discovery Plane Theory (DPT) and the downstream consequence boundary in Experience Architecture (EA), while keeping both formal frameworks distinct from the behavioral measure. We reanalyse two independent human–AI experiments comprising 5,810 real trial-level decisions from 381 participants. Loan decisions show anti-selective disagreement (OSI = −.095, participant-bootstrap 95% CI [−.152, −.037]), whereas chess decisions show positive selectivity (OSI = .292, 95% CI [.228, .350]). Participant-clustered models reproduce this divergence. We then use FiFAR as a synthetic-expert learning-to-defer benchmark and validate the Managerial Strategic Override Dataset (MSOD) v1.0 as a prospective causal instrument with 10 strategic cases, eight factorial conditions, 80 unique stimuli, and zero AI-criterion assignment mismatches. MSOD contains no collected manager responses, so no behavioral claims are drawn from it. The combined evidence suggests that the strategic value of human oversight lies not in retaining a veto, but in learning when that veto is informationally justified.

title: Bank Specialization within Production Networks
affiliations: Tilburg University, Tilburg University and KU Leuven - Department of Accountancy, Finance and Insurance (AFI)

detail.title: Bank Specialization within Production Networks
detail.abstract: Using firm-to-firm transaction and credit registry data from Belgium, we show that banks' common lending to supply chain partners is persistent and widespread. To study the benefits and costs of this lending specialization along supply chains, we develop and estimate a structural model of credit demand and supply in imperfectly competitive markets, where firms are connected through the production network. Our estimation results reveal that firms prefer to borrow from the same bank as their suppliers or customers, which gives common lenders market power and enables them to charge higher markups. At the same time, the network effects of common lending give banks an incentive to offer lower interest rates to maintain their role as common lenders. Exploiting the closure of a large manufacturing plant as an exogenous shock, we show that common lending also creates costs: the shock propagates through the production network, reducing credit demand along the supply chain and among common lenders, with banks more exposed to the affected network experiencing significantly larger declines in lending. A simulated counterfactual shows that the preference for borrowing from common lenders shapes how the losses are distributed across banks, concentrating them on the banks that lend directly to the disrupted firm and have a high exposure to the network.

title: Past Exposure, Future Innovation: CEO Board Experience and AI Innovation *
affiliations: University of Southampton, University of Southampton, University of Southampton and University of Southampton

detail.title: Past Exposure, Future Innovation: CEO Board Experience and AI Innovation *
detail.abstract: Why do otherwise similar firms differ in their ability to convert technological opportunities into innovation? This paper studies whether one explanation lies in CEO prior exposure to innovation at other firms where they previously served on boards. Linking BoardEx employment histories to USPTO AI patents, we construct grant-based measures of CEO external AI innovation exposure. Firms led by CEO with greater external AI innovation exposure subsequently produce more AI Innovation, robust to firm, CEO and industry-year controls, and the relation is specific to AI rather than general patenting. Event studies around CEO turnover, comparing firms with similar pre-turnover innovation potential, show that the arrival of exposed CEO is followed by increases in both AI Innovation Filings and AI Innovation, with no evidence of pre-existing filing trends. The effect is stronger in firms with greater absorptive capacity, and exposed insider and outsider CEO transitions have similar effects. Exposed CEO are also associated with the reallocation of AI inventors to the firm, including from firms on whose boards they previously served, and give rise to first-time AI inventors at the firm. The findings show that technology-specific CEO exposure is a form of managerial human capital that helps firms transform frontier technological opportunities into realized innovation.

title: MANAGERIAL AGENCY DECAY (MAD): A Theory of Cognitive Subordination and the Erosion of Human Capital in Algorithmically Mediated Workplaces
affiliations: , National University of science and Technology,Oman, University of Gondar and Injibara University

detail.title: MANAGERIAL AGENCY DECAY (MAD): A Theory of Cognitive Subordination and the Erosion of Human Capital in Algorithmically Mediated Workplaces
detail.abstract: We challenge the assumption that expanding workplace data linearly optimizes management effectiveness. Organizations are heavily investing in artificial intelligence (AI)-powered performance platforms to mitigate human bias. However, high-velocity dashboards often paralyze managers, shifting their focus from employee development to metric monitoring. We resolve this tension by introducing Managerial Agency Decay (MAD) Theory. We argue that high-intensity dashboards assert an epistemic hierarchy that devalues first-hand human observation. This dynamic induces Cognitive Subordination (CS), a metacognitive state where managers view their personal judgment as redundant next to actuarial data. Consequently, managers execute Coaching Withdrawal (CW), shifting feedback from exploratory development to short-term variance tracking. Using the Resource-Based View (RBV), we frame Managerial Cognitive Agency (MCA) as a critical VRIO asset that algorithmic reliance quietly liquidates. We conclude with a multi-method future research blueprint and prescriptive design interventions for strategic HR practices.

title: Valuing a Contested Technology: Public Acceptance and Willingness to Pay for Precision Livestock Farming
affiliations: Michigan State University

detail.title: Valuing a Contested Technology: Public Acceptance and Willingness to Pay for Precision Livestock Farming

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The study received IRB approval (STUDY00007833), and all respondents consented to participate in the study.
declarations.funderStatement: This work is supported by the Michigan Alliance for Animal Agriculture (M-AAA), project ID number AA-22-0044, from AgBioResearch and MSU Extension at Michigan State University, in partnership with the Michigan Department of Agriculture and Rural Development.

detail.abstract: I pair a two-wave attitudinal panel with a discrete choice experiment, fielded to the same adults in three major U.S. pork-producing states, to ask how residents of these states evaluate precision livestock farming (PLF), a real-time animal-level monitoring technology, and whether that evaluation carries economic value. The study yields three results. Mean acceptance of PLF is favorable, at about 3.0 on a 1–4 scale, and I detect no change within individuals over the year. Because the within-person design has a minimum detectable change of roughly 0.12 index points, I read this as stability that the study has limited power to distinguish from a small change. The clearest result is a contrast between the between-person and within-person dimensions: general attitudes predict acceptance across people but not within them, which suggests they are stable dispositions that interventions are unlikely to move. A within-person association with reported livestock experience is weaker, since it rests on 54 status-changers and does not survive dropping the largest changers. Stated willingness to pay for the labels — a verified animal-welfare claim and a verified environmental claim, each presented as substantiated by PLF-style monitoring — is positive, varies widely across respondents, and is higher for animal welfare than for environment. Because survey respondents tend to overstate what they would actually pay, I apply a standard hypothetical-bias correction; the adjusted premium is about $0.71–$1.53 per pound for animal welfare and $0.55–$1.19 for environment, down from raw stated premiums of $2.14 and $1.66. A latent-class model splits respondents into a high-value majority (about 61%), an indifferent minority (about 20%), and a moderate segment (about 19%). The sample covers three producing states, about 7% of the U.S. population, is markedly more educated than the U.S. adult population (61.5% versus 32.1% with a bachelor's degree), and reports stated rather than revealed valuations. Item non-response is high, with 'Don't Know' rates near 50-60% on many belief items, so the acceptance measure reflects opinion among those willing to express a substantive view about an unfamiliar technology. Because of the education skew in particular, the magnitudes are best treated as upper bounds even within these three states, and they should not be extrapolated into national estimates. The design cannot say whether the same animal welfare-above-environment ordering and the same heterogeneity would appear in more urban or coastal populations. The choice experiment identifies willingness to pay for the welfare and environmental labels themselves, presented as PLF-substantiated, rather than for PLF as a technology; the acceptance instrument, by contrast, measures how residents evaluate a neutral description of PLF directly. The paper measures both within the same respondents under a neutral frame. The policy readings that follow are interpretations consistent with these patterns, and the design does not identify them as causal effects.

title: Deprogramming Corporations
affiliations: Harvard Law School

detail.title: Deprogramming Corporations

publicationDetails.detailsText: European Corporate Governance Institute - Law Working Paper No. 954/2026
publicationDetails.journalName: European Corporate Governance Institute (ECGI) - Law Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
This essay explores the agenda of “deprogramming” the orthodox approach to U.S. corporate law and scholarship. Prompted by the Law and Political Economy (LPE) project but drawing largely on the Law and Economics (L&E) movement it critiques, it argues that central L&E frameworks—modularity, corporate law as contract, agency costs, and corporate law as product—operate as blinders: they artificially narrow corporate law’s subject matter and obscure issues of externalities, inequality, corporate power, and geopolitics. Key L&E theories such as “nexus of contracts” and the “market for corporate control” were not purely technocratic concepts but interventions in a broader agenda, including efforts to delegitimize corporate social responsibility, cabin antitrust scrutiny of mergers, and limit government intervention in corporations. Yet some blinders, such as the fetishization of limited liability, persist not because of L&E, but despite the critical resources L&E supplies for overcoming them.

Beyond mapping the familiar critical moves and calls for transformational institutional reform, this essay redirects attention to the overlooked social and political consequences of traditional corporate law mechanisms currently at risk of erosion. Corporate law is a polyfunctional governance technology that produces social spillovers: its familiar doctrines shape not only intra-firm governance but also broader patterns of accountability, distribution, and corporate power. For instance, expropriation by controlling shareholders through related-party transactions not only harms investors but is typically economically regressive and further concentrates wealth and political power. Likewise, liability schemes and transparency requirements may foster broader public accountability and forms of social control over corporate power. Deprogramming corporate law, in this sense, requires not only examining potential institutional transformation but also a fuller reckoning with the social and political consequences of tools already at hand.

title: GIS-Based Site Suitability Analysis for Wind Energy Development in Nigeria

detail.title: GIS-Based Site Suitability Analysis for Wind Energy Development in Nigeria

The research was developed as part of the Environmental Data Science Certificate Program (2025-2026) at the Yale School of the Environment.
