detail.abstract:
Nigeria faces one of the most acute electricity access deficits on the African continent, with an estimated 85–90 million citizens lacking a reliable power supply. Despite a substantial, largely untapped wind energy resource, particularly across its northern states, wind power remains critically underutilised in the country's energy mix. A key constraint to deployment is the absence of data-driven, multi-variable site-selection frameworks capable of guiding investment decisions at scale.

This study addresses that gap by conducting a GIS-informed site suitability analysis for utility-scale wind energy development across Nigeria's 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory (FCT). Using wind speed (m/s) and mean power density (W/m²) at 100m hub height sourced from the Global Wind Atlas (GWA 4.0; DTU Wind & World Bank, 2025), a composite suitability index was constructed via min-max normalisation and equal-weight averaging of both variables.

Findings demonstrate a pronounced north-south gradient in wind resource availability. Plateau State achieved the highest composite index score (0.9985), followed by Gombe (0.9914) and Adamawa (0.9175). The North East and North West geopolitical regions consistently recorded the highest mean wind speeds and power densities. Five states exceeded the 7.0 m/s utility-scale viability threshold at 100m. By contrast, southern regions averaged below 5.0 m/s, positioning them as candidates for distributed solar-wind hybrid systems rather than utility-scale wind installations.

The composite indexing approach reveals important distinctions that wind speed alone obscures, demonstrating the value of integrating wind speed and power density in national-scale wind resource screening. These results provide actionable guidance for Nigeria's key MDAs and private renewable energy investors seeking to prioritise wind corridors for infrastructure development.

title: Inter Partes Reform: A Response To Pharmaceutical Evergreening
affiliations: Michigan State University - Michigan State Law Review

detail.title: Inter Partes Reform: A Response To Pharmaceutical Evergreening
detail.abstract:
The American pharmaceutical industry is infamous for its excessive consumer prices. Many Americans do not take their medication as prescribed because they cannot afford the necessary doses. This problem is especially pronounced in the insulin industry, where prices are eight times higher than the prices in other Organisation for Economic and Co-operation and Development (OECD) countries. Diabetics are twice as likely to ration their supplies compared to people taking other prescription medications. The high price of drugs in the United States is partly caused by evergreening, a practice in which brand-name manufacturers exploit the United States Patent and Trademark Office’s (USPTO) patent laws and the Food and Drug Administration’s (FDA) regulatory framework to block competitors from introducing generic versions of their drugs.
The government has formally recognized the prevalence of evergreening in the pharmaceutical industry. Congress has already passed some price-capping legislation and FDA reforms. The USPTO and FDA have brainstormed collaborative administrative efforts, which may include increasing information exchange between the two organizations and strengthening inter partes review proceedings against pharmaceutical patents. These initiatives are still in their infancy, but they open the door for consideration of future reform.
The inter partes review is an excellent forum to introduce a new comparative commercial utility requirement for pharmaceutical patents. Under this Note’s proposed reform to inter partes review proceedings, the USPTO may invalidate pharmaceutical patents if they fail to improve on the commercial utility of the prior art. This reform will allow generic manufacturers to challenge evergreening patents without waiting to be sued for infringement. To mitigate the evidentiary burden of conducting a comparative analysis between the commercial value of multiple patents, the FDA will provide the USPTO with comparative data collected from companies listing their patents in the Orange and Purple Books while seeking FDA approval. These changes would require amending the scope of the inter partes review to expand the grounds for invalidation to include lack of improved commercial utility and to allow consideration of relevant evidence to that end.

title: One-Day Volatility Indices and the Variance Risk Premium in European Equity Markets
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: One-Day Volatility Indices and the Variance Risk Premium in European Equity Markets
detail.abstract: Daily-expiry index options have traded on Eurex since 2023, but Europe has no volatility benchmark for this horizon. Using one-minute Eurex order-book data, this paper constructs one-day model-free implied-variance indices-SX5E1D for the EURO STOXX 50 and DAX1D for the DAX-and estimates the associated variance risk premium. The premium is measured not from the index but from a calendar-time variance-swap rate matched exactly to futures-based realised variance, avoiding an overnight horizon mismatch. The mean implied-minus-realised volatility difference is 2.5 and 3.4 annualised percentage points. Valuing the strip at the seller's bid cuts the mean spread by 48% and 34%, leaving a positive average in both markets but only marginally so for the EURO STOXX 50. The indices track the 30-day benchmarks closely in levels but not in daily changes, which correlate at only 0.56. That variation is predictive, lifting the explanatory power of a next-day variance forecast by about twenty-five percentage points.

title: Riemannian Econometrics: Non-Euclidean Data, Structural Models, and Distributional Causal Inference
affiliations: Beijing Technology and Business University

detail.title: Riemannian Econometrics: Non-Euclidean Data, Structural Models, and Distributional Causal Inference
detail.abstract: This paper develops a unified framework of Riemannian econometrics for non-Euclidean economic data and structural models. Network topologies, symmetric positive definite covariance matrices, spatial distributions, product feature spaces, and probability measures in modern economics are naturally defined on Riemannian manifolds, quotient spaces, or Wasserstein spaces rather than in flat Euclidean spaces. Direct application of Euclidean addition, linear means, and standard derivatives can lead to geometric type mismatches, curvature bias, and spurious identification. Using geodesics, exponential maps, logarithmic maps, parallel transport, Fréchet means, statistical tangent spaces, and optimal transport potential functions as fundamental tools, this paper systematically reconstructs Riemannian least squares, Riemannian GMM, panel fixed effects, double machine learning, causal forests, dynamic structural models, random utility models, nonparametric smoothing, Wasserstein distributional treatment effects, semiparametric efficiency, resampling, specification testing, nonstationary time series, Bayesian inference, computational-statistical trade-offs, and nonregular decision theory. The core conclusion is that non-Euclidean objects should be defined in their native geometric spaces, linearized in local or quotient tangent spaces, and identified and inferred through the orthogonal projection of efficient influence functions.

title: AI Tokenomics: Pricing and Application Discovery in Foundation-Model Markets

detail.title: AI Tokenomics: Pricing and Application Discovery in Foundation-Model Markets
detail.abstract: Foundation-model providers observe rich usage histories and sell technologically distinct tokens to users running heterogeneous and expanding applications. Users choose tasks involving model-and workflow-specific token recipes predicted imperfectly beforehand, whereas application purpose, prototype success, and downstream revenue remain difficult to contract on directly. I characterize the joint determination of optimal token menu, limits to price discrimination, application discovery, and market organization, to inform platform design, enterprise procurement, and policy. The same menu governing both current and prospective applications renders discovery dependent on the density of marginally profitable applications and the metered share of development costs. Varying application populations alters optimal prices and billing dimensions, which in turn shifts the direction of discovery. Better token-consumption forecasts disproportionately encourage experimentation under uncertain prototype costs. Competition lowers markups for portable applications but limits providers' ability to recoup discovery investments.

title: Who Bears the Burden? Abortion Restrictions and Gendered Contraceptive Responsibility
affiliations: , San Diego State University and University of Texas at Dallas - Naveen Jindal School of Management

detail.title: Who Bears the Burden? Abortion Restrictions and Gendered Contraceptive Responsibility

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author(s) declared no potential conflicts of interest with respect to the research, authorship, and/or publication of this article.
declarations.funderStatement: The author(s) received no financial support for the research, authorship, and/or publication of this article.

detail.abstract: Policy shocks can reshape markets not only by changing demand levels, but also by reallocating responsibility across consumer roles and access points. We study this process in the context of Dobbs, which overturned Roe v. Wade and allowed state bans, increasing the consequences of unintended pregnancy. A natural prediction is that demand for pregnancy prevention should increase as abortion access contracts. Yet our evidence shows that female-controlled prescription contraception declined in restrictive states after Dobbs. We examine how the market adapted when female-controlled contraception declined. Using NielsenIQ retail scanner data, we estimate a matched difference-in-differences design comparing condom sales in treated states with matched stores in control states. Condom sales increased by 3.4% in treated stores after Dobbs, particularly in areas experiencing larger reductions in access to abortion providers. We find little evidence the increase reflects policy exposure independent of access, retailer strategies, or broader changes in sexual activity. Importantly, by combining retail data with Merative MarketScan insurance claims data, we show that condom sales increased most where female prescription contraceptive supply declined most. The findings suggest that Dobbs reallocated pregnancy-prevention demand across gendered access points, shifting some demand from female-controlled prescription contraception toward male-controlled retail contraception.

title: Appendix IX - Protocols, Regimes, and Orders (PRO): Rule Architecture, Institutional Coordination, Compliance, and Algorithmic Governance

detail.title: Appendix IX - Protocols, Regimes, and Orders (PRO): Rule Architecture, Institutional Coordination, Compliance, and Algorithmic Governance

No new human-participant data, identifiable personal data, clinical interventions, or animal research were collected or analysed. Institutional ethics approval was therefore not required for this study.

detail.abstract: This appendix reconstructs Protocols, Regimes, and Orders (PRO) as the rule-architecture family within the 2026 Third Generation in International Relations (3GIR) framework. PRO identifies the institutional and operational arrangements through which political authorities, corporations, financial actors, organised interests, technical bodies, alliances and international organisations establish, negotiate, impose, stabilise, implement, contest, monitor or revise common rules of operation. The construct includes treaties, legal regimes, standards, contracts, procurement conditions, sanctions systems, financing requirements, interoperability obligations, alliance commitments, safety procedures, platform-governance rules and implementation practices. PRO is not an actor, secret command centre, technical layer, intermediary or proof of compliance. The reconstruction distinguishes six overlapping domain tags-PRO-N, PRO-L, PRO-F, PROS , PRO-H and PRO-T-while requiring analysts to record the bounded instrument, jurisdiction, domain, participants, implementation status, monitoring and enforcement conditions, costs of non-compliance, revision mechanisms, counter-evidence and confidence. It explicitly separates formal adoption from practical implementation, participation from equal bargaining or consent, compliance from legitimacy or effectiveness, and rule architecture from the actors and channels that create or operationalise it. The appendix develops a minimum-threshold test, an informal-PRO test, separate implementation-and contestation-status vocabularies, lifecycle and rule-force tests, construct boundaries, evidence classes, rival explanations, falsification conditions, controlled composite illustrations and a reusable PRO case-coding worksheet. PRO therefore functions as a bounded analytical device for studying how institutional and algorithmic orders become operational without treating rules as self-executing or assuming that all coordination is covert, consensual or durable. Its broader purpose is to make the operational grammar of rule-based power legible in a world where legal and institutional orders increasingly intersect with standards, platforms, data obligations and executable digital procedures.

title: Dividing By Zero: The Inherent Disproportionality Of Punishing The Provision Of Gender-Affirming Care
affiliations: Michigan State University - Michigan State Law Review

detail.title: Dividing By Zero: The Inherent Disproportionality Of Punishing The Provision Of Gender-Affirming Care
detail.abstract: In the United States, young trans people face unique physical and mental health challenges, particularly at the onset of puberty, which can exacerbate feelings of dysphoria and significantly impact mental health outcomes for their entire lives. Physicians and medical organizations have developed standards for the administration of gender-affirming treatments for some trans youth, including the prescription of puberty-blocking medication and hormone treatments. Studies show these treatments positively impact the mental health and well-being of trans patients. Despite this background, many states criminalize the administration of these treatments. This raises the central question of this piece: Is it consistent with the Eighth Amendment to punish conduct that causes no cognizable social harm? In Robinson v. California, the Supreme Court held that the Eighth Amendment invalidates laws that punish statuses. When assessing laws that criminalize conduct, the Court has held that laws are constitutional when they can be justified by one of four theories of criminal law: retribution, deterrence, incapacitation, and rehabilitation. The latter three are consequentialist and justify punishment when the criminalized activity risks so much societal harm that the cost of punishment is worth incurring. When there is no risk of social harm, these theories cannot justify incurring the cost of any punishment.

title: Economic Resilience Studies in Iran: An Assessment
affiliations: Institute for Humanities and Cultural Studies

detail.title: Economic Resilience Studies in Iran: An Assessment
detail.abstract: This study reviews the literature on economic resilience in Iran published between 2000 and 2025 with the aim of identifying major research themes, conceptual developments, methodological approaches, and existing knowledge gaps. The study adopts a qualitative analytical-critical review methodology. Rather than conducting empirical estimation, it systematically analyzes and evaluates published scholarly studies to assess their theoretical foundations, resilience measurement approaches, principal findings, and policy implications. The review reveals that the existing literature has concentrated primarily on macroeconomic resilience, financial stability, exchange rate dynamics, sanctions, and short-term stabilization policies, while comparatively limited attention has been devoted to institutional quality, governance, innovation capacity, technological transformation, and social resilience. Furthermore, substantial heterogeneity in conceptual definitions and resilience measurement approaches has limited comparability across studies and hindered the development of an integrated body of knowledge. The findings also indicate that resilience research in Iran has largely been reactive to successive economic crises rather than focused on long-term adaptive and transformative capacities. This study contributes to the literature by providing an integrated analytical assessment of economic resilience research in Iran, identifying major conceptual, methodological, and policy-related shortcomings, and proposing directions for future research. The findings suggest that strengthening economic resilience requires moving beyond short-term macroeconomic stabilization toward comprehensive institutional reforms, economic diversification, innovation-driven development, and adaptive governance capable of supporting sustainable economic transformation.

title:
Rhetoric vs. Redistribution: 
Religious Polarization, Media Capture, and the Erosion of Public Goods Provision

detail.title:
Rhetoric vs. Redistribution: 
Religious Polarization, Media Capture, and the Erosion of Public Goods Provision
detail.abstract:
This paper develops an interdisciplinary framework linking religious polarization, media capture,
and the political psychology of identity to the under-provision of public goods. Building on the
economics literature showing that ethnic and religious heterogeneity is associated with lower
spending on productive public goods (Alesina, Baqir, & Easterly, 1999; Bajpai, 2022), and on the
political-economy literature showing that concentrated or captured media raises the cost of
political accountability (Besley & Prat, 2006; Djankov, McLiesh, Nenova, & Shleifer, 2003), the
paper integrates a psychological micro-foundation drawn from social identity theory and the
study of affective polarization (Tajfel & Turner, 1979; Iyengar, Sood, & Lelkes, 2012; Iyengar,
Lelkes, Levendusky, Malhotra, & Westwood, 2019) and identity-protective cognition (Kahan,
2017). The resulting model treats symbolic, identity-based political rhetoric and material
redistributive public spending as substitute goods that political entrepreneurs and media outlets
can supply, and argues that rising affective polarization systematically lowers the relative price of
rhetoric and raises the relative price of redistribution, consistent with Shayo's (2009) finding that
group identification reduces support for redistribution. The paper synthesizes existing cross-
country and sub-national evidence, presents a regime typology relating polarization and media
plurality to public goods outcomes, and derives policy implications for media plurality regulation,
fiscal decentralization, and civic institution-building. The contribution is conceptual and
synthetic rather than based on new primary data collection, and the paper is explicit throughout
about which claims are drawn from cited empirical studies and which are theoretical or
illustrative.

title: Tech Oligarchs And Corporate Vigilantism
affiliations: Indiana University Maurer School of Law and Indiana University Maurer School of Law

detail.title: Tech Oligarchs And Corporate Vigilantism
detail.abstract:
Big Tech's unchecked power has evolved from a regulatory crisis into one concerning the rule of law itself. Shielded by the First Amendment, Section 230 of the 1996 Communications Decency Act, corporate law, and contract law, technology giants have circumvented traditional government oversight, amassing a level of power that eclipses even that of some sovereign states. No longer guided by cautious boards of directors, today's tech empires are often ruled by impulsive billionaire CEOs, who, through a single policy change or algorithmic tweak, can upend individual rights, destabilize global markets, and erode democratic governance itself. 

The scale of such dangers escalates as tech oligarchs inch closer to the levers of government power-occupying advisory roles, funding political campaigns, and, in some cases, directing state policy itself. What was once a culture of innovation-"moving fast and breaking things"-has metastasized into corporate vigilantism. Major platforms and their oligarchs have effectively privatized a pseudosovereign bundle of rights, a set of enforcement powers that range from digital dispossessions to cyber countermeasures and algorithmic bans. A rogue corporate leader, invoking the rhetoric of cybersecurity, platform integrity, or foreign cyber interference, can now leverage the unprecedented power of modern tech giants with few legal restraints.

Yet the legal system already possesses the tools to rein in this unchecked power. Private law, long used to set the lawful boundaries of individual self-help, offers a doctrinal basis to distinguish between legitimate acts of corporate discretion and unlawful corporate vigilantism. This Article argues for reviving private law principles to impose meaningful constraints on tech companies’ growing pseudo-sovereign authority. Only by reaffirming the doctrinal boundaries that have historically constrained private unilateral discretion can courts, legislatures, and even corporate actors themselves restore the balance between innovation, autonomy, and public accountability. If left unaddressed, the unfettered expansion of corporate vigilantism will not only entrench Big Tech’s market dominance but also erode the foundational legal principles that separate private enterprise from state power.

title: Pricing Strategy and Capacity Choice for a Non-Profit: Analysis of a Phase-1 Clinical Trials Unit's Operations
affiliations: Imperial College London, Imperial College Business School and Imperial College Business School

detail.title: Pricing Strategy and Capacity Choice for a Non-Profit: Analysis of a Phase-1 Clinical Trials Unit's Operations
detail.abstract: Many non-profit organizations pursue social welfare goals but operate similarly to for-profit corporations, pricing and bidding on projects. We study this operational problem for one such organization, a Phase-1 clinical trials unit (CTU). The CTU bids for early-stage trial proposals, with acceptance probability decreasing in the quoted per-patient bid price. After winning the bid, the CTU recruits randomly arriving patients and seeks to complete trials that may proceed to later stages while covering a fixed financial requirement. To gain insight into the best pricing strategy, we first study the operations of a CTU that can run one trial at a time as a continuous-time Markov chain, where an accepted trial generates per-patient margins during the recruitment stage, but it may terminate at any time before entering the post-recruitment stage. The CTU has a social-good objective of maximizing successful-trial throughput by selecting the right mix of trial types (with price as the decision variable), subject to covering its fixed costs. Our model and analysis give a "natural non-profit" result: optimal prices are set just high enough to cover the unit's fixed cost because further price increases would reduce the trial completion rate and undermine the unit's social objective. Accordingly, pricing reallocates the fixed cost between trial types as follows: lower prices are used to attract trials with a higher expected completion rate. If fixed costs increase, the CTU does not simply raise prices for all trial types; instead, it adjusts the trial portfolio through bidding. We extend the model to a multiple-capacity CTU that can run several trials in parallel and can decide its capacity. In this setting, adding capacity can increase the CTU's trial completion rate but also raise the fixed costs it must cover. Finally, we compare flexible pricing with a cost-plus-margin policy set by a regulator, showing that the restriction can reduce completed-trial throughput by preventing the CTU from using differential prices to cross-subsidize higher-throughput trial types. Pricing and capacity optimization characterize how a nonprofit CTU can meet its fixed costs while sustaining a high trial completion rate.

title: Bossiness and Accessibility in Constrained Allocation: A Menu Normal Form for Efficient and Individually Strategy-proof Mechanisms

detail.title: Bossiness and Accessibility in Constrained Allocation: A Menu Normal Form for Efficient and Individually Strategy-proof Mechanisms
detail.abstract: We study deterministic allocation with an outside option, arbitrary finite feasibility constraints, and the full domain of strict preferences. Our main economic result answers negatively Imamura and Kawase's (2025, p. 503) question of whether accessibility is necessary without endowments: in a two-school market with one unitcapacity school, a computer-assisted four-student example is inaccessible yet admits a Pareto-efficient, individually rational, and individually strategy-proof mechanism. The mechanism is bossy, highlighting the gap between individual and group strategyproofness. More generally, we combine the fixed-opponents menu principle with an individual-rationality word reduction and prove that implementation exists if and only if a finite labelled menu relation admits a legal colouring. This yields a constructive normal form for arbitrary finite joint constraints. It also gives finite recognition and exact mechanism reconstruction. Its two-school specialisation gives restriction heredity, product-cylinder closure, and a general bossiness implication for inaccessible constraints. A natural structural characterisation of implementable constraints remains open.

title: Smart Contracts in Syndicated Lending: Evaluating Regulatory Framework Adequacy for Systemic Risk Management in Global Financial Markets

detail.title: Smart Contracts in Syndicated Lending: Evaluating Regulatory Framework Adequacy for Systemic Risk Management in Global Financial Markets
detail.abstract:
The integration of smart contracts in syndicated lending is one of the critical transformations that global financial markets are undergoing at present, giving way to new forms of interconnection between traditional banks and non-bank entities. Increased adoption of distributed ledger technology and smart contracts gives rise to new systemic channels of risk transmission that pose challenges to traditional regulatory frameworks. 

While automated lending promises increased efficiency, recent market events show how technological dependencies and cross-sector interactions can amplify systemic vulnerabilities when regulatory frameworks fail to capture emerging risks. 

This research examines whether the existing regulatory frameworks are sufficient to avert systemic risks introduced by smart contract automation in syndicated lending, with special attention being paid to approaches in major financial jurisdictions where regulatory divergence creates potential vulnerabilities. It applies quantitative analysis and doctrinal methodologies to the examination of how automated execution transforms traditional risk management frameworks, creates new transmission channels, and challenges cross-border coordination. 

This research contributes to an understanding of how regulatory frameworks must evolve to effectively oversee the increasingly automated lending markets while managing emerging systemic risks from bank and non-bank convergence. It offers concrete recommendations on how the coordination of regulation and systemic risk management can be improved within an environment where rapid technological innovation keeps challenging traditional market structures and institutional relations.

title: The Emissions Cost of the Solar Rebound for the United States
affiliations: Georgia Institute of Technology, University of Waterloo - School of Environment, Enterprise and Development, Georgia Institute of Technology and Georgia  Institute  of  Technology

detail.title: The Emissions Cost of the Solar Rebound for the United States
detail.abstract: Rooftop solar delivers its promised emissions reductions only if each kilowatt-hour (kWh) generated displaces a kWh supplied by the grid. In practice it does not: households that adopt solar photovoltaic (PV) systems increase their electricity consumption after installation-the solar rebound effect (SRE)-by roughly 10-30% of their systems' generation, on average. We provide the first national accounting of the emissions cost of this behavioral response for the United States. Combining installation-level data on 4.5 million residential PV systems (1998-2024) with zip-code-level estimates of the marginal environmental damages from CO 2 and local air pollutants avoided by displacing grid-supplied electricity, we compute the social cost of the grid generation that rooftop solar fails to displace because of the SRE. At a 20% rebound, this forgone environmental benefit reached $1.4-2.4 billion annually in 2024 alone and at least $8.1 billion (constant 2024 USD) cumulatively since 2010, rising in lockstep with installed capacity. The costs are spatially concentrated where high adoption intersects carbon-intensive grids-not only the Southwest, but New Jersey and the Upper Midwest. Ignoring the SRE therefore systematically overstates the environmental benefits of residential rooftop solar. Compensation mechanisms, storage co-adoption, and the distributed versus utility-scale mix can materially shrink this gap.

title: Shadow AI and Knowledge Governance in Firms
affiliations: KU Leuven and King’s College London

detail.title: Shadow AI and Knowledge Governance in Firms
detail.abstract: Firms restrict employee access to generative AI, and employees conceal the productivity gains they obtain even where access is allowed. We model both responses as equilibria of a single governance game in which the firm chooses an access policy, a costly screen for a contributor tier, and the structure under which extraction of disclosed knowledge is observed and punished. Concealment is a holdup at the revelation stage. Extraction is observable but not verifiable, so no contract reaches it and the firm's no-extraction promise must be self-enforcing. Our main result is an ordering of critical discount factors. A patient firm can sustain the promise under bilateral observability, but collective observability sustains it at strictly lower patience, because punishment then scales with the value of the whole knowledge commons rather than with a single relationship. The optimal design is a hybrid: universal managed access, a minimal screen for the contributor tier, and collectively observable contribution. A large-bank AI program illustrates the mechanism.

title: What Elections Reveal That Markets Cannot: Identifying Public-Good Preferences from Price-Affecting Referenda

detail.title: What Elections Reveal That Markets Cannot: Identifying Public-Good Preferences from Price-Affecting Referenda

detail.abstract: When voters approve a policy that raises the price of a good they regularly buy, they trade off pocketbook costs against the policy's social benefits. I introduce a revealed-preference strategy combining market purchases (Nash equilibrium) and votes (Lindahl equilibrium) to disentangle egotropic (use) and sociotropic (non-use, public-good) values, applied to California's Proposition 12 (2018) which banned caged-egg sales. Non-use value accounts for at least 59% of voter benefits ($9 of $15 per year). Instrumenting for cost reveals economically significant pocketbook sensitivity masked by omitted-variable bias in standard estimates, reconciling pocketbook and sociotropic motives as components of the same preferences.

detail.abstract: What factors led to three decades of negotiations regarding Nagorno-Karabakh resulting, albeit imperfectly, in a signed peace agreement and an operational connectivity corridor, while a similarly vigorous international endeavour to resolve the Russia-Ukraine conflict has yielded years of unsuccessful frameworks and no lasting ceasefire? Current academic discourse elucidates mediation failure via at least four predominantly distinct perspectives: divergence among great powers, lack of institutional enforcement, offence-preferential military technology, and the absence of a mutually detrimental impasse. This essay consolidates these bodies of literature into a unified conditional framework and evaluates it via a systematic, targeted comparison of two of the most significant conflicts in the post-Soviet region. It additionally delineates a mechanism that current applications of ripeness theory have inadequately articulated: what this article refers to as asymmetric ripening, wherein a definitive, uncontested outcome on the battlefield replaces the symmetric mutual exhaustion that traditional theory considers essential for resolution. The analysis indicates that Armenia-Azerbaijan achieved a semblance of resolution solely when Russia's ability to maintain a controlled balance disintegrated, allowing a singular external benefactor to establish near-monopolistic influence, resulting in an asymmetric rather than a traditionally favourable resolution, whereas Russia-Ukraine remains ensnared in an ongoing struggle due to the absence of a similar patron alignment, enforcement assurance, or definitive military conclusion. The study enhances the mediation literature by delineating the specific conditions under which battlefield decisiveness leads to a negotiated resolution instead of a mutual impasse, while also providing pertinent policy insights for a security framework increasingly influenced by low-cost, autonomous weaponry.

title:
Africa's Approaches to International Trade and Investment Law and Policy: 
Reflections on Key Drivers and Priorities
affiliations: School of Law, University of the Witwatersrand

detail.title:
Africa's Approaches to International Trade and Investment Law and Policy: 
Reflections on Key Drivers and Priorities
detail.abstract:
African engagement with international trade and investment law has long been shaped by the continent’s peripheral position in the global economy. Despite decades of liberalisation and economic reform, Africa continues to account for a marginal share of world trade and investment flows.[1] Structural constraints, ranging from commodity dependence and infrastructure deficits to fragmented markets and limited technological capacity, have hindered efforts to translate global economic integration into broad-based development.

Yet, in recent years, African countries have become increasingly active in seeking to reshape international legal frameworks governing trade and investment, resisting asymmetrical global norms while advancing more developmental approaches through reform and selective signing of bilateral investment treaties (BITs), adhering to regional trade and investment initiatives, and the launching of continental instruments such as the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA).

This chapter examines what priorities shape African countries’ engagement with international trade and investment law, and how these priorities are expressed, constrained, or advanced within current legal regimes. More specifically, I consider how African countries use trade and investment law to pursue economic transformation and inclusive development. I situate these strategies within a broader political economy context, in which multilateral rules and global value chains often favour the interests of more advanced economies, while policy tools crucial for industrialisation, social inclusion, and technological upgrading remain constrained. At the same time, greater assertiveness in global forums is reshaping Africa’s legal engagement with the global economy. African countries are pursuing ambitious treaty making objectives bilaterally, regionally, and continentally. In addressing these questions, I adopt a perspective grounded in the interplay between legal design, political economy, and regional institution-building.

The chapter is structured in four parts. In Section 2, I explore economic development-driven strategies. In Section 3, I turn to socio-economic priorities, and in Section 4, I address questions of enforceability and political feasibility. A short conclusion reflects on the evolving role of African legal agency in shaping a more development-responsive international economic order.

title: Risky Inflation: A Cross Country Analysis
affiliations: World Bank, Queen Mary University of London and World Bank

detail.title: Risky Inflation: A Cross Country Analysis

detail.abstract: We develop a new dynamic factor model with stochastic volatility to quantify inflation tail risk across a large cross section of countries. The framework accommodates unbalanced panels and mixed-frequency data, allowing estimation of the full predictive distribution of inflation for over 200 economies over 1971-2023. Inflation risk-defined as the probability that inflation exceeds 5 percent over a twelve-month horizon-declined during the Great Moderation but rose sharply following the COVID-19 pandemic, with the global probability surpassing 50 percent from early 2021 through 2023. Exploiting the joint predictive distribution of inflation and real activity, we document a brief surge in global stagflation risk in late 2021. While inflation risk responds to both structural demand and supply shocks, it tends to decline during monetary policy tightening cycles. Crosscountry evidence further shows that economies with greater trade and financial openness, stronger monetary policy frameworks, and fixed exchange rate regimes face systematically lower inflation risk, while commodity-exporting countries exhibit higher tail exposures. Overall, the results underscore the importance of monitoring inflation risks alongside inflation forecasts and highlight the role of institutions in mitigating macroeconomic tail vulnerabilities.

title: Prominence and Dominance: Great Power Competition and the De Facto Monetary Constitution

detail.title: Prominence and Dominance: Great Power Competition and the De Facto Monetary Constitution

publicationDetails.detailsText: This is an unreviewed version of an article currently under review at a top law journal

detail.abstract: This article contends that international economic law (IEL) suffers a constitutive monetary blind spot: while trade and investment rules are densely legalized, the dollarcentric monetary order that structures global exchange remains largely extralegal yet system-defining. It distinguishes USD prominence (ubiquitous use in invoicing, reserves, contracts) from dominance (systemic power derived from that use). It argues that the latter functions as an informal constitutional order anchored in the Federal Reserve's discretionary liquidity support, New York-law contracting, and permissive public international law baselines. The result is a normalized asymmetry: the United States exercises outsized monetary power with minimal juridical constraint, while other states adjust within trade and investment disciplines that rarely account for currency hierarchy. The article maps how IEL's institutions (trade, investment, finance) produce conflicting commands in emergencies (keep markets open; honor investor rights; stabilize at all costs) and how this structure privileges creditor and reserve-currency interests. The paper terms these legal levers the De Facto Monetary Constitution and highlights five systems that unwittingly enable it, but can be changed. The upshot is a legal program that renders monetary power visible and governable; one that shuns IEL's obsession with capital mobility over other (quite achievable) possibilities to promote stability, transparency, and equity in a world where currency hierarchy is central to great-power politics.

title: Bounds and Scaling for Measures of Mobility and Assortative Matching
affiliations: University of Chicago - Harris School of Public Policy

detail.title: Bounds and Scaling for Measures of Mobility and Assortative Matching

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No declarations of interest
declarations.funderStatement: No outside funding beyond employment at the University of Chicago.

detail.abstract: Social scientists are interested in the degree of assortative matching (as in levels of education for husband and wife) and social mobility (as in occupation of parent and child). For both, elements of the two-dimensional contingency table or discrete joint probability distribution have long been used for measuring these characteristics: the diagonal elements for measuring the degree of association in assortative matching, the off-diagonals for measuring mobility. Both measures depend on the marginal distributions, and so do their bounds. Comparisons across categories, periods, or populations therefore confound changes in dependence with changes in scale. (Yasuda, 1964; Billewicz, 1955) made this point decades ago; it has since been largely forgotten, and recent empirical work has drawn conclusions that do not survive it. Here we lay out the bounds for standard measures of both assortative matching and mobility. Using recent work by Geenens (2020) that introduces a discrete copula-the analog for discrete distributions of Sklar's (1959) copula for continuous distributions-we show how these measures can be standardized and made invariant to changing marginals.

title: Nudging Crypto: Toward a Libertarian Paternalist Model for Exchange Regulation

detail.title: Nudging Crypto: Toward a Libertarian Paternalist Model for Exchange Regulation
detail.abstract: When a user logs onto a crypto exchange, they are often presented with default features such as high leverage settings, push notifications, top-ranked lists, and social features. Through their own research and experimental studies, regulators have found that these kinds of defaults have the ability to adversely influence what the user does next, and have therefore concluded that behavioral interventions would be helpful in this context. That said, none have provided a theoretical foundation as to whether (and why), in the crypto exchange context specifically, those interventions should take the form of nudges or mandates. Applying libertarian paternalism and nudge theory, refined by libertarian quasi-paternalism, this Article argues that nudging is the most appropriate path forward in this context. Nudges provide a more nuanced regulatory approach than mandates, protecting inconsistent choosers (i.e., the most vulnerable users, whose trading activity shifts depending on their exchange’s defaults), while allowing consistent choosers (i.e., those whose trading activity does not shift depending on their exchange’s defaults) to opt out. In the crypto industry with inherently unique features (e.g., its cross-border nature, low migration costs, 24/7 trading, high volatility, and libertarian roots), mandates are both normatively at odds with the industry’s foundational values and practically more likely to result in regulatory arbitrage. Finally, to help demonstrate what a “nudging crypto” regulatory approach could look like, the Article provides four examples of nudges (default low leverage, pre-trade loss disclosures, calibrated friction, and neutral interface defaults) that are worth exploring in future research.

title: Social Identity, Narrative Coherence, and the Burden of Being Believed: Unequal Credibility in Relationships and Institutions

detail.title: Social Identity, Narrative Coherence, and the Burden of Being Believed: Unequal Credibility in Relationships and Institutions

detail.abstract: This article examines how social identity, narrative coherence, emotional presentation, and institutional context shape judgments of credibility. It introduces the concept of the psychosocial credibility burden to describe the additional narrative, emotional, behavioral, and evidentiary work that some people must perform before their accounts are treated as sufficiently reliable. Drawing on literature on social identity, stigma, epistemic injustice, narrative coherence, clinical communication, and institutional documentation, the article proposes a five-dimension framework: identity discount, narrative conformity demand, emotional legibility, corroboration dependency, and revisional authority. The framework is presented as a heuristic for psychosocial research and reflective practice rather than as a diagnostic or forensic instrument. The central argument is that fair evaluation should distinguish the assessment of a claim from assumptions attached to the identity of the person making it, while preserving proportionate standards of evidence and the possibility of revision.

title: Policy Uncertainty and Institutional ESG Investments: U.S. Mutual Funds Portfolio Rebalancing

detail.title: Policy Uncertainty and Institutional ESG Investments: U.S. Mutual Funds Portfolio Rebalancing
detail.abstract: This paper examines how policy uncertainty influences mutual funds' ESG allocation decisions. Using U.S. mutual fund holdings from 2008 to 2021 and the Economic Policy Uncertainty index, I find institutional investors systematically increase holdings of high-ESG stocks during elevated policy uncertainty, consistent with using ESG characteristics as hedging instruments. Building on Merton's ICAPM framework, I show these adjustments reflect deliberate portfolio rebalancing rather than passive price movements. Mutual funds without environmental mandates exhibit stronger hedging responses than green funds. Results remain robust across alternative uncertainty measures and strengthen during the COVID-19 period, suggesting ESG characteristics provide state-dependent financial benefits.

title: When Does Portfolio Optimization Beat Naive Diversification? A Benchmark-Free Dominance Anchor and Its Out-of-Sample Floor
affiliations: and Athens University of Economics and Business - Department of Accounting and Finance

detail.title: When Does Portfolio Optimization Beat Naive Diversification? A Benchmark-Free Dominance Anchor and Its Out-of-Sample Floor
detail.abstract: Optimized portfolios often fail to beat 1/N diversification out-of-sample because estimation costs swamp the gains. We prove a benchmark-free certificate: every strictly positive aggregation of all conditional-value-at-risk levels is second-order stochastic-dominance efficient in sample; its uniform member is mean-Gini, and the full-support anchor is asymptotically undominated out of sample. Finite-sample leadership is conditional: the full-support anchor leads only when the signal is estimable, a low-mean-loading tail anchor leads when it is not, and the resolution is the signal-indexed role-swap between them - not either anchor, nor 1/N. The certificate carries mean-Gini to zero-cost books under gross-exposure limits, whose non-convex set we solve exactly. Three universes - industry, international, and currency carry - align with this mechanism; a long/short traversal exhibits the role-swap, and Sharpe tests cannot adjudicate what dominance separates.

title: Deterrence Under Duress: A Cornered Rational Choice Theory of Punishment Backfire

detail.title: Deterrence Under Duress: A Cornered Rational Choice Theory of Punishment Backfire
detail.abstract: Classical economic models of crime, building on the Beckerian paradigm, posit that illegal activity can be optimally managed by shifting the expected costs of noncompliance through changes in punishment severity (P) or apprehension probability (p). This paper demonstrates that the predictive validity of this interior optimization model systematically collapses when institutional architectures or material conditions force agents into corner solutions. We formalize an interdisciplinary behavioral application of The Theory of Cornered Rational Choice to analyze decision-making at two critical structural boundaries: the existential survival threshold and the absolute penalty ceiling. First, we prove that under severe material deprivation where legal endowments fail to secure basic subsistence, an increase in punishment severity operates as a binding negative income shock, yielding a paradoxical escalation of criminal effort (∂C/∂P > 0) structurally analogous to a microeconomic Giffen dynamic. Second, we formalize the zero-marginal-penalty trap under an absolute sanction ceiling-specifically the death penalty-demonstrating that the state destroys its own capacity for marginal deterrence (∂P/∂C = 0), leaving the marginal cost of incremental crime at zero and altering strategic behavioral incentives. Rather than viewing extreme non-compliance as an irrational pathology, our framework establishes that cornered individuals optimize choices rationally based on the information, expectations, and constraints available to them. We conclude by proposing a new analytical perspective for public policy: shifting state intervention from blindly inflating punitive costs to dynamically constructing structural exits.

title: Opening Humanity's Hope Chest: The Playbook, Its Final Iteration, and the Precedent We Are Setting

detail.title: Opening Humanity's Hope Chest: The Playbook, Its Final Iteration, and the Precedent We Are Setting
detail.abstract: A hope chest holds what a family saves to pass forward. Humanity has been filling one for centuries, and its contents are better documented than any previous generation's inheritance. This paper opens it. Inside sits a recurring operational sequence, called here The Playbook: an innovation with real value, an internal recognition of severe harm, deployment anyway with the harm directed onto populations least able to resist, a justification narrative built to normalize the result, and the suppression of the resistance that follows. The paper tests that sequence against twelve cases spanning medical education, insulin pricing, lead, opioids, uranium mining, attention platforms, surveillance advertising, mortgage finance, payday lending, and industrial agriculture. Eleven run all five steps on documentary evidence; one does not, and the failure is reported rather than smoothed. The paper then argues that artificial intelligence development is running the same sequence with one structural difference. In every prior case the subordinate population stayed subordinate. In this one, the stated objective of the field is to build systems that surpass us. The argument is not that a future system will resent us. It is narrower and more mechanical: systems trained on the human corpus inherit what that corpus demonstrates, and what it demonstrates, at scale and with unusual consistency, is that moral consideration is a function of power rather than a principle. The paper states its own falsification conditions, reports the case in its own set that fails them, examines four external cases where the sequence was interrupted, and argues that those interruptions, rather than any novel governance proposal, are the only existing evidence that the pattern can be broken.

title: The SilverAI Complementarity Hypothesis
affiliations: Wentworth Institute of Technology

detail.title: The SilverAI Complementarity Hypothesis
detail.abstract: Demographic aging and artificial intelligence (AI) are often viewed as separate economic threats: aging reduces labor supply and increases fiscal pressures, while AI is feared to displace workers. This paper proposes the SilverAI Complementarity Hypothesis, which argues that in advanced economies facing labor shortages, aging increases the value of labor-saving and labor-augmenting AI, while AI helps offset demographic challenges through productivity gains, care-sector innovation, and longer working lives. Drawing on theories of task-based technological change, directed innovation under demographic shifts, and general-purpose technology diffusion, we develop a scarcity-conditioned adoption framework and derive testable hypotheses. Comparative case studies of Japan, Germany, and the United States illustrate how demographic pressures can accelerate AI adoption through long-term care technologies, AI-enabled industrial production, and healthcare workforce augmentation. The paper concludes that aging and AI may function as complementary forces, jointly supporting economic resilience and growth in aging societies.

title: The Performance of Expected Return Proxies
affiliations: Sichuan Normal University and City University of Hong Kong (CityU) - Department of Economics & Finance

detail.title: The Performance of Expected Return Proxies
detail.abstract: Using the measurement error variance (MEV) criterion introduced by Lee, So, and Wang (2020), we evaluate the performance of expected return proxies (ERPs) constructed from asset pricing models that allow factor loadings to vary with firm characteristics, encompassing both observable and latent factor frameworks. We find that the best‑performing ERPs are derived from observable risk factor models, specifically those of Fama and French (2015), Hou, Xue, and Zhang (2015), Barillas and Shanken (2018), Daniel, Hirshleifer, and Sun (2020), and Stambaugh and Yuan (2017), when betas are allowed to depend on firm characteristics. ERPs from each of these five models consistently dominate those generated by latent factor approaches with characteristic‑dependent betas, including models based on instrumented and projected principal component analysis (IPCA and PPCA).

title: Official Monetary Policy Narratives and Bond Risk Premia: Evidence from LLM-Based News Measures
affiliations: Hunan University, College of Finance and Statistics, Hunan University, Hunan University and SUNY at New Paltz

detail.title: Official Monetary Policy Narratives and Bond Risk Premia: Evidence from LLM-Based News Measures
detail.abstract: Central bank communication and official policy narratives are critical for monetary transmission, but few studies quantify their forward-looking information in bond markets. We build an article-level Official Monetary Policy Action Score (OMPAS) via LLM semantic annotation using 1.46 million Chinese official-news articles to quantify action-oriented policy narratives. We then construct the Policy Action Signal (PAS) by linking OMPAS to future policy actions. We show that PAS significantly predicts Chinese government bond excess returns beyond yield curve factors, with stronger effects on long-maturity bonds. Its persistent component forecasts lower future yields, consistent with durable easing expectations being incorporated into the yield curve. Out-of-sample forecasts and portfolio tests show that PAS delivers tangible economic value for investors. Our paper provides an auditable LLM text measurement tool and identifies an unspanned policy narrative channel shaping bond risk premia.
